Week 5

YARN, file formats and compression

Learn 6 topics, 8 comparisons and the formulas

  1. In one lineYARN is Hadoop 2's resource manager: one ResourceManager gives out containers, a NodeManager runs them on each node, and one ApplicationMaster manages each job.
    Key points
    • YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) arrived in Hadoop 2.0 (2013) and replaced the Hadoop 1.x JobTracker.
    • Hadoop 1.x JobTracker did resource management and job scheduling in one process: MapReduce only, ceiling about 4,000 nodes.
    • Splitting resource management (RM) from per-job logic (AM) removed the single JobTracker bottleneck: YARN scales past 10,000 nodes.
    Traps
    • NameNode and DataNode are HDFS (storage). They are not YARN parts and do not allocate CPU or RAM.
    • The AM is per job, the RM is per cluster. Q1's wrong favourite is the AM.
    • Hadoop 2.0 also added the Standby NameNode. That is HDFS high availability, not YARN (Q4 distractor).
    • The AM requests containers; it does not grant them. Only the RM's Scheduler grants.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  2. In one lineWhen a NodeManager stops heartbeating, the RM marks its containers failed and the AM requests replacements on other nodes.
    Key points
    • YARN handles failure in three layers: NodeManager, ApplicationMaster, ResourceManager.
    • NM failure: RM sees missing heartbeats (timeout over 10 minutes) and marks all containers on that node failed.
    • Fault handling is layered: YARN detects node loss, but the AM decides how to retry, because only it knows the framework.
    Traps
    • The AM, not the RM, re-requests the replacement containers. The RM only detects and marks.
    • The NM timeout is over 10 minutes, not seconds. The 60 seconds figure is RM failover.
    • Recovery from checkpoint depends on the framework: MapReduce can, early Spark could not.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  3. In one lineThe Capacity Scheduler splits the cluster into queues with guaranteed shares and lets queues borrow idle capacity.
    Key points
    • The RM Scheduler is pluggable with three policies: FIFO, Capacity, Fair.
    • FIFO (first in, first out): one queue in submission order; one long job blocks the rest.
    • Capacity guarantees protect SLAs (service level agreements, e.g. ETL done by 6 a.m.): analyst queries cannot starve production pipelines.
    Traps
    • Take the minimum of the by-RAM and by-CPU counts, never the RAM count alone.
    • The reserve queue has no container size, so it gets no count.
    • Capacity is not a hard cap: idle capacity is lent out and reclaimed by pre-emption.
    • 73% is 78/45 − 1, not 78 − 45 = 33 points.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  4. In one lineColumnar storage keeps each column's values together on disk, so a query reads only the columns it needs.
    Key points
    • Row store (CSV, JSON, Avro): one whole record after another on disk.
    • Columnar store (Parquet, ORC): all values of one column stored together.
    • Analytics queries touch few columns of many rows; a column store reads only those columns.
    Traps
    • Avro is a row format even though it is binary and self-describing.
    • The 33× assumes columns of equal size and an I/O-bound query; it is an estimate.
    • Skip a row group only when its range cannot match: for > 90 look at the max, for < 70 look at the min.
    • Pushdown is per row group; the whole file is not skipped unless every row group fails.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  5. In one lineAvro is a row format built for schema evolution; Parquet and ORC are columnar formats built for analytics.
    Key points
    • Five formats: Text/CSV (row, external schema), JSON (row, not splittable raw), Avro (row), Parquet (columnar), ORC (columnar).
    • Avro, Parquet and ORC are self-describing: the schema (field names and types) travels inside the file. Avro's schema is JSON.
    • Avro is row-oriented, so appending one event at a time is cheap: good for streams.
    Traps
    • Avro is self-describing and binary, but it is row-oriented, not columnar.
    • ORC is also correct for analytics on Hive; Parquet is the broader standard (Q2 note).
    • Missing field = default value; extra field = ignored. Do not swap them.
    • JSON lines is not splittable in raw form.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  6. In one lineA splittable file can be read from any point, so multiple Mappers process different parts at the same time.
    Key points
    • Snappy: fast, medium ratio, not splittable alone (Parquet row groups are).
    • Gzip: slow, high ratio, not splittable. LZO: fast, medium, splittable with an index.
    • Splittability decides parallelism: no splits means one Mapper and an idle cluster.
    Traps
    • HDFS splitting a gzip file into blocks does not make it splittable for MapReduce.
    • Snappy alone is not splittable; Parquet + Snappy is, at row-group boundaries.
    • Bzip2 is splittable, gzip is not; T/F 3 hinges on this.
    • Round splits up: a partial last block still needs a Mapper.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  7. Key differenceHadoop 1.x's single JobTracker mixed resource management with MapReduce job scheduling (MapReduce only, ~4,000-node ceiling); YARN (Hadoop 2.0, 2013) split this into a global ResourceManager and a per-job ApplicationMaster, so any framework can share a 10,000+ node cluster.
    Hadoop 1.x (JobTracker)Hadoop 2.x (YARN)
    DesignJobTracker = resource mgmt + job scheduling in one monolithResourceManager (global scheduler) separated from per-job ApplicationMaster
    Max nodes~4,000>10,000
    FrameworksMR onlyAny (Spark, Tez, Samza ...)
    Resource unitSlot (fixed)Container (flexible)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  8. Key differenceThe ResourceManager is the single global scheduler that hands out containers for the whole cluster, while an ApplicationMaster is a per-job process that negotiates containers from the RM and runs that one job's tasks.
    ResourceManager (RM)ApplicationMaster (AM)
    How manyOne per cluster, on a dedicated master nodeOne per running job (application)
    RoleGlobal cluster resource schedulerThe job's own scheduler
    Parts / dutiesScheduler (allocates containers; FIFO/Fair/Capacity) + ApplicationsManager (accepts jobs, starts first container for each AM)Requests containers from RM, tells NM to launch tasks, monitors progress, re-requests for failed tasks, releases containers
    Framework knowledgeFramework-agnosticHolds the framework-specific logic (MR AM, Spark AM, Tez AM, Samza AM)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  9. Key differenceA NodeManager failure is caught by the RM through missed heartbeats and the job's AM re-requests the lost containers elsewhere, whereas an AM failure is handled by the RM restarting the AM itself (default 2 attempts), recovering state from HDFS checkpoints if supported.
    NodeManager failureApplicationMaster failure
    Detected byRM, via missing heartbeat (>10 min)RM
    State changeAll containers on that node marked failedAM attempt counted (yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts, default 2)
    RecoveryAM is notified and re-requests containers elsewhereRM restarts a new AM
    Job stateTasks re-run in new containersNew AM recovers state from HDFS checkpoints if the framework supports it (MapReduce: yes; early Spark: no)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  10. Key differenceThe Capacity Scheduler gives each team's queue a guaranteed percentage of the cluster (lending idle capacity), whereas the Fair Scheduler shares resources equally among running jobs so short jobs finish fast; FIFO simply runs jobs in submission order and lets one long job starve the rest.
    Capacity SchedulerFair Scheduler
    PolicyCluster divided into queues with guaranteed capacity; elastically borrows unused capacityAll jobs get equal share of resources
    Slide exampleEngineering 60% / Finance 40%; a2i queues 60/30/10; LinkedIn 6 queues (production 40%)Latency-sensitive short jobs complete quickly even if a large job is running
    Default in / used byHDP/CDH; Yahoo!, LinkedInCloudera; Facebook, Twitter
    StrengthSLAs: production queue guaranteed minimum; adhoc queries cannot starve revenue pipelinesSmall jobs get fast turnaround
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  11. Key differenceA row store keeps each record's fields together so any query reads every column, while a columnar store keeps each column together so a query reads only the columns it needs (3 of 100 columns -> ~3% of the data).
    Row store (CSV / JSON / Avro)Columnar store (Parquet / ORC)
    Layout on diskRecord by record (id, name, age, score together)Column by column
    SELECT score FROM usersReads ALL columnsReads ONLY the score column
    100-col, 10 TB table, 3-col queryCSV reads all 10 TBParquet reads ~300 GB (33x speedup; 97% I/O reduction)
    Filter skippingNoneMin/max stats per row group -> predicate pushdown skips row groups
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  12. Key differenceAvro is a row-oriented format whose reader/writer schema handles schema evolution, so it suits append-heavy streaming ingest, whereas Parquet is columnar with per-row-group statistics, so it suits analytic reads that select few columns and filter.
    AvroParquet
    OrientationRowColumnar
    SchemaSelf-describing (JSON); reader vs writer schemaSelf-describing
    Key strengthSchema evolution: missing fields use defaults, extra fields ignored (backward + forward compatible)Row groups (~128 MB) with min/max stats -> predicate pushdown
    CodecSnappy / DeflateSnappy / Gzip
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  13. Key differenceA splittable file can be read from any point so many Mappers work on it in parallel, whereas a gzip-compressed CSV must be decompressed from the start, so one Mapper reads the whole file.
    Splittable (Parquet+Snappy, bzip2, LZO+index)Not splittable (Gzip CSV)
    DefinitionHDFS can start reading from any point in the file without decompressing from the beginningMust decompress from the beginning
    10 GB fileMultiple Mappers process different parts simultaneously (e.g. 3 row groups -> 3 Mappers)Exactly 1 Mapper - no parallelism
    WhyParquet splits at row-group boundaries; bzip2 natively splittableMapReduce cannot split across gzip boundaries even though HDFS stores it in blocks
    BenefitEnables data-local task scheduling-
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  14. Key differenceSnappy trades a medium compression ratio for high speed, whereas Gzip compresses more but slowly; neither is splittable on raw files, so both are used inside splittable containers like Parquet.
    SnappyGzip
    SpeedFastSlow
    RatioMediumHigh
    Splittable?No (but Parquet row groups are)No
    Matrix useAvro ingest; Parquet Spark analyticsParquet ML features
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  15. Columnar data read
    Read = D × k / N
    D table size, k columns selected, N total columns
    Columnar I/O reduction
    Reduction = 1 − k / N; speedup ≈ N / k
    10 TB, 3 of 100: 97%, 33×
    Pushdown saving
    Speedup = D / R
    R = bytes actually read; 10 TB / 50 GB = 200×
    Mappers per file
    Splits = ⌈F / B⌉, or 1 if gzip
    B = block or row group, about 128 MB
    Containers per queue
    min(nodes·f·RAM / c_ram, nodes·f·CPU / c_cpu)
    smaller term is the bottleneck
    Nodes for a job
    ⌈T / min(RAM / c_ram, CPU / c_cpu)⌉
    T containers needed at once
    Extra work from utilisation
    U_new / U_old − 1
    78/45 − 1 = 73%

Practise 11 worked examples from the slides, then 3 from the lecturer’s own files

  1. Given10 TB daily CDR on HDFS as gzip CSV. A Hive query selects 4 of 80 columns and takes 6 hours. Several teams share the cluster.
    1. Reason 1: CSV is a row store, so all 80 columns are read for a 4-column query.
    2. Reason 2: gzip is not splittable, so each file is read by one Mapper (little parallelism).
    3. Migration: Parquet (or ORC for Hive) + Snappy, partitioned by call date (and region).
    4. Column pruning alone: read 4/80 = 5% of the data = 10 TB x 4/80 = 500 GB.
    5. I/O reduction = 1 - 4/80 = 95%, speedup about 80/4 = 20x.
    6. If the job is I/O-bound: 6 h / 20 = 18 min, before any gain from partition pruning or splittable parallelism.
    7. Scheduler: Capacity (guaranteed queue per team, elastic borrowing) or Fair.
    AnswerRead 500 GB instead of 10 TB (95% less, 20x); about 18 min if I/O bound; Capacity Scheduler for multi-team sharing.
    Now try one

    Same company, new query reads 8 of 80 columns. Given: Parquet reads D x k/N. How much of the 10 TB does it read?

    10 TB x 8/80 = 1 TB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  2. GivenNM2 hosts 5 running containers of a MapReduce job and fails mid-run. RM marks a node lost after missed heartbeats (paper: >10 min). AM max attempts default 2. RM HA failover < 60 s.
    1. NM2 stops sending heartbeats to the RM.
    2. After the expiry interval (>10 min) the RM marks NM2 lost and all 5 of its containers FAILED; it removes NM2's capacity from the scheduler.
    3. The RM tells the job's AM that those 5 containers are gone.
    4. The AM re-requests 5 replacement containers from the RM.
    5. The RM grants containers on healthy nodes; the AM tells those NMs to launch the 5 tasks again (general knowledge: completed map output on NM2 is also re-run if reducers still need it).
    6. If the AM itself had been on NM2, the RM would restart the AM (up to 2 attempts) and MapReduce recovers job state from HDFS.
    AnswerDetection by RM heartbeat timeout; RM marks 5 containers failed; AM re-requests 5 containers; tasks rerun on other NMs.
    Now try one

    An AM restart limit is 2 attempts. The AM crashes once, restarts, then crashes again. Given: the RM restarts the AM up to max-attempts. Does the job survive?

    No. Two attempts are used (original + 1 restart = 2), so on the second failure the job fails.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  3. GivenA Spark AM requests 100 containers, each 4 cores and 8 GB RAM. The cluster is busy; the RM grants 80.
    1. Requested: 100 x 4 = 400 cores, 100 x 8 = 800 GB.
    2. Granted: 80 x 4 = 320 cores, 80 x 8 = 640 GB.
    3. Shortfall: 20 containers = 20% of the request (80 cores, 160 GB).
    4. The AM assigns tasks to the 80 executors it has and keeps asking for more as resources free up.
    Answer80 executors with 320 cores and 640 GB; the job runs at 80% of the parallelism it asked for.
    Now try one

    A MapReduce AM asks for 50 containers of {2 vCPU, 4 GB}. The RM grants 35. Given: granted resources = containers x size. How much RAM does the job hold?

    35 x 4 GB = 140 GB (and 35 x 2 = 70 vCPU).
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  4. GivenA 100-column table holds 10 TB. A query selects 3 columns. CSV (row store) vs Parquet (column store).
    1. Row store (CSV) must read every column of every row: 10 TB.
    2. Column store reads only the 3 needed columns: 10 TB x 3/100 = 0.3 TB = 300 GB (assumes columns of equal size).
    3. I/O reduction = 1 - 3/100 = 97%.
    4. Speedup from format alone = 100/3 = 33.33x, which the slide rounds to 33x.
    AnswerParquet reads about 300 GB instead of 10 TB: 97% less I/O, about 33x faster.
    Now try one

    A telecom keeps a 200-column, 20 TB call-record table. An analyst's query uses 5 columns. Given: a column store reads D x k/N. How much data does Parquet read?

    20 TB x 5/200 = 0.5 TB = 500 GB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  5. GivenA 10 GB gzip-compressed CSV on HDFS. Gzip is not splittable. Parquet row groups are about 128 MB and are splittable.
    1. Gzip has no internal block boundaries; a reader must decompress from the start.
    2. So MapReduce cannot start a second Mapper mid-file: 1 Mapper reads all 10 GB, no parallelism.
    3. Same data as Parquet + Snappy, row groups about 128 MB: 10 x 1,024 MB / 128 MB = 80 row groups.
    4. Each row group is one split, so up to 80 Mappers can run in parallel.
    AnswerGzip: 1 Mapper. Parquet with 128 MB row groups: about 80 parallel Mappers.
    Now try one

    A 2 GB bzip2 file on HDFS with 128 MB blocks. Bzip2 is splittable. How many Mappers?

    2 x 1,024 / 128 = 16 Mappers.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  6. Given5,000 nodes, each 64 GB RAM and 16 vCPU. Capacity Scheduler: production 40%, spark 25%, samza 15%, adhoc 10%, reserve 10%. Containers: Hive mapper {4 GB, 2 vCPU} (production and adhoc), Spark executor {8 GB, 4 vCPU}, Samza task {2 GB, 1 vCPU}.
    1. production: nodes 2,000, RAM 128,000 GB, vCPU 32,000; by RAM 32,000, by CPU 16,000; max 16,000 (CPU bound).
    2. spark: nodes 1,250, RAM 80,000 GB, vCPU 20,000; by RAM 10,000, by CPU 5,000; max 5,000 (CPU bound).
    3. samza: nodes 750, RAM 48,000 GB, vCPU 12,000; by RAM 24,000, by CPU 12,000; max 12,000 (CPU bound).
    4. adhoc: nodes 500, RAM 32,000 GB, vCPU 8,000; by RAM 8,000, by CPU 4,000; max 4,000 (CPU bound).
    5. Q2: every container asks 2 GB per vCPU but a node has 64/16 = 4 GB per vCPU, so CPU runs out first everywhere; half the RAM sits idle.
    6. Q3: per node min(64/4, 16/2) = 8 Hive mappers; 10,000 / 8 = 1,250 nodes (production owns 2,000, so it fits).
    AnswerMax containers: production 16,000, spark 5,000, samza 12,000, adhoc 4,000. Bottleneck: CPU. 10,000 Hive mappers need 1,250 nodes.
    Now try one

    Spark queue: 1,250 nodes, so 80,000 GB and 20,000 vCPU (given). Executors are {8 GB, 4 vCPU}. Find the max executors and the bottleneck.

    By RAM 80,000/8 = 10,000; by CPU 20,000/4 = 5,000; max 5,000, CPU is the bottleneck.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  7. GivenQuery WHERE score > 90. Footer stats: Row Group 1 score in [60, 85], Row Group 2 score in [85, 99]. Slide: a 10 TB Parquet query may physically read only 50 GB.
    1. Read the file footer only: min/max per column chunk per row group.
    2. Row Group 1: max 85 < 90, so no row can match. Skip the whole row group (no I/O).
    3. Row Group 2: range [85, 99] overlaps > 90, so it must be read.
    4. Inside Row Group 2 read only the score column chunk.
    5. Data read 50 GB of 10 TB = 0.5%, a reduction of 99.5%, about 200x less I/O.
    AnswerSkip RG1, read only the score chunk of RG2; 10 TB to 50 GB is 200x less data (99.5% saved).
    Now try one

    Footer stats for amount: RG1 [0, 4,000], RG2 [3,500, 9,000], RG3 [12,000, 20,000]. Query WHERE amount > 10,000. Which row groups are read?

    Only RG3 (min 12,000 > 10,000, all rows may match). RG1 max 4,000 and RG2 max 9,000 are below 10,000, so both are skipped.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  8. GivenThree siloed clusters ran at 45% average utilisation. One consolidated YARN cluster ran at 78%.
    1. Work done is proportional to utilisation x capacity; capacity is unchanged.
    2. Ratio = 78 / 45 = 1.733.
    3. Extra workload = 1.733 - 1 = 73.3%, about 73%.
    4. Note: the gain is 33 percentage points, but 73% in relative workload.
    Answer78/45 = 1.733: the same hardware served about 73% more workload.
    Now try one

    A bank merges two clusters running at 40% into one YARN cluster that runs at 70%. Given: extra work = U_new / U_old - 1. How much more work does the same hardware do?

    70/40 - 1 = 75% more.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  9. GivenCold data older than 2 years moves to ORC + Zstd, about 60% smaller than CSV.
    1. New size = old size x (1 - 0.60) = 0.40 x CSV size.
    2. Example: 100 TB of CSV becomes 100 x 0.40 = 40 TB.
    3. Saving = 60 TB of storage (before HDFS 3x replication; with it, 180 TB of raw disk).
    AnswerArchived size = 40% of the CSV size (100 TB to 40 TB).
    Now try one

    bKash has 250 TB of CSV older than 2 years. Given: ORC + Zstd is 60% smaller. What is the archived size?

    250 x 0.40 = 100 TB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  10. GivenPaper: YARN tested on 6,000 nodes with 100,000 concurrent tasks vs Hadoop 1.x's 4,000-node limit; RM handled 1,000 heartbeats/s. LinkedIn: PYMK recompute 18 h on MR1, 4 h on YARN; 400,000 peak containers on 5,000 nodes.
    1. Scale gain = (6,000 - 4,000) / 4,000 = 50% more nodes.
    2. PYMK speedup = 18 / 4 = 4.5x; time saved = 14/18 = 77.8%.
    3. Containers per node at peak = 400,000 / 5,000 = 80.
    4. Heartbeats: 6,000 NMs at 1,000/s means each NM can report about every 6 s.
    Answer50% beyond the old ceiling; PYMK 4.5x faster; about 80 containers per node at peak.
    Now try one

    A job took 12 h on MR1 and 3 h on YARN with Spark. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup and the time saved.

    12/3 = 4x; saved 75%.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  11. Givena2i cluster: Queue A 60% (DGHS batch), Queue B 30% (Spark streaming), Queue C 10% (ad-hoc Hive). LinkedIn 5,000 nodes: production 40%, spark 25%, samza 15%, adhoc 10%, tez 7%, reserve 3%.
    1. Guaranteed nodes = cluster nodes x queue share.
    2. LinkedIn: production 2,000, spark 1,250, samza 750, adhoc 500, tez 350, reserve 150 nodes.
    3. Check: shares sum to 100%.
    4. Idle capacity in one queue can be borrowed by others and is reclaimed by pre-emption (LinkedIn: 30-second warning).
    AnswerProduction 2,000, spark 1,250, samza 750, adhoc 500, tez 350, reserve 150 nodes; queue B on a2i can never take queue A's guaranteed 60%.
    Now try one

    a2i runs on a 400-node cluster with A 60%, B 30%, C 10%. Given: guaranteed = nodes x share. How many nodes is Queue B guaranteed?

    400 x 0.30 = 120 nodes.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. LinkedIn's Capacity Scheduler gives 40% of its 5,000 nodes to the production queue. A Spark job in the spark queue needs 2,000 containers, but only 1,250 are available. Describe what happens to the job under (a) the Capacity, (b) the Fair and (c) the FIFO scheduler.
    1. Setting: spark queue = 25% × 5,000 = 1,250 nodes, which hold about min(64/8, 16/4) = 4 executors each, so about 5,000 executors. Nodes are not containers.
    2. So 2,000 containers is within the queue's guarantee. Only 1,250 are free because other queues have borrowed spark's idle capacity (or spark's own jobs hold it). The job is short by 2,000 − 1,250 = 750.
    3. (a) Capacity: the job gets the 1,250 free containers at once.
    4. The other 750 come back by pre-emption: the borrowing queues get a warning (LinkedIn: 30 seconds), then their containers are killed and handed to spark. If spark itself is full, the tasks wait.
    5. Production keeps its 40% (2,000 nodes) whatever this job does: the SLA holds.
    6. (b) Fair: resources are split equally among running jobs; the job gets its fair share, not all 1,250, and grows as other jobs finish.
    7. Short jobs submitted later still finish quickly beside it.
    8. (c) FIFO: if it is first in line it takes every free container (1,250) and its last 750 tasks wait for containers to free up.
    9. Every job behind it waits too: one big job starves the cluster, which is why FIFO does not suit multi-tenant clusters.

    Based on Week 5 Part 1 (schedulers) and Part 2 (LinkedIn queues, pre-emption).

  2. LinkedIn's PYMK Spark job runs on a 300-million-node social graph using 600 executors, each with 8 GB RAM. Calculate the total memory requested as YARN containers and identify the dominant resource if each node has 64 GB RAM and 16 vCPUs.

    The question gives no vCPU figure; use the slide's Spark executor size {8 GB, 4 vCPU} (Week 5 Part 2 live exercise) and say so.

    1. Total memory = 600 × 8 GB = 4,800 GB (4.8 TB).
    2. Total vCPU = 600 × 4 = 2,400 vCPU.
    3. Share of one node per executor: RAM 8 / 64 = 12.5%; CPU 4 / 16 = 25%.
    4. CPU share is larger, so the dominant resource is CPU; DRF schedules on that share.
    5. Executors per node = min(64 / 8, 16 / 4) = min(8, 4) = 4 (CPU-bound).
    6. Nodes needed = 600 / 4 = 150 nodes; on each, 32 of 64 GB RAM stays idle.
    7. Cluster share: RAM 4,800 / (5,000 × 64 = 320,000 GB) = 1.5%; CPU 2,400 / (5,000 × 16 = 80,000) = 3%. CPU again dominates.
    8. It fits the spark queue easily (5,000 executors; see the live exercise).

    Beyond the slides: in practice Spark adds memory overhead to each container (max(384 MB, 10%)), so YARN would see about 8.8 GB × 600 = 5,280 GB.

  3. Compare YARN's two-level scheduling (the ResourceManager allocates containers; each ApplicationMaster places its tasks) with Kubernetes's one-level scheduling (kube-scheduler places pods directly). Under what workloads does two-level scheduling do better?
    YARN (two-level)Kubernetes (one-level)
    Who places workRM grants containers; the framework's AM decides which task runs whereOne central scheduler places every pod
    Framework knowledgeIn the AM (Spark stages, MapReduce data locality)Generic: CPU, RAM, labels
    Best fitData-heavy batch on HDFSLong-running services, mixed apps
    1. Many short tasks: the AM schedules its own tasks, so the RM only grants containers. Spark and Tez AMs keep long-lived containers (executors) and reuse them, and YARN ran 100,000 concurrent tasks on 6,000 nodes.
    2. Data locality: the AM knows which HDFS blocks each task needs and asks for containers on those nodes.
    3. Many frameworks on one cluster: MapReduce, Spark, Tez and Samza each bring their own AM and policy while the RM only shares resources.
    4. Scale and isolation: the RM does less work per job, and an AM crash affects only its own application.
    5. One-level wins for long-running services and microservices, where placing a pod once is enough (beyond the slides). The slides say Kubernetes inherited YARN's container idea, while Spark on YARN is still the main on-premise set-up.

    The slides give the YARN numbers and say Kubernetes inherited YARN's container idea. The one-level vs two-level framing, and where each wins, come from the old slides' question and go beyond the current deck.

Test 19 exam questions, then the predicted paper

  1. Which component in YARN is responsible for global resource allocation across the entire cluster?
    • (a) NodeManager
    • (b) ApplicationMaster
    • (c) ResourceManager
    • (d) NameNode
    (c) ResourceManager
    One RM per cluster allocates containers globally; the AM manages only its own job.
  2. Which Hadoop file format stores data in columnar format and is best suited for analytical, read-heavy workloads?
    • (a) Avro
    • (b) Text/CSV
    • (c) Parquet
    • (d) JSON
    (c) Parquet
    Columnar, with min/max stats for predicate pushdown; Avro, CSV and JSON are row formats. ORC is also columnar: the instructor accepts it as partly correct with a justification (best for Hive), but Parquet is the broader standard.
  3. What does “splittable” mean for a file format in Hadoop?
    • (a) The file can be deleted in parts by HDFS
    • (b) Multiple Mappers can process different parts of the file simultaneously
    • (c) The file format supports splitting schema across multiple NameNodes
    • (d) The file can be distributed across multiple data centres
    (b) Multiple Mappers can process different parts of the file simultaneously
    Reading can start anywhere in the file, which also allows data-local tasks.
  4. YARN was introduced in which major Hadoop version, and what did it replace?
    • (a) Hadoop 1.0; replaced the NameNode
    • (b) Hadoop 2.0; replaced the monolithic JobTracker with a decoupled ResourceManager + ApplicationMaster
    • (c) Hadoop 3.0; replaced DataNodes with Containers
    • (d) Hadoop 2.0; replaced the Secondary NameNode with a Standby NameNode
    (b) Hadoop 2.0; replaced the monolithic JobTracker with a decoupled ResourceManager + ApplicationMaster
    (d) is the trap: the Standby NameNode is HDFS, not YARN.
  5. Parquet is a row-oriented file format optimised for write-heavy workloads.
    False. Parquet is column-oriented and optimised for read-heavy analytics; the row-oriented, append-friendly format is Avro.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): Parquet is column-oriented and built for read-heavy analytical queries, not for row-by-row writes.

  6. YARN allows multiple computation frameworks such as Spark and Tez to share resources on the same Hadoop cluster.
    True. Each framework brings its own ApplicationMaster, so YARN runs MapReduce, Spark and Tez on one cluster.
  7. Gzip-compressed files are natively splittable in Hadoop, allowing multiple Mappers to process them in parallel.
    False. Gzip files are not splittable, so one Mapper reads the whole file; use bzip2 or Parquet + Snappy for parallel reads.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): Gzip is a streaming format with no internal block boundaries, so it must be decompressed from the start and cannot be split.

  8. ORC format is specifically optimised for Hive workloads and achieves among the highest compression ratios of any Hadoop format.
    True. ORC is columnar, best for Hive, with the highest compression, Hive ACID and vectorized reads.
  9. Explain YARN’s three-component architecture — ResourceManager, NodeManager, and ApplicationMaster. Draw a diagram showing how they interact when a Spark job is submitted to the cluster.

    See the diagram on the topic “YARN and its three components”

    ResourceManager (1 per cluster): Scheduler grants containers; ApplicationsManager accepts jobs and starts each AM.
    NodeManager (1 per node): launches and monitors containers, heartbeats to the RM, enforces CPU/RAM limits.
    ApplicationMaster (1 per job): requests containers, has NMs launch tasks, retries failures, releases containers.

    Diagram (see the diagram in the YARN and its three components card): Client, RM, Spark AM, NM1–NM3, with numbered arrows:

    1. Client submits the job to the RM.
    2. RM launches the Spark AM in a container.
    3. AM registers with the RM and requests containers; the RM Scheduler grants them.
    4. AM tells NM1–NM3 to launch executors.
    5. Executors report status to the AM.
    6. AM unregisters from the RM when done.

    Example: the Spark AM asks for 100 containers {4 cores, 8 GB}; the busy RM grants 80 and the AM runs executors in them.

  10. What is columnar storage? Why does it improve performance for analytics queries that select only a subset of columns? Use a concrete example with numbers to illustrate the I/O reduction.

    See the diagram on the topic “Row vs columnar storage and Parquet”

    Columnar storage keeps all values of one column together on disk (Parquet, ORC); a row store (CSV, Avro) writes whole records one after another.

    Why faster: the query reads only the columns it names; Parquet's min/max stats skip whole row groups (predicate pushdown); same-type values compress better.

    Example: 100 columns, 10 TB, query on 3 columns.

    FormatData read
    CSV10 TB
    Parquet10 × 3/100 = 0.3 TB = 300 GB

    I/O cut 97%, about 33× faster.

  11. Compare Avro and Parquet. Explain what “schema evolution” means and why Avro handles it better. In which scenarios would you use each?
    AvroParquet
    Layoutrowcolumnar
    Strengthschema evolution, appendsanalytic reads, pushdown
    CodecSnappy/DeflateSnappy/Gzip

    Schema evolution: the schema changes over time (e.g. a new field) while old files and readers keep working.

    Why Avro handles it: the writer schema is stored with the data, the reader supplies its own schema, fields match by name; missing fields get defaults, unknown fields are ignored. Backward and forward compatible.

    Use: Avro for Kafka → HDFS ingest and data exchange; Parquet for Spark, Presto and ML analytics.

  12. Data Lake Performance Migration: A Dhaka-based telecom company stores 10 TB of daily call-detail records (CDR) on HDFS as gzip-compressed CSV files. Their data engineers report that a Hive query selecting 4 of 80 columns takes 6 hours. – Identify two specific reasons why this configuration is slow – Propose a migration strategy: new format, compression codec, and partitioning scheme – Estimate the expected I/O reduction (show your calculation) – What YARN scheduler would you use and why, given that multiple teams share the cluster?

    i) Why slow

    1. Gzip is not splittable: one Mapper per file, the cluster idles.
    2. CSV is a row store: reading 4 columns parses all 80; no stats to skip data.

    ii) Migration: ORC (Hive) or Parquet (if Spark reads it too); Snappy for hot data (Zlib for ORC in Hive, Zstd for archive); partition by date and region, e.g. dt=YYYY-MM-DD/region=; convert once, then nightly.

    iii) I/O estimate

    Fraction read4/80 = 0.05
    Data read10 TB × 0.05 = 500 GB
    Reduction95% (20× less)
    Time if I/O-bound360 min × 0.05 ≈ 18 min

    iv) Scheduler: Capacity: guaranteed queues per team (ETL, analysts, data science), idle capacity borrowed, so no team starves another. FIFO lets one long job block all.

    From the lecturer’s files

    The lecturer's plan seeds this as 10 TB of web click data stored as gzip CSV; the same answer applies.

  13. YARN Failure Trace: A NodeManager (NM2) hosting 5 running containers for a MapReduce job fails mid-execution. Trace the complete failure recovery sequence: which components detect the failure, in what order, what state changes occur in the ResourceManager, and how are the 5 containers’ tasks restarted.
    1. NM2 crashes; its 5 containers die; heartbeats stop.
    2. RM detects the missed heartbeats after the timeout (>10 min) and declares NM2 lost.
    3. RM state: NM2 removed from schedulable capacity; its 5 containers marked failed.
    4. RM notifies the MapReduce AM.
    5. AM requests 5 replacement containers.
    6. RM grants them on healthy nodes (e.g. NM1, NM3), preferring nodes with HDFS replicas of the input.
    7. AM has those NMs relaunch the 5 tasks from their input splits; finished maps whose output was on NM2's disk may rerun.

    If the AM was on NM2, the RM restarts it (default 2 attempts); MapReduce recovers state from HDFS checkpoints.

  14. Resource consolidation increases utilisation: merging 3 siloed clusters into one raised average utilisation from 45% to 78% — the same capacity served 73% more workload

    Claim: one shared cluster uses hardware better than three silos.

    For: LinkedIn's silos (MapReduce, Spark, Samza) were idle at different times; merged, utilisation rose 45% → 78%, and 78/45 = 1.73, so 73% more work on the same hardware. No cross-cluster copying, one config instead of three.

    Against: workloads now compete, so queues, pre-emption and RM high availability become essential.

  15. Capacity Scheduler enables SLAs: production queues guaranteed minimum resources; analyst adhoc queries cannot starve revenue-generating pipelines

    Claim: guaranteed queues protect SLAs (promised finish times).

    For: production holds 40% at LinkedIn, so the 10% adhoc queue cannot delay revenue pipelines, while idle capacity is still lent out.

    Against: fixed percentages need tuning, and analysts may wait at busy times; Fair gives short jobs faster turnaround.

  16. Pre-emption needs tuning: aggressive pre-emption killed long-running Spark jobs; LinkedIn set 30-second grace periods and added Spark checkpoint-on-preempt hooks

    Claim: pre-emption is needed but must match the workload.

    For: without reclaiming borrowed containers, queue guarantees are empty promises.

    Against: killing a container wastes its work; long Spark jobs restarted repeatedly. LinkedIn's fix: a 30-second grace period and checkpoint-on-preempt hooks so jobs resume.

  17. YARN is the OS; frameworks are processes: the paradigm shift — the cluster is the computer, YARN is its kernel

    Claim: YARN is to a cluster what an OS kernel is to a computer.

    For: the RM allocates CPU and RAM as containers, NMs isolate them with cgroups, and frameworks are just applications with their own AM; the same three-tier design lives on in Kubernetes.

    Against: YARN sizes containers only by CPU and RAM, relies on HDFS for storage, and Kubernetes has replaced it for most new deployments.

  18. Samza on YARN: stream processing is just another set of long-running containers; YARN’s fault tolerance restarts failed Samza tasks

    Claim: a stream job is just long-running containers.

    For: Samza shares the cluster in its 15% queue, no separate stream cluster, and YARN restarts failed tasks on other nodes.

    Against: the containers hold capacity permanently, and the >10 min NodeManager timeout is slow for real-time data, so Samza must resume from the right Kafka offset itself.

  19. Task (20 minutes, pairs) Model LinkedIn’s 5,000-node YARN cluster in Python. Given: • 5,000 nodes; each: 64 GB RAM, 16 vCPUs • Capacity Scheduler: production 40%, spark 25%, samza 15%, adhoc 10%, reserve 10% • Container sizes: Hive mapper: {4 GB, 2 vCPU}; Spark executor: {8 GB, 4 vCPU}; Samza task: {2 GB, 1 vCPU} Questions: 1 Max concurrent containers per queue? 2 Which resource is the bottleneck (CPU or RAM)? 3 If production needs 10,000 Hive mappers, how many nodes are required?
    NODES    = 5_000
RAM_GB   = 64
VCPUS    = 16

queues = {
  "production": 0.40,
  "spark":      0.25,
  "samza":      0.15,
  "adhoc":      0.10,
  "reserve":    0.10,
}
containers = {
  "production": {"ram": 4, "cpu": 2},
  "spark":      {"ram": 8, "cpu": 4},
  "samza":      {"ram": 2, "cpu": 1},
  "adhoc":      {"ram": 4, "cpu": 2},
}

for q, frac in queues.items():
    nodes_q = NODES * frac
    ram_q    = nodes_q * RAM_GB
    cpu_q    = nodes_q * VCPUS
    if q in containers:
        c = containers[q]
        by_ram = ram_q // c["ram"]
        by_cpu = cpu_q // c["cpu"]
        max_c = int(min(by_ram, by_cpu))
        bottleneck = ("RAM" if by_ram < by_cpu
                             else "CPU")
        print(f"{q}: {max_c} containers "
              f"(bottleneck: {bottleneck})")

    Task: run the skeleton; add Q3:

    import math
c = containers["production"]
per_node = min(RAM_GB // c["ram"], VCPUS // c["cpu"])
print(per_node, math.ceil(10_000 / per_node))

    Expected output:

    production: 16000 containers (bottleneck: CPU)
spark: 5000 containers (bottleneck: CPU)
samza: 12000 containers (bottleneck: CPU)
adhoc: 4000 containers (bottleneck: CPU)
8 1250

    1. production 16,000; spark 5,000; samza 12,000; adhoc 4,000; reserve has no container size, so none.

    2. CPU. A node has 64/16 = 4 GB per vCPU; every container asks 2 GB per vCPU, so vCPUs run out with half the RAM idle.

    3. Per node min(64/4, 16/2) = 8 mappers; 10,000 / 8 = 1,250 nodes, which fits in production's 2,000.

    1. i)

    2. ii)
      FIFO runs jobs in submission order, so one long nightly batch job starves the streaming and ad-hoc work. It does not suit a multi-tenant cluster.

    4. iv)
      Dominant Resource Fairness (Ghodsi 2011) defines fairness across several resources (CPU and RAM), not memory alone. Here some jobs are CPU-heavy and some RAM-heavy, so sharing by one resource would be unfair.
    (b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
    A Dhaka telecom stores 10 TB of daily call-detail records on HDFS as gzip-compressed CSV. A Hive query that selects 4 of the 80 columns takes 6 hours.
    1. i)

    2. ii)

    1. i)
      1) Gzip is not splittable: each file is read by exactly one Mapper, so there is no parallelism within a file. 2) CSV is a row store: the query reads all 80 columns from disk to use 4.
    2. ii)
      Parquet + Snappy (or ORC + Zlib if the workload is Hive only), partitioned by date, e.g. dt=YYYY-MM-DD/ (optionally region=). Columnar, splittable at row-group boundaries, and date filters prune whole directories.
    3. iii)

    4. iv)
      Predicate pushdown: the reader first reads only the file footer, which holds min/max statistics per column chunk per row group. Any row group whose max duration is 600 or less is skipped with no I/O; in the rest only the needed column chunks are read.

    Before YARN, LinkedIn ran three separate clusters: MapReduce for Hive ETL, an experimental Spark cluster and Samza stream nodes. In 2013 it merged them into one 5,000-node YARN cluster with the Capacity Scheduler.

    2. ii)

Row format also suits appending events.
