Week 6

Apache Spark: RDDs and in-memory computing

Learn 6 topics, 6 comparisons and the formulas

  1. In one lineMapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS, so iterative algorithms pay disk I/O on every pass; Spark caches the data in RAM once.
    Key points
    • MapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS (the cluster's shared disk) before the next step can start.
    • Iterative algorithms (K-Means, logistic regression, PageRank) pass over the same data many times, so MapReduce pays disk I/O every iteration.
    • RAM is much faster to read than disk, and Spark also skips the HDFS write after every step.
    Traps
    • The 200× is disk I/O, not time. Here RAM is only 10× faster than HDFS, so the time speedup is about 18×.
    • Spark iterations 2–100 still read 50 GB each, from RAM. That is 99 RAM passes, not 100.
    • If the HDFS write speed is not given, say you assume it equals the read speed.
    • Spark does not skip the shuffle. Wide operations like reduceByKey still shuffle.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  2. In one lineSpark has three tiers: a Driver that builds the DAG and schedules tasks, a Cluster Manager that allocates resources, and Executors that run tasks and cache data.
    Key points
    • Driver: runs the user's main(), creates SparkContext, builds the DAG (directed acyclic graph of steps) and coordinates execution.
    • Cluster Manager: allocates cluster resources. Options: YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos or Spark Standalone.
    • A separate Cluster Manager lets the same Spark program run on YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos or Standalone.
    Traps
    • Spark does not need YARN. Kubernetes, Mesos and Standalone also work.
    • Cached data lives in the Executors, not in the Driver.
    • SparkContext did not disappear in Spark 2; it sits inside SparkSession.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  3. In one lineAn RDD is a read-only, partitioned collection of records that Spark rebuilds from its lineage if a partition is lost.
    Key points
    • Created only two ways: by transforming an existing RDD (map, filter) or by loading from stable storage (HDFS, S3).
    • Five properties: immutable, partitioned, lazy, lineage, resilient.
    • Replicating in-memory data 3 times would triple RAM use and send every write over the network. Lineage stores only the steps.
    Traps
    • Checkpointing is an optional add-on for long chains. Lineage is the main mechanism.
    • Copying each partition to two Executors is replication, which RDDs avoid.
    • cache() is lazy. Nothing is stored until an action runs.
    • Resilient means recomputable, not replicated.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  4. In one lineLazy evaluation means Spark records transformations in a DAG and runs nothing until an action is called.
    Key points
    • Transformation: builds the DAG and returns a new RDD, without running. map, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, cache.
    • Action: triggers DAG execution and returns a value to the Driver or writes to storage. collect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach.
    • Spark sees the whole plan before running anything, so it can optimise it.
    Traps
    • cache() is a transformation (lazy), not an action.
    • reduceByKey is a transformation; reduce is an action.
    • map and filter exist in PySpark, not only in Scala.
    • A transformation's result is not written to HDFS automatically.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  5. In one lineA wide dependency is one where an output partition needs data from many input partitions, which forces a shuffle and a new stage.
    Key points
    • Narrow dependency: each output partition depends on at most one input partition. map, filter, flatMap, union, mapPartitions, coalesce.
    • Wide dependency: an output partition may depend on many input partitions. groupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, sortByKey, join, repartition, distinct.
    • A shuffle costs network traffic, disk writes and a barrier where every task must finish. It is Spark's main cost.
    Traps
    • reduceByKey is still wide. It shuffles, only less data.
    • coalesce is narrow (no shuffle); repartition is wide.
    • join is narrow only when both RDDs are co-partitioned on the key.
    • Part 2 slide 2 says “3.5× fewer machines”, but 2,100 / 206 ≈ 10.2×, as slide 14 says.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  6. In one lineA DataFrame is a distributed table with named columns and a schema, optimised by Catalyst.
    Key points
    • DataFrame: a distributed collection organised into named columns with a schema, like a database table or a distributed Pandas DataFrame.
    • Built on RDDs internally; every DataFrame operation compiles to an RDD plan when it runs.
    • The schema tells Catalyst what each column is, so it can optimise the query; raw RDD lambdas are opaque to it.
    Traps
    • HBase is not a Spark ecosystem component.
    • DataFrames do not replace the engine: they compile down to RDDs.
    • Catalyst optimises DataFrames/SQL; RDD code goes through the DAG scheduler only.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  7. Key differenceMapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS, so iterative jobs pay disk I/O on every pass, whereas Spark caches the working set in memory as RDDs and recovers from lineage, making iterative work 10-100x faster.
    MapReduceSpark
    Intermediate storageDisk (HDFS) after every stepMemory (spill to disk if needed)
    Iterative algorithmsSlow (disk per iteration); K-Means 100 iters = 10 TB I/OFast (cache RDD; 10-100x); 50 GB read once
    Fault toleranceRe-execute task from HDFSRecompute from lineage
    Programming model / languagesMap + Reduce only; Javamap, filter, join, groupBy, SQL, ML, stream; Python, Scala, Java, R
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  8. Key differenceHDFS tolerates failures by storing three copies of the data, whereas an RDD stores only how it was derived and recomputes a lost partition from its parents, so there is no replication overhead.
    HDFS replication (traditional)RDD lineage (Spark)
    What is kept3 copies of the dataThe computation graph (log of transformations)
    Recovering a lost partitionRead another copyRe-read the HDFS input for that partition and re-apply the same transformations
    OverheadReplication overheadNo data replication overhead - 'the computation is the backup'
    Weak spot-Expensive for wide dependencies (many ancestors); checkpoint long chains to HDFS
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  9. Key differenceA transformation lazily defines a new RDD and only adds to the DAG, while an action forces the DAG to run and returns a value to the Driver or writes output.
    TransformationAction
    EvaluationLazy: builds the DAG, does not executeEager: triggers execution of the DAG
    ReturnsA new RDDA value to the Driver, or writes to storage
    Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, cachecollect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach
    RuleNo transformation executes until an action is calledSpark then analyses the full DAG, pipelines, runs only needed partitions
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  10. Key differenceIn a narrow dependency each child partition needs at most one parent partition, so it pipelines in one stage with no shuffle, whereas a wide dependency needs many parent partitions, forcing a network shuffle and a new stage.
    Narrow dependencyWide dependency
    Partition mappingEach output partition depends on at most one input partition (1-to-1)Each output partition may depend on multiple input partitions (all-to-all)
    Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, union, mapPartitions, coalescegroupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, join (not co-partitioned), repartition, distinct, sortByKey
    Data movementNo shuffleShuffle across the network
    StagesPipelined within a single stageCreates a stage boundary
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  11. Key differenceBoth shuffle, but reduceByKey pre-aggregates values on each partition before the shuffle (like a Combiner), so far less data crosses the network than with groupByKey.
    reduceByKeygroupByKey
    DependencyWide (shuffle)Wide (shuffle)
    Before shufflingApplies a local combine (like a MapReduce Combiner)Ships all values per key
    Network trafficGreatly reducedLarger
    Slide advicePrefer reduceByKeyAvoid when an aggregate is all you need (inference from 'prefer reduceByKey')
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  12. Key differenceA DataFrame adds named columns and a schema so the Catalyst optimiser can rewrite the query before running it (10-100x faster on structured data), whereas an RDD is schema-less records processed with functional operators.
    DataFrameRDD
    StructureDistributed collection organised into named columns with a schemaRead-only partitioned collection of records
    OptimiserCatalyst (predicate pushdown, join reordering, constant folding)DAG scheduler only
    Speed (structured data)10-100x faster than RDDsBaseline
    APISQL syntax + Python/Scala method chainingFunctional: map, filter, lambdas
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  13. MapReduce iterative disk I/O
    MR_IO = k × (D_read + D_write)
    k iterations; slide: 100 × (50 + 50) GB = 10 TB
    Spark HDFS I/O
    Spark_IO = D (read once)
    later iterations read RAM, not HDFS
    Transfer time
    t = size / speed
    50,000 MB / 500 MB/s = 100 s
    Iterative wall-clock time
    T_MR = k × (D/R_hdfs + D/W_hdfs); T_Spark = D/R_hdfs + (k − 1) × D/R_ram
    k − 1 RAM passes, not k
    Speedup
    Speedup = T_old / T_new
    A1: 20,000 / 1,090 ≈ 18.3×; RDD paper 127 / 0.96 ≈ 132×
    Hash partitioner
    partition = key.hashCode() % numPartitions
    17 % 4 = 1
    Shuffle records
    groupByKey = all pairs; reduceByKey ≤ partitions × distinct keys per partition
    4,000 vs 200 records
    Efficiency per node
    (T_old × N_old) / (T_new × N_new)
    GraySort (72 × 2,100) / (23 × 206) ≈ 32×

Practise 10 worked examples from the slides, then 4 from the lecturer’s own files

  1. Given50 GB bKash data, 100 iterations. HDFS read speed 500 MB/s, RAM cache read 5,000 MB/s. Assume HDFS write runs at the same 500 MB/s (not stated on the slide).
    1. One HDFS pass: 50,000 MB / 500 MB/s = 100 s.
    2. MapReduce per iteration = read + write = 200 s; total = 100 x 200 = 20,000 s = 5.56 h. Total HDFS I/O 10 TB.
    3. Spark: first read from HDFS 100 s; 99 more passes from RAM at 50,000/5,000 = 10 s each = 990 s.
    4. Spark total = 100 + 990 = 1,090 s, about 18.2 min. HDFS I/O 50 GB.
    5. Speedup = 20,000 / 1,090 = 18.3x.
    AnswerMapReduce about 20,000 s (5.56 h); Spark about 1,090 s (18.2 min); about 18.3x faster. Spark loses its edge if the data does not fit in RAM, or the job is a single pass.
    Now try one

    Given: one HDFS pass over 50 GB takes 100 s and one RAM pass takes 10 s. Spark reads HDFS once, then RAM for the remaining iterations. Total Spark time for 10 iterations?

    100 + 9 x 10 = 190 s.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  2. Giveninput -> filteredRDD -> mappedRDD -> reducedRDD, 10 partitions each. The executor holding partitions 3 and 7 of reducedRDD crashes.
    1. Driver: the executor stops heartbeating and its tasks fail; the driver marks partitions 3 and 7 (and anything else cached there) lost.
    2. Lineage lookup: reducedRDD <- mappedRDD <- filteredRDD <- input (HDFS).
    3. If all steps are narrow: recompute only partitions 3 and 7 of filteredRDD and mappedRDD from HDFS blocks 3 and 7: 2 input partitions, 2 x 3 = 6 partition computations. (8 counting the 2 input reads, as the card does)
    4. If reducedRDD comes from groupByKey (wide): partition 3 of reducedRDD needs data from all 10 mappedRDD partitions.
    5. Worst case (shuffle files lost with the executor and nothing cached): recompute all 10 partitions of filteredRDD and mappedRDD, re-shuffle, then rebuild partitions 3 and 7: 10 + 10 + 2 = 22 partition computations, plus re-reading all 10 HDFS blocks. (32 counting the 10 input reads)
    AnswerNarrow: 2 partitions per RDD (from 2 HDFS blocks). Wide (groupByKey) worst case: all 10 parent partitions recomputed and re-shuffled, 5x the input re-read.
    Now try one

    A job with 20 partitions, all narrow (map, filter). An executor holding 4 partitions dies. Given: narrow recovery recomputes only the lost partitions from their single parents. How many input partitions are re-read?

    4 (one parent per lost partition).
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  3. GivenHadoop record (Yahoo! 2012): 100 TB in 72 min on 2,100 nodes. Spark (Databricks 2013): 100 TB in 23 min on 206 EC2 i2.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 244 GB RAM, 8 x 800 GB SSD each). Input stored with 3x replication.
    1. Faster: 72 / 23 = 3.13x (slide: 3.1x).
    2. Fewer nodes: 2,100 / 206 = 10.19x (slide: 10.2x).
    3. Efficiency per node = (72 x 2,100) / (23 x 206) = 151,200 / 4,738 = 31.9x (slide: 32x).
    4. Total RAM = 206 x 244 GB = 50,264 GB = 50.3 TB; SSD per node 8 x 800 GB = 6.4 TB, total 206 x 6.4 = 1,318 TB = 1.32 PB.
    5. On disk with 3x replication: 100 x 3 = 300 TB.
    6. Throughput = 100 TB / 23 min = 4.35 TB/min (the slide prints 4.27, which would need 23.4 min).
    Answer3.1x faster on 10.2x fewer nodes, about 31.91x more work per node; 4.35 TB/min by recomputation.
    Now try one

    Yahoo! 2009 sorted 100 TB on 3,800 nodes in 173 min. Spark: 206 nodes, 23 min. Given: efficiency per node = (T_old x N_old) / (T_new x N_new). Compute it.

    (173 x 3,800) / (23 x 206) = 657,400 / 4,738 = 138.8x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  4. Given50 GB on HDFS, 100 iterations. MapReduce reads and writes 50 GB per iteration. Spark reads once and caches in RAM.
    1. MapReduce: 100 x (50 GB read + 50 GB write) = 10,000 GB = 10 TB.
    2. Spark: iteration 1 reads 50 GB from HDFS; iterations 2-100 read RAM. HDFS I/O = 50 GB.
    3. Ratio = 10,000 / 50 = 200x less disk I/O.
    Answer10 TB vs 50 GB: about 200x less disk I/O for Spark.
    Now try one

    A bKash model trains for 20 iterations over 200 GB. Given: MapReduce disk I/O = k x (read + write). Find MapReduce's total disk I/O.

    20 x (200 + 200) = 8,000 GB = 8 TB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  5. GivenLogistic regression, 10 iterations: Hadoop 127 s/iteration, Spark (MEMORY_ONLY) 0.96 s/iteration. K-means, 10 iterations: Hadoop 150 s vs Spark 5 s.
    1. LR speedup = 127 / 0.96 = 132.3x, about 132x.
    2. LR total over 10 iterations: Hadoop 1,270 s vs Spark 9.6 s.
    3. K-means speedup = 150 / 5 = 30x.
    AnswerAbout 132.29x for logistic regression (1,270 s vs 9.6 s over 10 iterations) and 30x for k-means.
    Now try one

    A Spark LR job takes 1.2 s per iteration; Hadoop takes 120 s. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup.

    120 / 1.2 = 100x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  6. GivenMapReduce's sort phase writes intermediate data to disk twice per byte (spill + merge). Spark's sort-based shuffle writes sorted runs once, eliminating about 120 TB of extra I/O at 100 TB.
    1. MapReduce extra disk I/O = 2 writes x 100 TB = 200 TB.
    2. Spark removes about 120 TB of that, leaving about 80 TB of shuffle I/O.
    3. Reduction in extra I/O = 120 / 200 = 60%.
    AnswerAbout 200 TB of extra disk I/O for MapReduce; Spark's sort shuffle saves about 120 TB (60%).
    Now try one

    A 40 TB sort on MapReduce writes every intermediate byte twice. Given: extra I/O = 2 x data. How much extra disk I/O?

    2 x 40 = 80 TB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  7. GivenSpark's default partitioner sends a key to partition key.hashCode() % numPartitions. For an integer key, hashCode() is the value itself (Java behaviour, general knowledge).
    1. Take the key's hash.
    2. Divide by the number of partitions and keep the remainder.
    3. Example: key 17, 4 partitions: 17 % 4 = 1, so partition 1.
    4. All pairs with the same key land in the same partition, which is what reduceByKey and join need.
    Answerpartition = hash(key) mod numPartitions; key 17 with 4 partitions goes to partition 1.
    Now try one

    An RDD of (customer_id, amount) has 8 partitions. Given: partition = key % 8. Where does customer_id 1,234 go?

    1,234 % 8 = 2, partition 2.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  8. GivenFor k iterations MapReduce pays k x HDFS read + k x HDFS write. Spinning disk 100 MB/s, 10 iterations, 100 GB.
    1. Reads only: 10 x 100 GB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 10,000 s = 2.78 h, about 3 h.
    2. Reads + writes (the slide's own formula): 2,000 GB / 100 MB/s = 20,000 s = 5.56 h.
    3. So the slide's 3 hours matches the read side only; with writes included it is about 5.6 h. Either way it is hours of pure I/O, which Spark avoids by caching after the first read.
    AnswerAbout 2.8 h counting reads only (the slide's 3 h); 5.6 h if writes are counted too.
    Now try one

    A graph job runs 20 iterations over 50 GB on disk at 100 MB/s. Given: read time per iteration = 50,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 500 s. Total read time?

    20 x 500 = 10,000 s = 2.78 h.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  9. GivenWord count on README.md with sc local[4]: flatMap -> map -> reduceByKey. Time counts.count() before and after cache(); compare reduceByKey with groupByKey in the Spark UI. Sample timings (not on the slide): first count 2.40 s, cached count 0.012 s.
    1. Before any action, toDebugString shows the lineage only: no job has run (lazy evaluation).
    2. First count() triggers the whole DAG: read, flatMap, map, shuffle for reduceByKey.
    3. counts.cache() marks the RDD for caching; the warm-up count() fills the cache; toDebugString now shows the RDD as cached in memory.
    4. Speedup = 2.40 / 0.012 = 200x.
    5. groupByKey ships every (word, 1) pair across the shuffle; reduceByKey combines locally first, so shuffle read/write bytes are much smaller.
    AnswerCached count is served from memory; with the sample timings the speedup is 200x. reduceByKey shuffles fewer bytes than groupByKey.
    Now try one

    A student times count(): 3.6 s uncached, 0.045 s cached. Given: speedup = uncached / cached. Report the speedup.

    3.6 / 0.045 = 80x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  10. GivenSpark is 10-100x faster on iterative workloads; for single-pass ETL larger than RAM, 2-5x. DataFrames are 10-100x faster than RDDs for structured data. Spark executors need about 8 GB minimum. Use Spark for >2 iterations over the same data.
    1. A 10-hour iterative MapReduce job at 10-100x becomes 6 min to 60 min.
    2. A 10-hour single-pass ETL at 2-5x becomes 2 h to 5 h.
    3. Executor memory floor: 50 executors x 8 GB = 400 GB of RAM before any data is cached.
    AnswerIterative: 10 h becomes 6-60 min; single pass: 2-5 h; 50 executors need at least 400 GB RAM.
    Now try one

    A nightly single-pass ETL takes 6 h on MapReduce. Given: single-pass gains are 2-5x. What range of Spark run times should you expect?

    6/5 = 1.2 h to 6/2 = 3 h.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. K-Means runs over 50 GB for 100 iterations. Reading or writing one 128 MB HDFS block takes 100 ms. (i) Compare the HDFS I/O time of MapReduce and Spark. (ii) An executor holding cached partitions crashes. How does Spark recover, and what is the worst-case cost?
    1. Blocks = 50 × 1,024 MB / 128 MB = 51,200 / 128 = 400 blocks.
    2. One full pass = 400 × 0.1 s = 40 s.
    3. MapReduce (slide model: each iteration reads its input from HDFS and writes its output back): 2 × 40 = 80 s per iteration.
    4. 100 iterations × 80 s = 8,000 s ≈ 2.2 h (reads alone: 4,000 s ≈ 67 min).
    5. Spark: reads the 400 blocks once (40 s) and caches them; iterations 2 to 100 read RAM, not HDFS.
    6. HDFS I/O time: 8,000 s / 40 s = 200× less (100× if you count reads only).
    7. Crash: the Driver sees the lost executor and its tasks fail; it looks up the lineage textFile → parse → cache.
    8. Only the lost partitions are rebuilt: with 10 executors, about 40 blocks × 0.1 s = 4 s of re-reading, then the current iteration's lost tasks rerun.
    9. The 99 earlier iterations are not redone: the centroids live in the Driver, and the points come from the input.
    10. Worst case (all cache lost): re-read the whole input, 40 s, and rerun one iteration. That is still less than one MapReduce iteration (80 s).

    With 1 GB = 1,000 MB: 391 blocks, 39.1 s per pass; the ratios are the same. This is the lecturer's plan's version of slide question A1, which uses MB/s instead.

  2. A Spark job runs logistic regression over 50 GB on a 10-node cluster with 32 GB RAM per node. (a) Can the full dataset be cached at MEMORY_ONLY? (b) If not, which StorageLevel would you choose and why? (c) Estimate how many iterations are needed before the cached speedup (130×) pays for the caching cost (1 extra HDFS read).
    1. (a) Cluster RAM = 10 × 32 = 320 GB, so 50 GB of raw bytes would fit.
    2. It is not safe, though. The OS, the NodeManager and shuffle (execution) memory also need RAM, and Java objects in memory are usually 2–5× larger than the file. At 3×, 50 GB becomes 150 GB, about half the cluster.
    3. Under MEMORY_ONLY, partitions that do not fit are dropped (LRU) and recomputed from HDFS every iteration, so the speedup disappears.
    4. (b) MEMORY_AND_DISK: partitions that overflow go to local disk and are read back from there, not rebuilt from HDFS. Choose MEMORY_ONLY_SER (Kryo bytes, smaller but slower) if there is spare CPU.
    5. (c) Let T = one HDFS pass. A cached iteration costs T / 130, and caching costs one extra T.
    6. Uncached, n iterations: nT. Cached: first pass T + caching T + (n − 1) × T/130.
    7. Break-even: n = 2 + (n − 1)/130, so 130n = 260 + n − 1, 129n = 259, n ≈ 2.01.
    8. Check: n = 2 costs 2T uncached vs 2.008T cached (not yet); n = 3 costs 3T vs 2.015T. Caching pays from the 3rd iteration.
    9. At 10 iterations: 10T vs 2T + 9T/130 = 2.07T, about 4.8× faster overall.

    Slides: StorageLevels, LRU eviction, LR 127 s vs 0.96 s per iteration (slide: 132×; the question rounds to 130×). Beyond the slides: the object-size blow-up and the memory set aside for the OS and shuffles.

  3. A groupByKey on an RDD with 1 billion records and 500 distinct keys produces 500 shuffle partitions. Identify two data-skew scenarios that would cause out-of-memory errors and propose a fix for each.
    1. Even spread: 1,000,000,000 / 500 = 2,000,000 records per key. groupByKey ships every value and holds all of a key's values in one task's memory.
    2. Skew 1, a hot key: one key (for example a default value such as "unknown") has 30% of the rows, 300 M records. That is 150× the average, all in one task, so it runs out of memory while the other tasks sit idle.
    3. Fix 1: if the goal is an aggregate, use reduceByKey or aggregateByKey, which combine on each partition before the shuffle.
    4. Textbook numbers: 108 values of 16 B for one key = 1.6 GB shuffled by groupByKey. With reduceByKey over 200 partitions only 200 partial sums move.
    5. If all the raw values really are needed (for example a median), salt the key: key + "_" + random(0..N−1), group in two phases, then merge.
    6. Skew 2, hash collisions: the hash partitioner (key.hashCode() % 500) can send several heavy keys to the same partition. Three keys of 100 M each put 300 M records in one partition.
    7. Fix 2: a custom partitioner that gives each heavy key its own partition, or more partitions (repartition) or a range partitioner, plus salting.
    8. Check in the Spark UI: one task's shuffle read is far above the median.

    Slides: reduceByKey vs groupByKey, and the hash partitioner “can hot-spot on skewed data”. Salting and the 1.6 GB example come from the lecturer's textbook (ch 6).

  4. Compare RDD lineage fault tolerance with HDFS-style 3× replication for a 10-iteration ML job. Under what failure rate does lineage become slower than replication?
    1. Replication pays on every iteration, failure or not: two extra copies of each output cross the network.
    2. Lineage pays nothing until a failure, and then recomputes only the lost partitions.
    3. Rule: lineage is slower when failures × recompute cost > iterations × replication overhead.
    4. Assume an iteration takes 60 s and replication adds 20%: 12 s × 10 = 120 s per job.
    5. Assume 10 executors, so one failure loses 1/10 of the partitions.
    6. Narrow chain or cached input: recompute about 1/10 of one iteration = 6 s. Break-even 120 / 6 = 20 failures per job; lineage wins easily.
    7. Wide chain, no checkpoint, shuffle files lost (worst case): recompute back to the input, on average 5 iterations × 60 s = 300 s. Break-even 120 / 300 = 0.4 failures per 10-minute job, that is one failure per 25 minutes of run time.
    8. Conclusion: lineage is slower only when failures are frequent and chains are long and wide. Checkpoint every few iterations to cap the recompute cost.

    The slides give the principle (lineage has no replication overhead and is expensive for wide dependencies, so checkpoint long chains). The 60 s, 20% and 10 executors are assumed numbers, beyond the slides.

Test 22 exam questions, 1 from the lecturer’s own files, then the predicted paper

  1. What makes Spark significantly faster than MapReduce for iterative algorithms?
    • (a) Spark uses more CPU cores per node
    • (b) Spark writes intermediate results to faster SSDs
    • (c) Spark caches intermediate data as RDDs in memory
    • (d) Spark skips the shuffle phase entirely

    (c) Spark caches intermediate data as RDDs in memory

    Later iterations read from RAM instead of re-reading and re-writing HDFS; the hardware is the same.

  2. How does Spark achieve fault tolerance in RDDs without full data replication?
    • (a) Checkpointing to HDFS every 60 seconds
    • (b) Tracking lineage and recomputing lost partitions from parent RDDs
    • (c) Copying each RDD partition twice across two Executors
    • (d) Using a write-ahead log on the Driver node

    (b) Tracking lineage and recomputing lost partitions from parent RDDs

    The recipe is kept, not copies; (c) is replication.

  3. Which of the following is NOT a component of the Spark ecosystem?
    • (a) MLlib
    • (b) GraphX
    • (c) Structured Streaming
    • (d) HBase

    (d) HBase

    HBase is a separate NoSQL database on HDFS; Spark can only read it as a data source.

  4. In Spark, a “transformation” such as map() or filter() is:
    • (a) Immediately executed when called and materialised to memory
    • (b) Lazily evaluated — only executed when a subsequent action is called
    • (c) Automatically persisted to HDFS after execution
    • (d) Only available in the Scala API, not in PySpark

    (b) Lazily evaluated — only executed when a subsequent action is called

    rdd.filter(f) alone does nothing; rdd.filter(f).count() runs it.

  5. Spark can only run on top of Hadoop YARN and has no other deployment option.

    False. The Cluster Manager can be YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos or Spark Standalone.

    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): Spark runs on YARN, Kubernetes, Apache Mesos or its own Standalone manager.

  6. RDDs are mutable — individual elements can be modified in place after creation.

    False. RDDs are immutable; every transformation creates a new RDD.

    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): RDDs are immutable; a transformation creates a new RDD and never changes the original.

  7. Spark's DataFrame API provides schema-aware, named-column operations similar to SQL tables.

    True. A DataFrame has named columns and a schema, like a relational table, and accepts SQL.

  8. MapReduce is generally better than Spark for machine learning workloads that require many iterations over the same dataset.

    False. Spark is better: it caches the data in RAM and is 10–100× faster on iterative work, while MapReduce hits disk every iteration.

    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): For iterative ML Spark is 10–100× faster because it caches the training data in memory; MapReduce re-reads HDFS on every iteration.

  9. Explain the concept of a Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD). What does “resilient” mean in this context? How does Spark recover a lost RDD partition without replication?

    RDD: a read-only, partitioned collection of records, created from stable storage (HDFS, S3) or by transforming another RDD. Properties: immutable, partitioned, lazy, lineage, resilient.

    Resilient: it survives a node failure by recomputing lost partitions from its lineage (the steps that built it) instead of keeping 3 copies. The computation is the backup.

    Recovery:

    1. Spark detects Part 2 of mappedRDD is lost.
    2. Traces lineage: mappedRDD ← filteredRDD ← inputRDD.
    3. Re-reads input Part 2 from HDFS.
    4. Re-applies filter, then map.
    5. Part 2 restored; the job is not restarted.

    Diagram: draw the lineage chain shown in the diagram in the RDD card: inputRDD → filteredRDD → mappedRDD, with Part 2 of mappedRDD crossed out and the recovery path going back to inputRDD Part 2 on HDFS.

    Cheap for narrow dependencies; checkpoint long chains.

  10. Differentiate between Spark transformations and actions. Give two concrete examples of each. Why does Spark not execute transformations immediately?
    TransformationAction
    RunsLazily, only recorded in the DAGImmediately, triggers the DAG
    ReturnsA new RDDA value to the Driver, or output to storage
    Examplesmap(f), filter(f)count(), collect()

    Why wait: with the whole DAG in view, Spark can

    • optimise the plan (DAG scheduler, or Catalyst for DataFrames);
    • pipeline filter and map in one pass, with no intermediate disk writes;
    • run only the partitions needed, e.g. first() stops at the first match.
  11. Describe Spark's lazy evaluation model. What is the advantage of deferring computation until an action is called? Use the example rdd.filter(x > 1000).first() to illustrate.

    See the diagram on the topic “Transformations, actions and lazy evaluation”

    Model: transformations are only recorded in the DAG. When an action is called, Spark analyses the DAG, optimises it, pipelines compatible steps in one pass per partition, and runs only the partitions it needs.

    Advantages: less work (early stop, skipped partitions), no intermediate disk writes, whole-plan optimisation.

    Example:

    1. filter(x > 1000): recorded, no data read.
    2. first(): action; Spark starts reading the first partition.
    3. It returns the first value above 1000 and stops.
    4. Eager execution would filter the entire dataset, then keep one value.
  12. Iterative I/O Cost Analysis: You need to train a K-Means clustering model over 50 GB of bKash transaction data with 100 iterations. Assume HDFS read speed = 500 MB/s and RAM cache read speed = 5,000 MB/s.
    • Calculate the total HDFS I/O for MapReduce (all 100 iterations)
    • Calculate the total I/O for Spark (50 GB fits in cluster RAM)
    • Estimate the wall-clock time for each approach
    • Under what conditions would Spark NOT outperform MapReduce?

    Given: D = 50 GB = 50,000 MB, k = 100, HDFS 500 MB/s (write assumed = read), RAM 5,000 MB/s.

    MapReduceSpark
    HDFS I/O100 × (50 + 50) = 10 TB50 GB (read once); RAM reads 99 × 50 = 4,950 GB
    Per pass50,000/500 = 100 s read + 100 s write = 200 s100 s first, then 50,000/5,000 = 10 s
    Total time100 × 200 = 20,000 s ≈ 5.56 h100 + 99 × 10 = 1,090 s ≈ 18.2 min

    Disk I/O 200× less; time speedup 20,000 / 1,090 ≈ 18.3×.

    Spark does not win when: the job is single-pass (nothing to reuse); the data does not fit in RAM (spill or evict and recompute); Executor memory (~8 GB minimum) is too costly; stable MapReduce code is already fast enough.

    From the lecturer’s files

    The lecturer's plan words this with 100 ms per 128 MB block instead of MB/s; see the worked version “K-Means, 50 GB, 100 iterations at 100 ms per 128 MB block” in Practise.

  13. RDD Failure Recovery Trace: A Spark job computes input → filteredRDD → mappedRDD → reducedRDD over 10 partitions. Mid-execution, the Executor holding partitions 3 and 7 of reducedRDD crashes. Trace the complete recovery sequence: what does the Driver detect, which partitions of which RDDs need to be recomputed, and what is the worst-case recovery cost if reducedRDD involves a wide dependency (groupByKey)?

    Stages: filter, map narrow → Stage 1 (input → filteredRDD → mappedRDD). groupByKey wide → Stage 2 (reducedRDD).

    Driver detects: the Executor is lost; tasks for reducedRDD partitions 3 and 7 failed. The other 8 partitions are fine.

    Lineage: reducedRDD ← groupByKey ← mappedRDD ← map ← filteredRDD ← filter ← input.

    CaseRecomputed
    If all narrowPartitions 3 and 7 at each level: 2 × 4 = 8 computations (20%)
    Wide, shuffle files surviveOnly reducedRDD 3 and 7, re-fetching from all 10 mappedRDD outputs
    Wide, worst caseShuffle output lost too: all 10 input, filteredRDD and mappedRDD partitions (30) + reshuffle + reducedRDD 3, 7 (2) ≈ the whole job

    Limit the cost: reduceByKey instead of groupByKey, cache mappedRDD, checkpoint long chains.

    From the lecturer’s files

    The lecturer's plan pairs this with the K-Means question: executor crash recovery via lineage, and its worst-case cost.

  14. In-memory is a multiplier, not a panacea: Spark is 10–100× faster on iterative workloads; for single-pass ETL over data larger than RAM, gains are smaller (2–5×)

    Claim: memory speeds up reuse; it does not fix every workload.

    For: iterative jobs reuse the working set. RDD paper: logistic regression 127 s vs 0.96 s per iteration (132×).

    Against: single-pass ETL reads each byte once, and data larger than RAM spills to disk, so the gain falls to 2–5×.

    Choose by workload: more than 2 iterations favours Spark.

  15. The lineage model scales elegantly: re-computing a lost partition from lineage is cheaper than maintaining 3× replicated in-memory state

    Claim: lineage beats replication for in-memory data.

    For: 3× replication triples RAM and network writes on every step; lineage costs nothing until a failure and then rebuilds only lost partitions.

    Against: with wide dependencies or long chains, one lost partition can need many ancestors recomputed, so checkpoints are still needed.

  16. Shuffle is the bottleneck: both at GraySort and in production; minimising wide dependencies (shuffle) is the primary Spark tuning skill

    Claim: shuffles dominate Spark's cost.

    For: a shuffle moves data over the network, writes to disk and forces a stage barrier. Spark's GraySort win came from a cheaper shuffle: sort-based shuffle (about 120 TB less I/O), all 8 SSDs as shuffle directories, one sortByKey. Tuning: reduceByKey over groupByKey, co-partition before joins.

    Against: sorts and un-partitioned joins need a shuffle; you minimise it, you cannot remove it.

  17. Benchmark marketing is real: GraySort made Spark famous; it also hid cases where Spark's JVM memory overhead hurt performance (many small files, high-cardinality groupBy)

    Claim: a headline benchmark sells a system but shows one workload.

    For: 100 TB in 23 min on 206 nodes vs Hadoop's 72 min on 2,100 drove Spark's adoption.

    Against: it ran on tuned large nodes (244 GB RAM, 8 SSDs). Many small files (per-task overhead) and high-cardinality groupBy (too many keys for JVM memory, GC pauses) were not tested.

    Test on your own workload.

  18. Open-source velocity: the Apache Spark community grew to 1,000+ contributors in 5 years; Databricks’ business model (cloud + support) aligned commercial incentives with open-source development

    Claim: a free engine plus a paid service sped up Spark.

    For: Databricks earns from cloud and support, not licences, so improving open Spark helps its business. 1,000+ contributors in 5 years produced Spark SQL, MLlib, Structured Streaming, GraphX.

    Against: one company steering the project can shape the roadmap and push features to its paid product first (lock-in risk).

  19. Task (25 minutes, pairs)
    Run the following PySpark script locally (Spark local mode).
    Goal: build and inspect an RDD lineage; observe lazy evaluation; compare cached vs. uncached timing.
    from pyspark import SparkContext
import time
sc = SparkContext("local[4]", "RDDDemo")
sc.setLogLevel("WARN")
# Build lineage (lazy - no compute yet)
lines = sc.textFile("README.md")
words = lines.flatMap(lambda l: l.split())
pairs = words.map(lambda w: (w.lower(), 1))
counts = pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a+b)
# Inspect lineage BEFORE action
print(counts.toDebugString().decode())
# First action - triggers full DAG
t0 = time.time()
n = counts.count()
print(f"count={n}  time={time.time()-t0:.2f}s")
# Cache and re-run
counts.cache()
counts.count()          # warm up cache
t1 = time.time()
n = counts.count()      # served from cache
print(f"cached count={n} "
      f"time={time.time()-t1:.4f}s")
sc.stop()

    local[4] = local mode, 4 threads. textFile, flatMap, map, reduceByKey only build lineage; the first count() runs the DAG. Key additions for the questions (run with python rdd_demo.py):

    print(counts.toDebugString().decode())   # Q1 before cache
for i in (1, 2):                          # Q2 two uncached runs
    t0 = time.time(); counts.count()
    print(i, time.time() - t0)
counts.cache()
print(counts.toDebugString().decode())   # Q1 after cache
counts.count()                            # fills the cache
t1 = time.time(); counts.count()
print("cached", time.time() - t1)
# Q3: counts = pairs.groupByKey().mapValues(sum)
input("open localhost:4040, then Enter")

    Expected: the lineage shows HadoopRDD → Python RDDs, with a +- indent at the reduceByKey shuffle; count = number of distinct lower-cased words.

  20. Call rdd.toDebugString() before and after cache() — what changes?

    The parent chain does not change, because cache() is lazy and lineage is kept for recovery. After cache() the top line shows a storage level (e.g. [Memory Serialized 1x Replicated]). After an action fills the cache it also shows CachedPartitions and memory size (expected).

  21. Time rdd.count() twice without cache(). Then add .cache() and time again. Report the speedup.

    Speedup = uncached time / cached time. Expected: run 1 slowest (start-up, read, shuffle); run 2 a bit faster (shuffle files reused, Stage 1 skipped); cached run fastest. On a small README start-up overhead dominates, so the ratio is modest; the RDD paper shows 127 s → 0.96 s (132×) at scale.

  22. Change reduceByKey to groupByKey. Use the Spark UI (localhost:4040) to compare shuffle read/write bytes between the two.

    Use pairs.groupByKey().mapValues(sum), then read Shuffle Write/Read on the UI's Stages tab. Expected: same counts, larger shuffle bytes for groupByKey, because reduceByKey combines each partition's pairs before the shuffle and groupByKey sends every (word, 1) pair.

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. True or false, with a one-line justification: calling rdd.collect() is a safe way to look at a 300 GB result.

    False. collect() sends every partition to the Driver's memory. On hundreds of GB the Driver runs out of memory, which ends the whole application.

    Use take(n), sample(False, 0.01) or saveAsTextFile(path); keep collect() for small final aggregates.

    Slides: collect() returns all elements to the Driver. The out-of-memory warning is the lecturer's textbook “Driver memory trap” (ch 6).

Predicted paper

  1. Write it closed book, then tap each part to check.

    (a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
    bKash's fraud team trains a logistic-regression model for 10 iterations over the same transaction data. On MapReduce each iteration takes 127 s; on Spark with the data cached in memory it takes 0.96 s (the RDD paper's benchmark).
    1. i)
      Why is MapReduce slow for this kind of algorithm? (1)
    2. ii)
      What does Spark do differently? (1)
    3. iii)
      Calculate the per-iteration speedup and the total time of each system for 10 iterations. (1)
    4. iv)
      When should the team call cache(), and when is caching a mistake? (1)
    1. i)
      MapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS and reads it back at the next step, so each of the 10 iterations pays a full disk read and write of the data.
    2. ii)
      Spark reads the data from HDFS once, caches it as an RDD in executor memory, and runs iterations 2 onward from RAM. Intermediate results stay in memory.
    3. iii)
      Speedup = 127 / 0.96 = 132x. Totals: MapReduce 10 x 127 = 1,270 s; Spark 10 x 0.96 = 9.6 s.
    4. iv)
      Cache an RDD that is reused by more than one action (iterative ML, interactive queries). Caching a single-use RDD wastes RAM and pushes other cached data out (LRU eviction).
    (b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
    The fraud pipeline on the slide is: txns = textFile -> map(parse) -> filter(amount > 50000) -> map((sender, 1)) -> reduceByKey(+) -> filter(count > 3) -> count(). It runs on 8 partitions.
    1. i)
      Which of these calls are transformations and which is the action? When does Spark actually start work? (1.5)
    2. ii)
      Is reduceByKey a narrow or wide dependency? How many stages does the job have, and where is the boundary? (1.5)
    3. iii)
      reduceByKey uses the default hash partitioner. A sender key has hashCode 1,234,567. Which partition gets it? (1)
    4. iv)
      The executor holding one partition of the parsed RDD crashes. How does Spark rebuild it without replicas, and why would losing a partition after reduceByKey cost more? (2)
    1. i)
      Transformations: map, filter, map, reduceByKey, filter (textFile is lazy too). Action: count(). Nothing runs until count() is called; until then Spark only records the DAG (lazy evaluation).
    2. ii)
      Wide: an output partition needs records for its keys from every input partition, so data is shuffled. 2 stages: stage 1 = textFile, map, filter, map (pipelined); the boundary is the shuffle at reduceByKey; stage 2 = reduce, filter, count.
    3. iii)
      Partition = key.hashCode() % numPartitions = 1,234,567 % 8. 8 x 154,320 = 1,234,560, remainder 7, so partition 7.
    4. iv)
      Spark follows the lineage: it re-reads that partition's HDFS block and re-applies map(parse) for that one partition only (narrow dependency, one parent). After reduceByKey each output partition depends on all 8 parent partitions, so if the shuffle output is lost, Spark must recompute the parents of all 8 partitions. Long lineages should be checkpointed to HDFS.

    Open it in the mock papers

  2. Write it closed book, then tap each part to check.

    (a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
    An analyst runs rdd.filter(lambda x: x > 1000).first() on a 1 TB dataset and is surprised it returns in seconds. A colleague says the same 10-iteration job over 100 GB on MapReduce spent about 3 hours on disk I/O.
    1. i)
      What is lazy evaluation? (1)
    2. ii)
      Why does first() return so quickly here? (1)
    3. iii)
      Check the colleague's figure: 10 iterations over 100 GB at 100 MB/s. (1)
    4. iv)
      Name two transformations and two actions. (1)
    1. i)
      Transformations such as filter and map only record a step in the DAG and return a new RDD; nothing executes until an action (count, collect, first, saveAsTextFile) is called.
    2. ii)
      When first() triggers the DAG, Spark pipelines the filter and stops as soon as it finds the first matching element; it never filters the whole 1 TB. Without lazy evaluation the full filter would run first.
    3. iii)
      Reads only: 10 x 100 GB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 10,000 s = about 2.8 h, the slide's 'about 3 hours'. Counting the writes too doubles it to 20,000 s = about 5.6 h.
    4. iv)
      Transformations: map, filter (also flatMap, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, distinct). Actions: count, collect (also first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach).
    (b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
    In November 2013 Databricks sorted 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 EC2 nodes. The previous Hadoop record was 72 minutes on 2,100 nodes. The sort is a single sortByKey.
    1. i)
      Why is the shuffle the bottleneck of a distributed sort, and what did Spark change in it? (1.5)
    2. ii)
      Spark was 3.1x faster on 10.2x fewer nodes. What is its efficiency per node relative to Hadoop? (1.5)
    3. iii)
      Define narrow and wide dependencies with one example each, and say how each affects stages. (1.5)
    4. iv)
      Why should a word count use reduceByKey rather than groupByKey? (1.5)
    1. i)
      Every record crosses the network between map and reduce sides, and MapReduce's shuffle spills, merges and re-reads intermediate data on disk many times (about 200 TB of extra I/O at 100 TB). Spark used a sort-based shuffle that writes sorted runs once and then merges, spread over 8 SSDs per node, with off-heap sort buffers that avoid GC pauses.
    2. ii)
      Per-node efficiency = 3.1 x 10.2 = about 31.6, about 32x (72/23 = 3.13 and 2,100/206 = 10.19 give 31.9).
    3. iii)
      Narrow: each output partition depends on at most one input partition (map, filter, union); no shuffle, pipelined in one stage. Wide: an output partition depends on many input partitions (groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, sortByKey); needs a shuffle and starts a new stage.
    4. iv)
      reduceByKey combines values locally on each partition before the shuffle (like a MapReduce Combiner), so only one partial sum per key per partition crosses the network. groupByKey ships every (word, 1) pair, so it moves far more data.

Week 7

Hive, HiveQL and SQL-on-Hadoop

Learn 6 topics, 4 comparisons and the formulas

  1. In one lineHive is a data warehouse layer on Hadoop that compiles SQL-like HiveQL queries into MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs over files on HDFS.
    Key points
    • HiveServer2: the JDBC/ODBC server. It authenticates users and accepts HiveQL from Beeline, BI tools (Tableau, Power BI) and JDBC drivers.
    • Driver: the query pipeline Parser → Semantic Analyser → Logical Planner → Query Optimizer → Physical Plan Generator.
    • Before Hive, a simple GROUP BY was a 100+ line Java MapReduce program and an answer took days. Analysts know SQL, not Java.
    Traps
    • Hive never runs HiveQL directly on HDFS. It compiles the query to MR, Tez or Spark jobs first.
    • Schemas live in the Metastore, not the NameNode. The NameNode only knows files and blocks.
    • Switching to Tez changes the plan and the speed, never the answer.
    • ORDER BY needs one reducer for a global order, so the final sort stage is a bottleneck.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  2. In one lineSchema-on-read means Hive applies the table's column types when data is queried, not when it is loaded.
    Key points
    • Schema-on-read: Hive applies column types at query (SELECT) time. Loading just copies raw files to HDFS.
    • Schema-on-write: an RDBMS such as MySQL checks each row at INSERT time and rejects bad rows.
    • Fast loading: a plain file copy, no validation cost.
    Traps
    • Schema-on-read does not mean the schema is inferred. You still write CREATE TABLE (MCQ 2 option d).
    • The schema is stored separately under both models. The key word is when it is applied.
    • HiveQL looks like SQL but runs as batch jobs: minutes, not milliseconds. A COUNT(*) on 1 TB can take 5–10 min on MapReduce; use Presto or Spark SQL for interactive speed. Exam Tip (old slides v1); still on current slide 17Very likely
    • Hive ACID is not on all tables, only transactional ORC tables.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  3. In one linePartitioning stores a Hive table in separate HDFS sub-directories by the value of a column, so queries filtering on it read only matching directories.
    Key points
    • Partition pruning: when WHERE filters on the partition key, Hive reads only the matching sub-directories and skips the rest.
    • Good key: a low-cardinality column (few distinct values) used often in WHERE: date, country, region, status.
    • Avoids a full table scan, so data read and job time drop in proportion.
    Traps
    • Partitioning splits by directory; bucketing splits into files inside a partition. Only partitioning skips directories.
    • In a dynamic insert, partition columns must be last in SELECT and in PARTITION order, or Hive assigns values wrongly without error.
    • Pruning needs a filter on the partition column itself. A filter on any other column scans every partition.
    • The fraction formula assumes equal-size partitions. Say so.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  4. In one lineBucketing splits each Hive partition into a fixed number of files by hash(column) % N.
    Key points
    • A row goes to bucket hash(column) % N. For an integer key the hash is the value itself.
    • DDL: CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS STORED AS ORC. Add SORTED BY for a sort-merge bucket join.
    • Joining two large tables no longer shuffles both of them, a large speed-up.
    Traps
    • Bucketing does not skip directories. It cuts join cost.
    • Buckets are numbered from 0: with 4 buckets the files are 0 to 3.
    • Same key and same bucket count on both tables, or no bucket map join.
    • The 5 TB question gives no years or countries. State your assumptions before sizing.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  5. In one linePresto is Meta's in-memory SQL engine that answers interactive queries over HDFS in seconds by never writing intermediate results to disk.
    Key points
    • Presto (Meta, 2013; fork: Trino) runs interactive SQL over petabytes on HDFS: 5 to 60 seconds versus Hive+MR's 5 to 15 minutes.
    • No intermediate disk writes: data flows through an in-memory pipeline (split → stage → output).
    • Disk writes between stages are the main cost of Hive+MR; Presto removes them.
    Traps
    • Presto's speed comes from no intermediate disk writes, not from extra SQL functions, connectors or Python UDFs.
    • Presto replaces the engine, not the catalogue: it reads the Hive Metastore.
    • The slide title says 10× faster; the ranges (5–15 min vs 5–60 s) give 5× to 180×.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  6. In one lineDiscover Weekly is Spotify's weekly recommendation playlist, built from playlist co-occurrence in HiveQL and ALS collaborative filtering in Spark, scheduled by Luigi.
    Key points
    • Scale (2015): about 3 billion events/day, 30 million songs, 2 billion playlists, 75M users; output 30M personalised playlists.
    • Data path: Kafka events → HDFS → HiveQL (analytics, features) and Spark MLlib (collaborative filtering).
    • Implicit feedback (2 billion playlists) was a richer signal than explicit star ratings.
    Traps
    • ALS size uses users plus songs, not users times songs.
    • The slides give no RAM per node. State the assumption (e.g. 64 GB).
    • Bucketing playlist_songs by playlist_id speeds the self-join, not the GROUP BY on song pairs.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  7. Key differenceSchema-on-write validates data against the table schema when it is loaded and rejects bad rows, while schema-on-read stores raw files as-is and applies the schema only when queried, so bad values silently become NULL.
    Schema-on-write (RDBMS / MySQL)Schema-on-read (Hive)
    When schema enforcedAt INSERT / LOAD timeAt SELECT / query time
    Invalid dataRejected immediately (INSERT fails if amount is text)Stored; NULL returned at query ('abc' in amount -> NULL)
    Write speed / query speedSlower write (validation); faster queryFast write (raw file copy); slower query (parse per query)
    Schemas per dataOne schema per tableMany schemas on same data
    From the lecturer’s files

    Schema on write vs on read is the first row of the lecturer's “important exam topics” table.

    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  8. Key differenceHiveQL looks like SQL but compiles to distributed batch jobs over HDFS, so it scales to petabytes yet has minute-level latency, limited ACID/UPDATE and no traditional indexes, unlike an RDBMS's millisecond OLTP SQL.
    SQL (RDBMS)HiveQL
    SchemaOn write (checked at INSERT)On read (applied at SELECT)
    ACID / UPDATE / DELETEFull; any row, any timeLimited: only ORC tables in ACID (transactional) mode
    IndexingB-tree, hash, bitmapPartitions + buckets (no traditional indexes)
    Sub-queriesCorrelatedNon-correlated only (some limitations)
    From the lecturer’s files

    The lecturer's course plan lists this table (schema, ACID, UPDATE/DELETE, indexes vs partitions + buckets, latency) as “important exam topics”.

    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  9. Key differencePartitioning splits a table into directories by a low-cardinality column value so WHERE filters skip whole directories, while bucketing hashes a (high-cardinality) column into a fixed number of files so tables bucketed the same way can be joined bucket-to-bucket without a full shuffle.
    PartitioningBucketing
    Physical unitSeparate HDFS sub-directory per column value (year=2024/month=01/)Fixed number of files (buckets) inside each partition
    Decided byValue of the partition columnhash(column) % N
    Main benefitPartition pruning: skips non-matching directories, avoids full-table scanBucket map join: bucket i x bucket i, no full sort-merge shuffle
    Good columnLow-cardinality, used in WHERE (date, country, region, status)The join key, e.g. user_id (slide example; 'high-cardinality' is general knowledge)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  10. Key differenceHive compiles queries into batch MapReduce/Tez jobs that write intermediate results to HDFS (minutes), whereas Presto pipelines data through memory with no intermediate disk writes, giving second-level interactive SQL.
    Hive (+MapReduce)Presto / Trino
    OriginFacebook, 2008Meta (Facebook), 2013
    Execution modelCompiled to MR / Tez / Spark jobsIn-memory pipeline execution (split -> stage -> output)
    Intermediate resultsMaterialised to HDFS between every MapReduce stageNo intermediate disk writes
    Latency5-15 min (minutes)5-60 sec (seconds); '10x faster than Hive+MapReduce'
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  11. Map-side aggregation
    reduction = N_rows / G (with M mappers: N_rows / (M × G))
    50M rows, 200 countries: 250,000×
    Partition pruning
    fraction read = P_read / P_total
    P_total = product of values per partition column
    Bucket number
    bucket = hash(column) % N
    integer key: hash = value; 98 % 4 = 2
    Bucket file size
    size = S / (P × N); files = P × N
    aim near the 128 MB HDFS block
    ALS model size
    (users + items) × k × bytes
    (75M + 30M) × 50 × 4 B = 21 GB
    Speed-up
    T_old / T_new; saved = (T_old − T_new) / T_old
    8 h to 2 h: 4×, 75% saved
    Pairs in a playlist
    L(L − 1) / 2
    20 songs: 190 pairs

Practise 11 worked examples from the slides, then 1 from the lecturer’s own files

  1. Given5 TB table (txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date). Reports filter by country and txn_date; joins with a 10 M-row user profile table on user_id. Assume 1 year of data and 10 countries (assumption, not on slide). The topic card's A1 answer assumes 3 years, 5 countries and 8 buckets instead; both are valid, since the slide gives no dates or country count. In the exam, state your assumptions and the method carries the marks.
    1. Partition on txn_date and country (both low-cardinality and in every WHERE). Never on user_id.
    2. Partitions = 365 x 10 = 3,650; average partition = 5,000,000 MB / 3,650 = 1,370 MB.
    3. Bucket on user_id, the join key, with the same bucket count in the user table.
    4. Pick N so files are near the 128 MB HDFS block: 1,370 / 128 = 10.7, so 8 or 16 buckets; N = 16 gives 85.62 MB files (58,400 files).
    5. DDL: CREATE TABLE txns (txn_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT, product_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE) PARTITIONED BY (country STRING, txn_date DATE) CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 16 BUCKETS STORED AS ORC;
    AnswerPARTITIONED BY (country, txn_date), CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 16 BUCKETS, ORC; about 85.62 MB per bucket file.
    Now try one

    A 2 TB table has 1,000 partitions. Given: partition size = 2,000,000 MB / 1,000 = 2,000 MB. How many buckets give files of about 128 MB?

    2,000 / 128 = 15.6, so 16 buckets (125 MB files).
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  2. GivenALS factorises a 75 M-user x 30 M-song matrix at rank k = 50, 4 bytes per float. Compare with the 5,000-node YARN cluster (64 GB per node, W05 Live Exercise).
    1. ALS stores one k-vector per user and per song: (users + songs) x k floats.
    2. (75,000,000 + 30,000,000) x 50 = 5,250,000,000 floats.
    3. x 4 bytes = 21,000,000,000 bytes = 21 GB.
    4. Cluster RAM = 5,000 x 64 GB = 320,000 GB = 320 TB.
    5. Model is 21 / 320,000 = 0.0066% of cluster RAM: it fits easily.
    Answer21 GB; fits in the 320 TB of aggregate RAM many times over.
    Now try one

    Rank is raised to k = 100, everything else the same. Given: size = (users + songs) x k x 4 B. New model size?

    105,000,000 x 100 x 4 = 42 GB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  3. GivenCLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO N BUCKETS. Rows where hash(column) % N = k go to bucket file k. Slide examples: 4 buckets in the diagram, 32 in the DDL. For an integer key, hash = the value (general knowledge).
    1. user_id 98 with 4 buckets: 98 % 4 = 2, bucket 2.
    2. Both tables bucketed on user_id with the same N: rows with equal user_id sit in the same bucket number in both.
    3. Bucket map join pairs bucket i of sales with bucket i of users only: with 32 buckets, 32 small joins instead of one full shuffle join.
    4. Each partition (e.g. year=2024/month=01) holds N bucket files.
    AnswerBucket = hash % N (98 % 4 = 2); a bucket map join does N matched bucket-pair joins with no full shuffle.
    Now try one

    A users table is CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS. Given: bucket = user_id % 32. Which bucket holds user_id 1,000?

    1,000 % 32 = 8, bucket 8.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  4. GivenCo-occurrence query GROUP BY song_a, song_b over 2 billion playlist rows, 30 M songs, pairs counted once (song_a < song_b), HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.
    1. Upper bound on distinct pairs = 30 M x (30 M - 1) / 2 = 4.500e+14 (about 4.5 x 10^14).
    2. Real output is far smaller: only pairs that actually co-occur, and HAVING > 5 drops rare ones; it is bounded by the pairs generated from playlists.
    3. A playlist of L songs gives L(L-1)/2 pairs: 20 songs give 190 pairs.
    4. To shrink the shuffle: bucket playlist_songs by playlist_id (so the self-join is bucket-local) and partition by week/dt so only recent data is read.
    AnswerAt most about 4.50e+14 pairs; actual output limited to co-occurring pairs above the HAVING threshold. Bucket on playlist_id, partition on date.
    Now try one

    A playlist has 30 songs. Given: pairs per playlist = L(L-1)/2. How many song pairs does it emit?

    30 x 29 / 2 = 435.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  5. GivenSELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY country on 50 million rows with 200 countries. Hive does partial aggregation in the mapper (combiner pattern) before shuffling.
    1. Without map-side aggregation every row is shuffled as (country, 1): 50,000,000 records.
    2. With it, the output is at most one (country, partial count) per country: 200 records (if one mapper; M mappers send up to M x 200).
    3. Reduction = 50,000,000 / 200 = 250,000x.
    4. With 10 mappers: 10 x 200 = 2,000 records, still 25,000x less.
    Answer50,000,000 records become 200: about 250,000x less shuffle data.
    Now try one

    A Hive table of 80 million click rows is grouped by 400 browser versions. Given: with map-side aggregation, one record per group leaves the map side. What is the shuffle reduction?

    80,000,000 / 400 = 200,000x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  6. GivenTable partitioned by (year, month) over 3 years: 36 sub-directories. Query WHERE year=2024 AND month=01. Warning: partitioning a 100 M user table on user_id would create 100 M directories.
    1. Partitions = 3 years x 12 months = 36.
    2. The query reads 1 of 36 = 2.78%; 35 directories skipped.
    3. If data is even and the job is I/O bound, job time drops by about 36x.
    4. On user_id: one directory per distinct value = 100,000,000 directories, each a NameNode metadata object, which overflows NameNode memory.
    Answer1 of 36 directories (2.8%); partitioning on user_id would mean 100 M directories.
    Now try one

    Daily partitions (dt) over 2 years. Given: partitions = 2 x 365. A dashboard query reads the last 7 days. What fraction is read?

    7 / 730 = 0.96%.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  7. Givenplay_events partitioned by (dt, country): 365 days x 200 countries. Query WHERE p.dt = '2024-10-01' AND p.country IN ('BD','IN','US').
    1. Total partitions = 365 x 200 = 73,000.
    2. The filter fixes one dt and three countries: 1 x 3 = 3 partitions.
    3. Fraction read = 3 / 73,000 = 0.0041%; 72,997 partitions skipped.
    4. The Metastore holds each partition's HDFS path, so Hive picks the 3 directories without listing all files.
    AnswerHive reads 3 of 73,000 partitions (0.0041%).
    Now try one

    A sales table is partitioned by (year, month) over 3 years. Given: total partitions = years x 12. A query asks for year=2024 AND month IN (1, 2). How many partitions are read out of the total?

    2 of 3 x 12 = 36; fraction 5.6%.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  8. GivenPartitioning play_events by week reduced the co-occurrence HiveQL from 8 hours to 2 hours. Daily retraining would cost 7x the compute of weekly.
    1. Speedup = 8 / 2 = 4x.
    2. Time saved = (8 - 2) / 8 = 75%.
    3. Retraining: weekly costs 1 unit per week; daily costs 7 units per week (7x).
    Answer4x faster, 75% of the time saved; daily retraining would cost 7x the weekly compute.
    Now try one

    A HiveQL report drops from 6 h to 45 min after partitioning by date. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup.

    360 / 45 = 8x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  9. GivenSELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM transactions WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2023 GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5. Sample: 3 mappers, each sees all 1,000 products.
    1. Job 1 Map: read rows, apply the 2023 filter, emit (product_id, amount); map-side aggregation emits (product_id, partial sum).
    2. Shuffle key: product_id.
    3. Job 1 Reduce: SUM per product -> (product_id, revenue).
    4. Job 2: global sort by revenue DESC and LIMIT 5 (one reducer sees all totals). With 3 mappers x 1,000 products the shuffle carries at most 3,000 partial sums.
    5. On Tez: the two jobs become one DAG; no HDFS write between the aggregate and the sort.
    AnswerMap emits (product_id, amount); shuffle on product_id; reduce sums; a second stage sorts and takes 5. Tez fuses the stages into one DAG with no intermediate HDFS write.
    Now try one

    Mappers emit partial sums per product. 5 mappers, 2,000 products, each mapper sees every product. Given: records shuffled = mappers x groups. How many records are shuffled?

    5 x 2,000 = 10,000.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  10. GivenFacebook 2010: 2 PB stored, 15 TB/day growth, 7,500+ queries/day, <15% failure rate, 200+ analysts. Spotify: about 3 billion events/day; its Hive Metastore catalogs over 1 million tables on a cluster processing 600 billion events/day.
    1. Yearly growth = 15 TB x 365 = 5,475 TB = 5.47 PB.
    2. Failures at most 15% of 7,500 = 1,125 queries/day.
    3. Queries per analyst = 7,500 / 200 = 37.5 per day.
    4. Spotify 3 B events/day / 86,400 s = 34,722 events/s.
    AnswerAbout 5.47 PB/year growth; up to 1,125 failed queries/day; about 34,722 Spotify events per second.
    Now try one

    A data lake grows 15 TB per day. Given: yearly growth = daily x 365. How much after 2 years if it started at 2 PB?

    2 PB + 2 x 5.475 PB = 12.95 PB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  11. GivenHive+MR: 5-15 min; Presto: 5-60 s. A COUNT(*) on 1 TB takes 5-10 min on MapReduce. Presto processes column chunks in batches of 1,024 rows. Presto is about 10x faster than Hive+MapReduce.
    1. Hive best and worst: 5 min = 300 s, 15 min = 900 s.
    2. Ratios: 300/60 = 5x (worst Presto vs best Hive) up to 900/5 = 180x; about 10x typical.
    3. Vectorised batches: 10,000,000 rows / 1,024 = 9,766, so 9,766 batches instead of 10 million row-at-a-time calls.
    AnswerPresto is roughly 5x to 180x faster across the ranges (about 10x typical); 10 M rows run as 9,766 batches.
    Now try one

    A Hive+MR query takes 12 min. Given: Presto is about 10x faster for interactive queries. Estimate Presto's time.

    12 x 60 / 10 = 72 s.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. Using the 5 TB transactions table (txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date), partitioned by (txn_date, country) as in A1 (assume 3 years and 5 countries, as in the A1 answer), write HiveQL for the monthly average transaction amount per country in Q1 2024. Explain how many partitions it reads and the MapReduce stages Hive generates.
    SELECT country, MONTH(txn_date) AS mon, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM transactions
WHERE txn_date >= '2024-01-01' AND txn_date <= '2024-03-31'
GROUP BY country, MONTH(txn_date)
ORDER BY country, mon;
    1. Pruning: Q1 2024 = 31 + 29 (leap year) + 31 = 91 days; 91 × 5 countries = 455 of 5,475 partitions (the A1 count, 3 × 365 × 5). Counting 2024's extra day gives 5,480; the share is still 8.3%.
    2. 455 / 5,475 = 8.3%, about 5,000 GB × 0.083 ≈ 416 GB read instead of 5 TB. A plain range on the partition column makes pruning certain.
    3. Job 1, Map: emits key (country, month) and value (amount, 1).
    4. Combiner: partial (sum, count) per key. Never partial averages: an average of averages is wrong.
    5. Shuffle key: (country, month), so 5 × 3 = 15 keys.
    6. Reduce: AVG = total sum / total count, giving 15 rows.
    7. Job 2: ORDER BY uses one reducer to sort the 15 rows. On Tez the two jobs become one DAG with no HDFS write in between.
    8. Tiny check: BD, January. Mapper 1 sees 100 and 300, giving (400, 2); mapper 2 sees 500, giving (500, 1). AVG = 900 / 3 = 300. The wrong average of averages is (200 + 500) / 2 = 350.

    If “monthly average” means average monthly revenue, first SUM(amount) per (country, month) in a sub-query, then AVG over the three months per country. This is the lecturer's plan question; the slides' A2 asks only for the 2023 top 5.

Test 21 exam questions, 1 from the lecturer’s own files, then the predicted paper

  1. In Hive, where is table schema metadata (column names, types, partition info) stored?
    • (a) HDFS NameNode
    • (b) Hive Metastore (relational DB such as MySQL)
    • (c) HBase
    • (d) ZooKeeper
    (b) Hive Metastore (relational DB such as MySQL)
    The NameNode holds HDFS block metadata, not table schemas.
  2. What does "schema-on-read" mean in the context of Hive?
    • (a) Schema is validated when data is inserted into the table
    • (b) Schema is applied when data is queried, not when it is stored on HDFS
    • (c) Schema is stored separately from data in HDFS metadata
    • (d) Schema is inferred automatically from column names in the file header
    (b) Schema is applied when data is queried, not when it is stored on HDFS
    (a) describes schema-on-write, how MySQL works.
  3. Which Hive optimization technique physically organises data into separate HDFS sub-directories by a column's value to avoid full table scans?
    • (a) Bucketing
    • (b) Indexing
    • (c) Partitioning
    • (d) Compression
    (c) Partitioning
    Bucketing splits files inside a partition; it does not skip directories.
  4. Presto's primary performance advantage over Hive+MapReduce for interactive queries is:
    • (a) Presto supports more SQL functions than HiveQL
    • (b) Presto has better native integration with HBase and Cassandra
    • (c) Presto executes queries entirely in memory without writing intermediate results to disk
    • (d) Presto has native Python UDF support
    (c) Presto executes queries entirely in memory without writing intermediate results to disk
    Hive+MR writes to HDFS between every stage.
  5. HiveQL supports full ACID transactions on all table types, just like MySQL.
    False. Corrected: HiveQL supports ACID only on ACID-enabled transactional ORC tables; MySQL (InnoDB engine) gives full ACID: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and ROLLBACK on any row.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): ACID exists only on ORC-backed transactional tables created with TBLPROPERTIES ('transactional'='true').

  6. Partitioning in Hive reduces query time by eliminating irrelevant data partitions from the HDFS scan.
    True. A WHERE filter on the partition key makes Hive read only the matching sub-directories (partition pruning).
  7. Hive directly executes a HiveQL query on HDFS without any intermediate translation step.
    False. Corrected: Hive compiles HiveQL (parse, analyse, plan, optimise) into MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs, which then read HDFS.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): The Driver parses HiveQL, builds and optimises a logical plan, and compiles it into a DAG of MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs before any data is touched.

  8. Bucketing in Hive is particularly useful for optimising JOIN operations between two large tables.
    True. Both tables bucketed on the join key with the same N let Hive join bucket i with bucket i, with no full shuffle.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): A bucket map join pairs matching bucket numbers (same hash), so the full shuffle-sort phase is skipped.

  9. Explain the Hive architecture: what is the role of HiveServer2, the Driver, and the Metastore? How is a HiveQL query compiled into executable jobs? Draw the component diagram.
    • HiveServer2: JDBC/ODBC front door; authenticates users, accepts HiveQL from Beeline, BI tools, JDBC.
    • Driver: Parser → Semantic Analyser → Logical Planner → Optimizer → Physical Plan Generator; manages the query lifecycle.
    • Metastore: MySQL/PostgreSQL catalogue of schemas, types, partitions, HDFS paths.

    Compilation: parse to AST → check names and types in the Metastore → logical plan (Filter, Join, GroupBy, OrderBy) → optimise (partition pruning) → MR/Tez/Spark jobs → submit to YARN; results to HDFS and client.

    Diagram:

    See the diagram on the topic “Hive architecture and query compilation”
  10. Differentiate between partitioning and bucketing in Hive. When would you choose each? Describe a scenario in Bangladesh e-commerce data where both are used together.
    PartitioningBucketing
    UnitDirectory per valueFixed N files, hash(col) % N
    BenefitPruning for WHERE filtersBucket map join
    ColumnLow cardinality (date, division)High cardinality key (customer_id)

    Choose partitioning when queries filter on a few-valued column; bucketing when large tables are joined on a many-valued key.

    Scenario: a Bangladeshi e-commerce orders table, PARTITIONED BY (order_date, division) and CLUSTERED BY (customer_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS. The Dhaka daily report reads one folder; the join with customers (also 32 buckets on customer_id) pairs bucket i with i.

  11. What is "schema-on-read"? What are its advantages and disadvantages compared to "schema-on-write" in a traditional RDBMS such as MySQL? Give one example where schema-on-read causes a data quality problem.

    Schema-on-read: Hive applies column types at query time; loading is a raw file copy. MySQL (schema-on-write) checks each row at INSERT.

    AdvantagesDisadvantages
    Fast load, no validationSlower queries (parse every time)
    Load before the schema is known; many schemas on the same files; no ETL at ingestBad data silent: becomes NULL
    Open formats (ORC, Parquet, CSV, JSON, Avro)Unfit for OLTP (banking, orders)

    Example: abc in a DOUBLE amount column. MySQL rejects the INSERT; Hive stores it and returns NULL, so SUM(amount) under-reports revenue with no warning. Fix: Great Expectations or dbt tests downstream.

  12. Partitioning & Bucketing Design: You have a 5 TB e-commerce transaction table with columns: (txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date). Design a complete partitioning and bucketing strategy to optimise: – Daily revenue reports filtered by country and txn_date – JOINs between this table and a 10 M-row user profile table (keyed on user_id). Write the complete CREATE TABLE DDL. Justify why you chose a specific number of buckets and which column(s) you partitioned on.

    Partition on txn_date, country (low cardinality, used in report filters). Bucket on user_id (high-cardinality join key), same N on both tables for a bucket map join. Never partition on user_id or txn_id.

    Bucket count (assume 3 years, 5 countries):

    Partitions3 × 365 × 5 = 5,475
    Per partition5,000 GB / 5,475 ≈ 0.913 GB
    8 buckets≈ 114 MB/file (near 128 MB block), 43,800 files
    32 buckets≈ 28.5 MB/file, 175,200 files: too small
    CREATE TABLE transactions (
  txn_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT,
  product_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE)
PARTITIONED BY (txn_date STRING, country STRING)
CLUSTERED BY (user_id) SORTED BY (user_id) INTO 8 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

CREATE TABLE user_profile (
  user_id BIGINT, name STRING, city STRING)
CLUSTERED BY (user_id) SORTED BY (user_id) INTO 8 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

    Result: a one-day, one-country report reads 1 of 5,475 partitions (≈ 0.018%); the join pairs bucket i with i.

  13. Query Compilation to MapReduce: Write HiveQL to find the top 5 products by total revenue in 2023. Then trace how Hive compiles this query into MapReduce stages: what is emitted by the Map phase, what is the shuffle key, and what does the Reduce phase compute? How would switching the execution engine from MapReduce to Tez change the execution plan?
    SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS total_revenue
FROM transactions
WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2023
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;
    Job 1: aggregateJob 2: sort + limit
    Map emits(product_id, amount) for 2023 rows; combiner gives partial sums(total_revenue, product_id); each mapper keeps its top 5
    Shuffle keyproduct_idtotal_revenue DESC, to one reducer
    ReduceSUM(amount) per product, written to HDFSFirst 5 rows

    Tiny check: (P1,100), (P2,50), (P1,30), (P3,80), (P2,20) → P1 130, P3 80, P2 70.

    Tez: one DAG, Map 1 → Reducer 2 → Reducer 3. No HDFS write between the jobs, one submission, container reuse. Same result, faster.

    From the lecturer’s files

    The plan also asks for the monthly average per country in Q1 2024; see that worked query in Practise.

  14. Spotify's co-occurrence query runs GROUP BY song_a, song_b over 2 billion playlist rows. Estimate the output size if there are 30M songs. Propose a partitioning + bucketing scheme for the playlist_songs Hive table that would reduce the shuffle size for this query. [CLO4 – Apply]

    Claim: output is far below the 30M-song bound. Bound: 30M × (30M − 1) / 2 ≈ 4.5 × 10^14 pairs. Realistic (assume 20 songs per playlist): 10^8 playlists × 190 = 1.9 × 10^10 pairs, ≤ 304 GB at 16 B/row, much less after HAVING > 5. (If you read it as 2 billion playlists of 20 songs: 2 × 10^9 × 190 = 3.8 × 10^11 pairs, ≈ 6.1 TB at 16 B; state which reading you use.)

    Scheme: PARTITIONED BY (week), CLUSTERED BY (playlist_id) SORTED BY (playlist_id, song_id) INTO 1024 BUCKETS. For: the self-join runs inside each bucket with no shuffle, and weekly partitions cut 8 h to 2 h. Against: it does not shrink the GROUP BY shuffle on song pairs; rely on map-side aggregation there.

    From the lecturer’s files

    This discussion question appeared in the old (v1) slides' Part 2 too, with the same CLO tag.

  15. The ALS collaborative filtering model is a matrix factorisation over a 75M-user × 30M-song matrix. At 4 bytes per float and rank k = 50, calculate the model size and explain whether it fits in a 5,000-node YARN cluster's aggregate RAM. [CLO4 – Analyse]

    Size: (75M + 30M) × 50 × 4 B = 21 GB (users 15 GB + songs 6 GB).

    Fits? Assume 64 GB/node: 5,000 × 64 GB = 320 TB; 21 GB ≈ 0.0066%, about 4.2 MB per node. For: it fits easily, even on one large server; the dense 9 PB matrix would not. Against: training also holds the interaction data, shuffled factor blocks and JVM overhead, several times the model size, but still well within the cluster.

    From the lecturer’s files

    This discussion question appeared in the old (v1) slides' Part 2 too, with the same CLO tag.

  16. Spotify uses Luigi while other companies use Apache Airflow. Compare the two on: dependency declaration style, backfill capability, and UI/observability. Which would you choose for a 100-step daily pipeline? [CLO3 – Evaluate]

    Claim: choose Airflow for a 100-step daily pipeline. Luigi: target-based requires()/output(), skips finished outputs, backfill by date parameters, simple UI. Airflow: DAG with a scheduler, built-in catchup/backfill, rich UI with logs, retries and alerts.

    For: at 100 steps you need to see which step failed, read its logs and re-run past days, which Airflow gives out of the box. Against: Luigi is lighter and its skip-if-output-exists model fits file-based Hadoop pipelines like Spotify's.

    From the lecturer’s files

    This discussion question appeared in the old (v1) slides' Part 2 too, with the same CLO tag.

  17. Task (25 minutes, pairs): Simulate a Hive session using PySpark's SQL interface (which reads the same Hive Metastore). Dataset: a 10,000-row synthetic play_events CSV (generate with the skeleton below).
