    50,000,000 / 25,000 = 2,000x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  6. GivenLie factor = size of effect shown in graphic / size of effect in data. Y-axis starts at 50; the data rise 10% but the bar appears to double.
    1. Effect in data = +10%.
    2. Effect shown = bar doubles = +100%.
    3. Lie factor = 100 / 10 = 10: the graphic overstates the change 10 times.
    AnswerLie factor about 10 (truthful = 1).
    Now try one

    Revenue rises from 50 to 55 (+10%). The chart's y-axis starts at 45, so the bars are drawn 5 and 10 units tall. Given: shown effect = (10 - 5)/5. Find the lie factor.

    Shown = +100%; data = +10%; lie factor = 10.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  7. GivenData-ink ratio = ink used to display data / total ink used in the graphic. Example (not on slide): a chart uses 200 units of ink, 60 of which draw the bars.
    1. Ratio = 60 / 200 = 0.3.
    2. Remove the 3-D effect (40 units), redundant legend (20) and heavy gridlines (60): total becomes 200 - 120 = 80.
    3. New ratio = 60 / 80 = 0.75.
    Answer0.30 before, 0.75 after removing chartjunk.
    Now try one

    A bar chart uses 500 units of ink; 150 draw data. Given: ratio = data ink / total ink. Find the ratio.

    150 / 500 = 0.3.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  8. Given5 topics x 7 days = 35 random values; count = floor(random x 50,000) + 10,000. y = d3.scaleLinear().domain([0, max]).range([260, 20]); bar height = 260 - y(count). Suppose max = 50,000.
    1. Count range: 10,000 to 59,999 (random in [0, 1)).
    2. Pixels per unit = (260 - 20) / 50,000 = 0.0048 px.
    3. Count 25,000: y = 260 - 25,000/50,000 x 240 = 140; height = 260 - 140 = 120 px.
    4. Because the domain starts at 0, bar heights are proportional to counts (lie factor 1).
    AnswerA 25,000 bar is 120 px tall and its top sits at y = 140.
    Now try one

    Same scale (domain [0, 50,000], range [260, 20]). Given: height = count / 50,000 x 240. Height of a 40,000 bar?

    40,000/50,000 x 240 = 192 px.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  9. GivenPie charts only when there are <= 4 categories and the question is 'what fraction of the whole?'. Above 5 categories use a horizontal bar chart ordered by value.
    1. Count categories and identify the question type.
    2. Example: 8 districts' share of dengue cases: 8 > 4, so use a horizontal bar chart sorted by value.
    3. Example: a 3-way split of revenue by channel as a fraction of total: a pie is acceptable.
    AnswerPie only for <= 4 categories and part-to-whole; otherwise bar (or line for time).
    Now try one

    A bKash report shows the share of 3 transaction types (send money, cash out, payment) in total volume. Given the <= 4 rule, is a pie acceptable?

    Yes: 3 categories and a part-of-whole question.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  10. GivenThe NYT used 7-day rolling averages to remove day-of-week reporting artefacts; the tracker loaded 800 million times in 2020; 6 million readers per day. Sample daily cases (not on slide): 120, 135, 128, 300, 140, 131, 126.
    1. 7-day average = sum / 7 = 1,080 / 7 = 154.3.
    2. The 300 spike (a reporting backlog) moves the average far less than it moves the daily line.
    3. 800 M loads / 366 days (2020 leap year) = 2,185,792 loads per day.
    Answer7-day average = 154.3; about 2,185,792 loads per day.
    Now try one

    Daily dengue cases for 7 days: 210, 190, 205, 400, 195, 200, 180. Given: 7-day average = sum / 7. Compute it.

    1,580 / 7 = 225.7.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. The NYT COVID tracker uses a 7-day rolling average instead of raw daily counts. (a) What reporting artefact does this remove? (b) What real signal might a 7-day window mask that a 3-day window would reveal? Relate your answer to Shneiderman's “zoom and filter”.
    1. (a) It removes day-of-week reporting artefacts: low counts at weekends, catch-up spikes on Monday, and one-day data dumps. Any 7-day window holds exactly one of each weekday.
    2. (b) A trailing average lags a real change by about half its window: 7-day ≈ (7 − 1)/2 = 3 days, 3-day ≈ 1 day.
    3. So a 7-day line shows the start of a surge or a turning point about 2 days later than a 3-day line, and makes it look gentler.
    4. Example: cases jump from 100 to 400 a day. On day 1 the 3-day mean is (100 + 100 + 400)/3 = 200, but the 7-day mean is (6 × 100 + 400)/7 ≈ 143.
    5. The cost of the 3-day window is that it keeps part of the weekly cycle, so it is noisier.
    6. Shneiderman: the 7-day line is the overview. Zoom and filter lets the reader narrow to the last few weeks and switch to raw or 3-day bars to see the onset. Details on demand shows the exact daily count on hover.

    Slides: the 7-day average reduces day-of-week artefacts, and the window choice is an editorial decision. The lag arithmetic and the 3-day comparison go beyond the slides.

Test 21 exam questions, 1 from the lecturer’s own files, then the predicted paper

  1. Edward Tufte's “data-ink ratio” principle states that a visualization should:
    • (a) Use more colours to highlight different categories of data
    • (b) Maximise the fraction of ink devoted to representing actual data, removing all decorative elements
    • (c) Use ink sparingly to reduce printing costs
    • (d) Always include data labels using a different ink colour from the chart body
    (b) Maximise the fraction of ink devoted to representing actual data, removing all decorative elements
    The ratio is about what the ink encodes, not saving ink.
  2. Which visualization type is most appropriate for showing the distribution and spread of a continuous variable?
    • (a) Pie chart
    • (b) Line chart
    • (c) Histogram
    • (d) Treemap
    (c) Histogram
    Bins along the number line show shape and spread.
  3. Shneiderman's visualization mantra begins with which step?
    • (a) Details first, then overview
    • (b) Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand
    • (c) Filter first, then provide an overview
    • (d) Details on demand first, then zoom out
    (b) Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand
    Filtering only makes sense after the overview shows what to filter.
  4. Which visualization tool is best suited for a real-time production operations dashboard monitoring server metrics and application error rates with 5-second refresh intervals?
    • (a) Tableau
    • (b) D3.js
    • (c) Power BI
    • (d) Grafana
    (d) Grafana
    Native time-series DB integration with 5 s auto-refresh; D3 would need custom code.
  5. A pie chart is a recommended choice for comparing more than 5 categories.
    False. People judge angles poorly. Corrected: use a horizontal bar chart; pies only for ≤ 4 categories.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): With more than 5 categories, people judge arc angles poorly; a horizontal bar chart sorted by value reads better.

  6. Hexbin plots are an effective technique for reducing overplotting when visualising millions of data points.
    True. Counting points per hexagon turns 10 million dots into ≈ 10,000 coloured cells.
  7. D3.js generates static PNG or PDF image files as its primary output format.
    False. Corrected: D3.js binds data to DOM elements and produces interactive SVG in the browser.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): D3.js binds data to SVG DOM elements in the browser; the output is interactive, scalable vector graphics, not static image files.

  8. Choropleth maps are used to visualise the geographic distribution of a quantitative variable.
    True. Regions are shaded by a value, best a rate such as cases per 100,000.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): A choropleth encodes a quantitative variable (e.g. dengue incidence per 100,000) as colour intensity on geographic polygons.

  9. Explain Tufte's data-ink ratio principle. Provide a “before and after” example: describe a cluttered bar chart (what chart-junk elements are present) and then describe the clean version after applying the principle.

    Principle: data-ink ratio = ink encoding data ÷ total ink; maximise it. If erasing an element loses no information, erase it.

    Before (quarterly sales)After
    Title "CHART TITLE!!!"Plain short title
    Legend for one seriesNo legend; Q1-Q4 on the x-axis
    3-D bars with shadowsFlat 2-D bars, one colour
    Gradient fill, borderRemoved
    Heavy dark gridlinesNone, or one light line; y starts at 0

    Same data, but almost all remaining ink is data, so the trend reads at once.

  10. What is overplotting? Describe three techniques to address it when visualising millions of data points in a scatterplot. For each technique, explain what information it preserves that the original overplotted chart lost.

    Overplotting: millions of dots overlap into a blob that only says "data exists here".

    TechniqueHowPreserves
    Alpha transparencyEach point α = 0.02; stacks look darkerRelative density (fails at very high density)
    HexbinCount points per hexagon, colour by count; 10 M → ≈ 10,000 cellsActual count per area
    KDE contourSmooth density, contour linesShape, modes (peaks), tails
  11. What is a data cube? How does pre-aggregating a billion-row fact table into a data cube enable interactive visualization at sub-second latency? What is the trade-off of this approach?

    Data cube: pre-computed aggregates (SUM, COUNT) of a fact table for combinations of dimensions, e.g. district × date × product × channel.

    • A nightly Spark/Hive job builds it once.
    • It holds millions of rows, not billions.
    • Tableau/Superset filters read the cube, so they answer in under 1 s instead of minutes.

    Trade-off: staleness up to 24 h; only pre-built dimensions can be sliced; extra storage. Alternative: AQP (sampling) trades accuracy for speed.

  12. Public Health Dashboard Design: A DGHS public health dashboard needs to communicate: (a) COVID-19 confirmed case counts by district over 24 months (b) Real-time hospitalisation rate updated every 5 minutes (c) Demographic breakdown (age group, gender) of confirmed cases For each sub-requirement: specify the appropriate visualization type, justify using Shneiderman's data-type taxonomy, identify which big data visualization challenge applies (if any), and name the tool you would use. Apply Tufte's data-ink principle to state one specific chart-junk element to eliminate.
    Req.Data typeChartChallengeTool
    (a) Cases by district, 24 monthsTemporal (+ 2-D map)Small multiples of line charts, same scale; choropleth of rate per 100,000Latency: pre-aggregate to daily counts per districtTableau / Power BI
    (b) Hospitalisation every 5 minTemporal (live)Stat panel + sparkline, 24 h line chartStreamingGrafana on InfluxDB/Prometheus
    (c) Age × genderCategorical / multi-dimensionalGrouped horizontal barNone (small table)Tableau / Power BI

    Sizes: (a) 730 days × 64 districts = 46,720 rows after aggregation. (b) 24 × 60 ÷ 5 = 288 points per day, so 5 s polling is ample.

    Mantra: national total → district dropdown and date slider → hover tooltip.

    Chartjunk to remove: 3-D effect on the demographic bars (also heavy gridlines on the line charts).

  13. Streaming Sentiment Visualization: Design a complete visualization system for a streaming Twitter (X) sentiment analysis pipeline processing 10,000 tweets per second. Specify: (a) which Kafka aggregation window you would use and why; (b) which chart types best convey sentiment drift over time and topic clustering; (c) how you would handle the velocity challenge at the visualization layer without overloading the browser; (d) which tools form the pipeline from Kafka to browser render.

    Givens: 10,000 tweets/s → 600,000 per minute, 864,000,000 per day.

    (a) 1-minute tumbling window per topic: count, mean sentiment, % positive/neutral/negative. One point replaces 600,000 tweets, smooths noise, still shows drift. Optional 15-min sliding window for a smoother trend.

    (b) Drift: line chart (or 100% stacked area) per topic as small multiples. Clustering: t-SNE/UMAP scatter drawn as hexbin or KDE to avoid overplotting.

    (c) Send only window aggregates (one refresh of 5 s replaces 50,000 tweets); keep a rolling buffer of the last 60 points; throttle redraws; pre-bin the cluster view server-side.

    (d) X API → Kafka → Spark Structured Streaming/Flink → InfluxDB/Prometheus or Elasticsearch → Grafana (5 s poll) or Kibana; WebSocket → D3.js for sub-second views.

  14. Data quality is a visualisation problem: the NYT's biggest engineering effort was cleaning data, not drawing charts; retroactive state corrections forced D3 charts to support negative bars (days where cases were revised down)

    See the diagram on the topic “Case study: NYT COVID-19 tracker”

    Claim: a chart is only as right as its data.

    For: most NYT work was normalising 50 state schemas; downward revisions made daily changes negative, so chart design had to show negative bars.

    Against: cleaning is really a data-engineering task, and no chart design can fix bad source data. Even so, the chart must show corrections honestly (negative bars) rather than hide them.

  15. Accessibility is non-negotiable at 6M readers/day: every chart had a data table alternative for screen readers; colour scales were tested for colour-blindness (deuteranopia, protanopia)

    Claim: at 6 M readers a day, even a small share of blind or colour-blind readers is many people.

    For: a screen reader cannot describe the shapes of a chart, so a data table gives blind readers the same facts; avoiding red/green scales serves red-green colour-blind readers of public-health data.

    Against: tables and testing cost time on daily deadlines and restrict palettes; the NYT judged it worth paying.

  16. Small multiples beat animation: the 50-state grid (Tufte small multiples) was more actionable than an animated map of spreading cases

    Claim: showing every state at once beats one frame at a time.

    For: a shared scale lets readers compare states side by side and find their own without waiting or remembering frames.

    Against: animation grabs attention and shows geographic spread vividly; 50 small charts can be dense on a phone. Grid for analysis, animation for a headline.

  17. Rolling averages are editorial decisions: choosing 7-day vs. 14-day average changes what story the chart tells; these are journalistic choices with ethical weight

    Claim: the window length shapes the story readers see.

    For 7-day: removes weekend reporting dips and reacts to a real turn within days.

    For 14-day: smoother, fewer false alarms, but hides a turning point longer.

    Readers made health decisions from it, so the choice should be stated on the chart.

  18. GitHub as data infrastructure: publishing the raw CSV on GitHub enabled 1,000+ derivative dashboards worldwide within days

    Claim: open data multiplies the value of expensive cleaning.

    For: others reused it for 1,000+ dashboards; version history makes corrections traceable and numbers checkable.

    Against: GitHub is not a database; others can misread the data, and the publisher must keep files consistent as corrections arrive.

  19. A Grafana dashboard shows daily API error counts for a Big Data pipeline. Identify three Tufte violations in a dashboard that uses: a 3-D bar chart with a y-axis starting at 500, a heavy grid, and gradient fill colours. Redesign the chart applying data-ink principles. [CLO3 — Apply]
    ViolationPrinciple brokenFix
    3-D barsChartjunk; depth and perspective distort bar heightsFlat 2-D bars (or a line, since daily counts are temporal)
    y-axis starts at 500Lie factor above 1: small differences look hugeStart y at 0
    Heavy gridChartjunk competing with the dataNo grid, or one light reference line (e.g. the error budget)
    Gradient fillChartjunk: colour encodes nothingOne flat colour

    Example: days with 600 and 700 errors are drawn 100 and 200 units tall (+100%) for a real +16.7%: lie factor = 100 ÷ 16.7 ≈ 6.

    Redesign: flat bars or line from 0, light axes, no legend for one series, label the axis directly, hover tooltip with the exact count (details on demand).

    From the lecturer’s files

    This discussion question was in the old (v1) slides' Part 2 only; the current deck keeps just the lessons.

  20. Design a Shneiderman-compliant interactive dashboard for a ride-sharing company's trip data (1M trips/day, 5 cities). Specify the overview view, the zoom/filter interactions, and the details-on-demand panel. Justify each design choice using the mantra. [CLO3 — Design]

    Givens: 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6 trips/s; about 200,000 trips per city per day.

    StageDesignWhy (mantra)
    OverviewKPI row (trips today, completion rate, active drivers) with sparklines; 5-city small multiples of trips per hour on one scale; pickup map as a hexbin (1 M points would overplot)The whole picture first, so the user sees which city or hour needs attention
    Zoom and filterCity selector, date-range slider, hour brush, map zoom to a zone; served from a pre-aggregated cube (city × zone × hour) so each change returns in under 1 sNarrow to the subset of interest only after seeing the overview; dynamic queries must feel instant
    Details on demandHover a hex or bar for count, average wait and fare; click a zone or driver for a table of individual tripsRaw records only when asked, so the screen is not swamped

    Live numbers: Kafka → Spark 1-min windows → time-series DB → Grafana 5 s refresh for the KPI row.

  21. Live Exercise — D3.js Bar Chart with Tufte Styling Task (25 minutes, pairs) Build a minimal D3.js bar chart that follows Tufte's data-ink principles: 1. No gridlines (or only a single light reference line) 2. y-axis starts at 0 3. No fill gradient — use a flat colour 4. Tooltip on hover (Shneiderman: details-on-demand) 5. Add a sparkline for each bar showing the 7-day trend Dataset: weekly Kafka message counts for 5 topics (generate 7×5 random values). Extension: add a dropdown filter to select one topic and zoom into its 7-day line chart.
    <!DOCTYPE html>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<style>
  .bar { fill: steelblue; }
  .bar:hover { fill: #b5651d; }
  .axis path, .axis line {
    stroke: #ccc; stroke-width: 0.5px; }
  .tooltip {
    position: absolute; background: #fff;
    border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 6px;
    font-size: 11px; pointer-events: none; }
</style>
<body>
<script src=
  "https://d3js.org/d3.v7.min.js"></script>
<script>
const topics = ["orders","clicks",
                "errors","logins","search"];
const data = topics.map(t => ({
  topic: t,
  count: Math.floor(Math.random()*50000)
         + 10000
}));
const svg = d3.select("body").append("svg")
  .attr("width", 500).attr("height", 300);
const x = d3.scaleBand()
  .domain(data.map(d=>d.topic))
  .range([50,480]).padding(0.3);
const y = d3.scaleLinear()
  .domain([0, d3.max(data,d=>d.count)])
  .range([260, 20]);
svg.append("g").attr("transform","translate(0,260)")
  .call(d3.axisBottom(x));
svg.append("g").attr("transform","translate(50,0)")
  .call(d3.axisLeft(y).ticks(4));
svg.selectAll(".bar").data(data).join("rect")
  .attr("class","bar")
  .attr("x",d=>x(d.topic))
  .attr("y",d=>y(d.count))
  .attr("width",x.bandwidth())
  .attr("height",d=>260-y(d.count));
</script>

    Key code (added to the skeleton; 7 daily values per topic, bar = weekly sum; SVG height raised to 340 for the sparklines; CSS .ref { stroke: #ddd; stroke-dasharray: 3 3; }):

    const data = topics.map(t => { const days = d3.range(7)
  .map(() => Math.floor(Math.random()*50000) + 10000);
  return {topic: t, days, count: d3.sum(days)}; });
svg.selectAll("g").attr("class","axis");   // skeleton forgot this
const mean = d3.mean(data, d => d.count);  // one light line at the mean
svg.append("line").attr("class","ref").attr("x1",50).attr("x2",480).attr("y1",y(mean)).attr("y2",y(mean));
const tip = d3.select("body").append("div").attr("class","tooltip").style("opacity",0);
svg.selectAll(".bar").on("mouseover",(e,d)=>tip.style("opacity",1)
      .style("left",(e.pageX+8)+"px").style("top",(e.pageY-28)+"px")
      .html(d.topic+": "+d.count))
    .on("mouseout",()=>tip.style("opacity",0));
const sx = d3.scaleLinear().domain([0,6]).range([0,x.bandwidth()]);
data.forEach(d => { const sy = d3.scaleLinear()
  .domain(d3.extent(d.days)).range([325,290]);
  svg.append("path").attr("fill","none").attr("stroke","#555").attr("transform",`translate(${x(d.topic)},0)`)
   .attr("d", d3.line().x((v,i)=>sx(i)).y(v=>sy(v))(d.days)); });
    1. Gridlines: D3 axes draw none; add only one dashed light line at the mean.
    2. y from 0: domain [0, max]; a higher start would push the lie factor above 1.
    3. Flat colour: fill: steelblue, no gradient.
    4. Tooltip: mouseover shows topic and count; mouseout hides it. This is details on demand.
    5. Sparkline: 7-point line, no axes, under each bar, own min-max scale (shape, not size).

    Extension: a select of the 5 topics; on change, fade other bars and draw that topic's 7-day line chart below.

    Expected: 5 flat bars; tallest reaches y = 20 (240 px); bar width ≈ 56.8 px (step 430 ÷ 5.3 ≈ 81.1); weekly totals between 70,000 and 419,993.

From the lecturer’s own files

  1. True or false, with a justification: a Grafana availability panel with an auto-scaled y-axis is fine, because the tick labels show the true values.

    False. Readers judge bar and line height, not tick labels. Auto-scaling to 99.975–99.995% makes a 0.01-point wobble span half the chart's height.

    Example: 99.98% is drawn at 25% of the height and 99.99% at 75%, a 200% visual rise for a real change of 0.01 / 99.98 ≈ 0.010%. The lie factor is 200 / 0.010 ≈ 20,000.

    Start availability and ratio charts at zero, or label the zoomed axis clearly.

    Slides: lie factor, and the y-axis should start at 0. The auto-scaling dashboard case is from the lecturer's textbook (ch 9).

    An analyst reports that four regional sales datasets have the same mean, variance and correlation (r = 0.816), so 'they behave the same'. Another report shows revenue up 5%, but the bar is drawn 40% taller because the y-axis does not start at 0.

Sparklines: word-sized line charts embedded in text or table cells, adding trend context, e.g. a tiny 7-day trend beside each district's case count.

    bKash fraud operations want a live chart of transaction volume. Week 10

Big data in real applications

Learn 6 topics, 6 comparisons and the formulas

  1. In one lineCommunity detection finds groups of nodes more densely linked to each other than to the rest of the graph, usually with the Louvain algorithm.
    Key points
    • Four data dimensions of social media: graph-structured, temporal, text (NLP), multimedia.
    • The graph (who follows or retweets whom) is the main object of analysis, not the single post.
    • Louvain is greedy and local, so it scales to billion-node graphs in Spark GraphX.
    Traps
    • PageRank measures importance, not community membership; K-Means clusters vectors, not graph links.
    • The hop estimate is an upper bound: it counts shared followers again (clustering, overlapping neighbourhoods).
    • Kempe's result: the problem is NP-hard, the greedy answer is approximate (63%), not exact.
    • Sparse means few edges per node, not few nodes.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  2. In one lineVADER is a lexicon-and-rule-based sentiment analyser for social media that outputs a compound score in [−1, +1].
    Key points
    • VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary for Sentiment Reasoning (Hutto & Gilbert 2014), lexicon-and-rule based, tuned for social media text.
    • VADER handles capitalisation, punctuation (!!!), degree words (very, kind of), negation (not good) and emojis.
    • Rules and a lexicon need no labelled training data, so VADER works out of the box on short, noisy posts.
    Traps
    • The slide's cut-offs are strict (> 0.05, < −0.05), so 0.05 itself is neutral by the slide. VADER's own documentation uses ≥ 0.05 and ≤ −0.05, so if a boundary value is asked, state the slide's rule you are using.
    • Trending depends on the ratio to baseline, not on absolute volume.
    • VADER is rule-based, not a deep-learning classifier.
    • LSH here is for detecting trends, not for sentiment.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  3. In one lineProphet is a time series forecasting model that splits a series into trend, seasonality, holidays and noise: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t).
    Key points
    • Time series properties: order matters, autocorrelation, seasonality, trend, non-stationarity (mean and variance change over time).
    • ARIMA(p, d, q): AR uses past p values, I differences d times for stationarity, MA uses past q forecast errors.
    • Shuffling a time series destroys trend and seasonality, so standard i.i.d. regression is invalid.
    Traps
    • A sudden wave is a trend changepoint, not seasonality; h(t) only covers dates you list in advance.
    • Weekly seasonality on weekly data learns nothing: every point is the same weekday.
    • Prophet's default interval is 80%; set interval_width=0.95 for 95%.
    • ARIMA's d is the number of differences, not the number of seasons.
    Be ready to draw this

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  4. In one lineAn anomaly is a data point that does not conform to the expected pattern of the series.
    Key points
    • STL: Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS. Splits a series into trend, seasonal and residual.
    • STL rule: flag a point if |residual| > k × IQR of the residuals (IQR = Q3 − Q1).
    • Removing trend and seasonality first stops a normal winter peak from being flagged.
    Traps
    • Use the absolute value of the residual: big negative residuals are anomalies too.
    • The threshold uses the IQR of residuals, not of the raw series.
    • In Isolation Forest, anomalies have shorter paths, not longer.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  5. In one lineFederated learning trains a model at each hospital and shares only model updates, so raw patient records never leave the site.
    Key points
    • Four modalities: EHR (ICD-10, notes, FHIR), genomics (≈200 GB per genome; 10,000 patients = 2 PB), wearables (per-second), imaging (DICOM, 200 MB-2 GB, unstructured).
    • EHR ML beats physician rules: ICU mortality (random forest, AUROC > 0.90), 30-day readmission (20% fewer), sepsis 6 hours earlier. Needs 1M+ records.
    • Images are binary DICOM files, so they need deep learning (CNN, ViT), not SQL.
    Traps
    • Stored in a file does not mean structured: DICOM images are unstructured.
    • HIPAA is for health data; US financial data falls under GLBA.
    • Federated learning moves the model, not the data; differential privacy adds noise, it does not encrypt.
    • AlphaFold predicts structure from sequence; it is not anomaly or fraud detection.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  6. In one lineSyndromic surveillance uses non-traditional signals, such as posts, pharmacy sales and ER notes, that show illness before a diagnosis is reported.
    Key points
    • Physician-reported cases reach CDC 1 to 2 weeks after symptoms (ILINet: >3,000 sentinel physicians, weekly).
    • Syndromic surveillance uses pre-diagnosis signals: posts peak 7 to 10 days before ER visits; pharmacy antipyretic sales spike 3 to 5 days before confirmation.
    • Outbreaks grow exponentially, so a 1 to 2 week reporting lag is costly.
    Traps
    • GFT did not replace CDC surveillance; it failed and was discontinued.
    • Syndromic signals are early warnings, not ground truth.
    • Twitter enters the post-GFT model as a covariate, not as the main signal.
    • r² = 0.97 was in-sample; it says nothing about future seasons.

    More detail: the full topic, scenarios and longer answers

  7. Key differenceLouvain finds groups of densely connected nodes by maximising modularity, whereas PageRank scores how important each individual node is; K-Means clusters feature vectors, not graphs.
    Louvain (community detection)PageRank
    AnswersWhich community/group is a node in?How important is a node?
    MethodStart each node alone; greedily merge to maximise modularity; aggregate super-nodes; stop when gain is zeroNode importance score (high-PageRank nodes)
    OutputCommunity labelsScore per node
    Complexity / scaleO(n log n); billion-node graphs in Spark GraphXGraphX runs PageRank (W06 P1 s29)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  8. Key differenceTwitter is a directed, mostly non-reciprocal follower graph (22.1% mutual) that behaves like a news medium, while Facebook is a mutual-friendship social network (~100% reciprocal).
    Twitter (Kwak et al. 2010)Facebook
    Graph typeDirected, asymmetricMutual friendship required (undirected)
    ReciprocityOnly 22.1% mutual; 77.9% of users have a non-reciprocating follower~100%
    Size41.7 million users, 1.47 billion edges (2010)3 billion users
    What it isNews medium: 85% of trending topics were headline newsSocial network
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  9. Key differenceARIMA is a classical model that needs a stationary series and expert-chosen (p, d, q), while Prophet decomposes a series into trend, multiple seasonalities and holidays with automatic changepoints, so analysts can fit thousands of series at scale.
    ARIMA(p, d, q)Facebook Prophet
    KindClassical statistical: AR(p) past values, I(d) differencing, MA(q) past errorsAdditive decomposable model y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t)
    StationarityAssumes stationary input (difference d times)Piecewise trend with automatic changepoints
    SeasonalityStruggles with complex multi-seasonal patternsFourier series; multiple seasonalities (annual, weekly, daily)
    Holidays-h(t): user-specified events (Eid, Puja, elections, cricket World Cup)
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  10. Key differenceSTL flags points whose residual after removing trend and seasonality is unusually large, which is interpretable but needs regular seasonality, whereas Isolation Forest flags points that random trees isolate in few splits, with no distribution assumption and Spark-scale speed.
    STL decompositionIsolation Forest
    IdeaDecompose into trend, seasonal, residual (LOESS)Ensemble of random trees isolating points by partitioning feature space
    Anomaly ruleResidual whose |value| > k x IQR of residualsFewer splits to isolate -> shorter path length
    AssumptionWorks well for regular seasonalityNo assumption about data distribution
    StrengthInterpretableScales to millions of observations in Spark MLlib
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  11. Key differenceTraditional surveillance counts physician-reported cases (accurate but 1-2 weeks late), while syndromic surveillance watches non-clinical signals such as tweets, pharmacy sales and searches for earlier but noisier warnings - a supplement, not a replacement.
    Traditional surveillance (ILINet)Syndromic surveillance
    Source>3,000 sentinel physicians report weekly ILI countsSocial media, pharmacy OTC sales, ER chief complaints, search query volume
    Speed1-2 weeks behind real timeTwitter peaks 7-10 days before ER visits; pharmacy 3-5 days before confirmation
    AccuracyGround truthEarly signal; Twitter ~30% higher error
    RoleMain recordSupplement, not replace
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  12. Key differenceHIPAA is the US healthcare-specific law requiring removal of 18 identifiers before research use, while GDPR is the EU's general data-protection law built on data minimisation, purpose limitation and the right to erasure; Bangladesh's PDPA is being modelled on GDPR.
    HIPAA (USA)GDPR (EU)
    CoversHealthcare data: patient records, medical informationPersonal data generally (general knowledge)
    Key requirementDe-identify 18 PHI identifiers before research use; consent requiredData minimisation; purpose limitation; right to erasure
    Bangladesh PDPA (third law)-PDPA: under development, based on GDPR principles; NID-linked records require explicit consent
    DistractorNot financial data (that is GLBA / Basel III)-
    More detail: full table and scenario cue
  13. Prophet model
    y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t)
    trend + seasonality + holidays + noise
    Prophet trend
    g(t) = (k + a(t)ᵀδ) t + (m + a(t)ᵀγ)
    δ slope changes at changepoints, sparse prior
    Fourier seasonality
    s(t) = Σ [aₙ cos(2πnt/P) + bₙ sin(2πnt/P)], n = 1..N
    P = 365.25 yearly, 7 weekly

    Speedup
    T_sequential / T_parallel
    480 min / 12 min = 40× (5,000 SKUs)
    Reach in h hops
    d + d² + … + d^h

    Greedy influence bound
    spread ≥ (1 − 1/e) × optimal ≈ 0.632 × optimal

Practise 15 worked examples from the slides

  1. GivenTwitter: average shortest path 4.12 hops over 41.7 M users. A tweet is retweeted by a high-PageRank account. Assume an average out-degree of 45 and estimate reach within 3 hops.
    1. Hop 1: 45 users.
    2. Hop 2: 45^2 = 2,025.
    3. Hop 3: 45^3 = 91,125.
    4. Total within 3 hops = 45 + 2,025 + 91,125 = 93,195, about 0.22% of 41.7 M users.
    5. It is an overestimate: real networks are clustered (followers share followers), so the same users are counted many times; reciprocity (22.1%) and overlapping neighbourhoods mean paths loop back.
    AnswerUpper bound 93,195 users; an overestimate because of clustering/overlapping neighbourhoods (the tree assumption ignores repeated users).
    Now try one

    A Bangla-language rumour starts at an account whose followers each have 30 followers on average. Given: reach in h hops = d + d^2 + ... + d^h. Reach within 2 hops?

    30 + 900 = 930.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  2. GivenSources: Twitter/Facebook posts and pharmacy purchase records. Validate against DGHS ground truth. Example: 120 pharmacies upload hourly; 2 million posts per day (assumptions).
    1. Ingest: social posts via REST API -> Kafka; pharmacy POS: Kafka producers (real time) or nightly Sqoop from their RDBMS.
    2. Load: 120 pharmacies x 24 uploads = 2,880 files/day; 2 M posts / 86,400 = 23.1 posts/s.
    3. Features: keyword counts (flu, fever, can't taste), VADER sentiment, spike ratio vs baseline per district; pharmacy: daily antipyretic units, ratio to a 7-day baseline.
    4. Model: Prophet with social and pharmacy signals as covariates (they lead by days); validate by back-testing against DGHS case counts week by week.
    5. Ethics: privacy (aggregate by district, de-identify), misinformation-driven false alarms, Bangla-English code-switching bias.
    AnswerKafka ingestion, NLP + pharmacy ratio features, Prophet with exogenous signals, validation on DGHS history, privacy by aggregation.
    Now try one

    Antipyretic sales in a district average 400 units/day over the last 7 days; today 1,000 units sold. Given: spike = today / baseline. Spike ratio?

    1,000 / 400 = 2.5x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  3. GivenA single whole-genome sequence is about 200 GB. A clinical study of 10,000 patients. DICOM images are 200 MB to 2 GB each.
    1. Total = 200 GB x 10,000 = 2,000,000 GB.
    2. = 2,000 TB = 2 PB.
    3. With HDFS 3x replication: 6 PB of raw disk.
    Answer2 PB (6 PB raw with 3x replication).
    Now try one

    A Bangladesh study sequences 2,500 patients at 200 GB each. Given: total = genomes x size. Total storage?

    2,500 x 200 = 500,000 GB = 500 TB.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  4. Given41.7 M users, 1.47 billion following edges, 106 M tweets. 77.9% of users have a follower they do not follow back; 22.1% of relationships mutual. Power law P(k) ∝ k^-2.276. Top 0.05% have >1 M followers. 85% of trending topics are news; median trend lasts 17.5 h.
    1. Average out-degree = 1.47e9 / 41.7e6 = 35.25 follows per user.
    2. Mutual relationships = 22.1% of 1.47 B = 324.87 million.
    3. Top 0.05% of 41.7 M = 20,850 users with >1 M followers.
    4. Power law: doubling k cuts P(k) by 2^2.276 = 4.84x.
    5. Of 200 trending topics, 85% = 170 news, 15% = 30 memes.
    AnswerAverage 35.3 follows per user; 20,850 celebrities; P(k) falls 4.8x when k doubles.
    Now try one

    A graph has 2 million users and 70 million directed edges. Given: average out-degree = edges / users. Compute it.

    70e6 / 2e6 = 35.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  5. Given90-day forecasts for 5,000 store-product SKUs. Sequential Prophet on one machine: 8+ hours. Spark applyInPandas, grouped by sku_id, on a 20-executor cluster: about 12 minutes.
    1. Speedup = 8 x 60 / 12 = 40x.
    2. Models per executor = 5,000 / 20 = 250.
    3. Sequential time per model = 480 min / 5,000 = 5.76 s.
    4. One model at a time per executor would take 250 x 5.76 s = 24 min; the measured 12 min is half that, which implies about 2 models running at once per executor (multi-core executors; inference, not stated on the slide).
    5. Forecast output rows = 5,000 x 90 = 450,000.
    Answer40x speedup; 250 models per executor; 450,000 forecast rows.
    Now try one

    A chain has 12,000 SKUs; Prophet takes 6 s per SKU on one machine. Given: sequential time = SKUs x time per model. How long sequentially?

    12,000 x 6 = 72,000 s = 20 h.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  6. GivenA phrase normally appears 10 times/hour and suddenly 10,000 times/hour: trending regardless of absolute volume. #QurbaniEid showed a 1,200x spike over 6 hours with 92% positive sentiment. A bKash agent's hourly volume jumps from 10 to 10,000 transactions.
    1. Spike ratio = current rate / baseline = 10,000 / 10 = 1,000x.
    2. The rule is relative: a phrase going 1,000 to 10,000 (10x) trends less than one going 10 to 10,000.
    3. #QurbaniEid: if the baseline was 50 per hour, 1,200x gives 60,000 per hour.
    4. 92% positive of 60,000 tweets = 55,200 positive.
    Answer1,000x spike ratio; same arithmetic flags the bKash agent for Isolation Forest review.
    Now try one

    A hashtag's baseline is 25 posts/hour; it now has 15,000/hour. Given: spike = current / baseline. Spike ratio?

    15,000 / 25 = 600x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  7. GivenTrained on 170,000 experimentally determined structures; released 200 million predicted structures (2022). MSA search over 250 million UniProt sequences (>200 GB compressed). Training used 128 TPU v3 cores. Median GDT > 92%.
    1. Predictions per training structure = 200,000,000 / 170,000 = 1,176x.
    2. Average compressed size per UniProt sequence = 200 GB / 250 M = 800 bytes.
    3. Each prediction searches all 250 M sequences to build the MSA, which is why it is a big data problem.
    AnswerAbout 1,176x more predicted structures than training structures; about 800 bytes per sequence.
    Now try one

    A lab predicts 2 million structures from a model trained on 20,000. Given: ratio = predicted / trained. Ratio?

    2,000,000 / 20,000 = 100x.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  8. GivenGradient boosting on discharge records reduces 30-day readmissions by 20%. Streaming sepsis model detects onset 6 hours before clinical criteria. ICU mortality model AUROC > 0.90. Needs 1 million+ records. HIPAA Safe Harbour removes 18 identifiers.
    1. Readmissions: 1,500 per year x (1 - 0.20) = 1,200; 300 avoided.
    2. Sepsis onset by clinical criteria at 14:00 -> model alert at 08:00.
    3. De-identification: a record with name, DOB, phone, NID and zip has all 5 removed under Safe Harbour (part of the 18).
    Answer1,500 readmissions become 1,200 (300 avoided); sepsis flagged 6 hours earlier.
    Now try one

    A Dhaka hospital has 800 readmissions per year. Given: the model cuts readmissions by 20%. How many remain?

    800 x 0.8 = 640.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  9. GivenGFT correlated 45 search queries with ILINet; initial r² = 0.97 on 2003-2008 data. In 2012-13 it over-predicted flu by 2x. Twitter signals arrive 2 weeks earlier than ILINet but with 30% higher error.
    1. r² = 0.97: 97% of variance explained in training (r ≈ 0.985).
    2. Over-prediction by 2x: true ILI rate 3% -> GFT predicted 6%.
    3. Twitter error: if ILINet-based error is 10%, Twitter's is 10 x 1.3 = 13% (30% higher), but 2 weeks sooner.
    4. Three causes (Lazer 2014): big-data hubris, autocomplete changed the features, media coverage drove searches.
    Answerr^2 = 0.97 in-sample, yet a 2x over-prediction out of sample.
    Now try one

    True ILI in a week was 2.4%. GFT over-predicted by 2x. Given: predicted = 2 x true. What did GFT report?

    2 x 2.4 = 4.8%.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  10. GivenChoosing k seed nodes for maximum spread is NP-hard (Kempe et al., KDD 2003); the greedy algorithm guarantees at least (1 - 1/e) of the optimal spread.
    1. 1 - 1/e = 1 - 0.3679 = 0.6321, about 63%.
    2. If the best possible seeding reaches 100,000 users, greedy reaches at least 63,212.
    3. Greedy: repeatedly add the node with the largest marginal gain in spread.
    AnswerGreedy reaches at least 63.2% of optimal.
    Now try one

    A campaign's optimal 10-seed spread is 40,000 users. Given: greedy >= 0.632 x optimal. Minimum greedy spread?

    0.632 x 40,000 = 25,280.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  11. GivenSTL splits a series into trend, seasonal and residual, and flags residuals whose absolute value exceeds k x IQR. Example (not on slide): residual Q1 = -0.65, Q3 = 1.25, k = 3.
    1. IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 1.25 - (-0.65) = 1.9.
    2. Threshold = 3 x 1.9 = 5.7.
    3. New residuals to check (quartiles come from the agent's history): Residuals [1.2, -0.8, 0.5, 2.0, -1.5, 9.4, 0.3, -0.2]: only 9.4 has |r| > 5.7, so that hour is the anomaly.
    AnswerIQR 1.9, threshold 5.7; the residual 9.4 is flagged.
    Now try one

    bKash residuals for one agent have Q1 = -2 and Q3 = 4. Given: IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 6 and k = 2. What is the flag threshold?

    2 x 6 = 12: flag |residual| > 12.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  12. GivenPhysician reports reach CDC 1-2 weeks after symptoms. Twitter posts with 'flu', 'fever', 'can't taste' peak 7-10 days before ER visits. OTC antipyretic sales spike 3-5 days before clinical confirmation. ILINet: >3,000 sentinel physicians; BioSense: 3,500+ EDs.
    1. ER visits peak on 20 October.
    2. Twitter signal peaks 7-10 days earlier: 10-13 October.
    3. Taking 20 October as the clinical confirmation date, the pharmacy spike comes 3-5 days earlier: 15-17 October.
    4. Traditional report reaches CDC 1-2 weeks after symptoms: 27 October to 3 November (if symptoms start 20 October).
    AnswerTwitter about 10-13 Oct, pharmacy 15-17 Oct, ER peak 20 Oct, CDC reports 27 Oct-3 Nov.
    Now try one

    Dengue ER visits in Dhaka peak on 15 September. Given: social posts peak 7-10 days before ER visits. When does the social signal peak?

    5-8 September.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  13. Given156 weekly points (3 years). ili = 5 + 3 sin(2π t / 52 - π/2) + N(0, 0.5), clipped at 0. Fit Prophet with yearly and weekly seasonality, forecast 12 weeks, add an Eid holiday (upper_window 3), change changepoint_prior_scale 0.05 -> 0.5.
    1. t = 0: 5 + 3 sin(-π/2) = 2 (trough).
    2. t = 13: 5 + 3 sin(0) = 5.
    3. t = 26: 5 + 3 sin(π/2) = 8 (peak).
    4. Period 52 weeks = 1 year; 156 / 52 = 3 seasons.
    5. Forecast 12 weeks beyond week 155 (weeks 156-167).
    6. changepoint_prior_scale 0.05 -> 0.5 is 10x looser: the trend bends more easily (more flexible, risk of overfitting).
    7. Discussion Q2: a sudden COVID wave is a trend changepoint, caught by g(t); the changepoint_prior_scale sets how readily new changepoints are accepted.
    AnswerTrough 2 at week 0, mean 5 at week 13, peak 8 at week 26; 3 full seasons; prior scale raised 10x.
    Now try one

    Same formula. Given: sin(2π·39/52 - π/2) = sin(π) = 0. What is the expected ILI at week 39?

    5 + 3 x 0 = 5.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  14. GivenYouTube: 500 hours uploaded per minute. Twitter/X: 500 M tweets/day. BioSense 2019-20: 38 million ED visits; Prophet ran on 60 HHS regions in parallel; 3,500+ EDs. Facebook ran Prophet on 500,000+ series.
    1. YouTube per day = 500 x 60 x 24 = 720,000 hours of video.
    2. Tweets per second = 500e6 / 86,400 = 5,787.
    3. ED visits per ED = 38e6 / 3,500 = 10,857 per season.
    4. 500,000 Prophet series on 1,000 executors = 500 series each.
    Answer720,000 hours/day of video; about 5,787 tweets/s; about 10,857 visits per ED.
    Now try one

    A platform receives 100 million posts per day. Given: per second = daily / 86,400. Rate?

    100e6 / 86,400 = 1,157 posts/s.
    More detail: the other variant and the why question
  15. GivenVADER outputs a compound score in [-1, +1]: positive if > 0.05, negative if < -0.05, otherwise neutral. Sample scores (not on slide): 0.62, 0.04, -0.03, -0.41, 0.05.
    1. 0.62: positive.
    2. 0.04: neutral.
    3. -0.03: neutral.
    4. -0.41: negative.
    5. 0.05: neutral.
    6. Share positive = 1/5 = 20%. Note 0.05 itself is neutral (the rule is strictly greater).
    Answer1 positive, 3 neutral, 1 negative.
    Now try one

    Three tweets score 0.30, -0.06 and 0.05. Given the thresholds, classify each.

    0.30 positive; -0.06 negative; 0.05 neutral.

Test 22 exam questions, then the predicted paper

  1. Facebook's Prophet library is primarily designed for:
    • (a) Graph analytics and community detection in social networks
    • (b) Real-time stream processing of events
    • (c) Time series forecasting with decomposable trend, seasonality, and holiday components
    • (d) Text sentiment classification using deep learning
    (c) Time series forecasting with decomposable trend, seasonality, and holiday components
    Prophet fits y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t).
  2. Which algorithm is most commonly used for community detection in large-scale social network graphs?
    • (a) K-Means clustering
    • (b) PageRank
    • (c) Louvain algorithm
    • (d) ARIMA
    (c) Louvain algorithm
    It maximises modularity in O(n log n); PageRank ranks importance, not groups.
  3. HIPAA in the United States primarily regulates the privacy and security of:
    • (a) Financial transaction data and bank records
    • (b) Healthcare data including patient records and medical information
    • (c) Social media user data and behavioural profiles
    • (d) Government data retention and public records
    (b) Healthcare data including patient records and medical information
    HIPAA is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act; financial data falls under GLBA.
  4. DeepMind's AlphaFold used big data and deep learning to solve:
    • (a) Real-time financial fraud detection at bank-card transaction scale
    • (b) Social network influence maximisation over billion-node graphs
    • (c) The protein structure prediction problem, predicting 3D structure from amino acid sequence
    • (d) Time series anomaly detection in IoT sensor streams
    (c) The protein structure prediction problem, predicting 3D structure from amino acid sequence
    Trained on 170,000 PDB structures with MSAs from 250M sequences; 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
  5. Google Flu Trends successfully replaced traditional CDC flu surveillance and has been used as the primary source ever since.
    False. GFT over-predicted flu by 2× in 2012-2013 and was discontinued.
    Corrected: Google Flu Trends failed, and CDC still relies on clinical reporting, with big data signals only as a supplement.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): Google Flu Trends over-predicted flu by about 2× in 2013 (over-fitted to search terms) and was dropped as a primary source; it only supplements traditional surveillance.

  6. Time series data is order-sensitive: randomly shuffling the records in a time series changes the analysis result.
    True. Autocorrelation, trend and seasonality exist only in time order; shuffling destroys them.
  7. Social network graphs are typically sparse, with most nodes connected to only a small fraction of all possible neighbours.
    True. Real social networks are scale-free (power-law degrees): most nodes have few links and a few hubs have millions. Twitter had 1.47B edges among 41.7M users, about 35 follows each out of millions possible.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): Real social networks are scale-free (power-law degrees): most nodes have few links while a few hubs have millions. So the average degree (about 35 follows among 41.7 M users) is tiny: the graph is sparse.

  8. Medical imaging data such as MRI and CT scans is classified as structured data because it is stored in files.
    False. Being in a file does not make data structured.
    Corrected: MRI and CT scans are unstructured binary DICOM files (200 MB to 2 GB), analysed by deep learning, not SQL.
    From the lecturer’s files

    Model justification (old slides): MRI/CT images are unstructured binary DICOM files with no row-column schema; they need computer-vision models, not SQL.

  9. Describe three types of analysis commonly performed on social media data (e.g., community detection, sentiment analysis, influence maximisation). For each, state one specific ethical risk that arises when the analysis is deployed at scale.
    AnalysisWhat it doesEthical risk at scale
    Community detectionLouvain finds groups more densely linked inside than outside, by maximising modularity.Profiling: group labels expose political or religious ties users never shared.
    Sentiment analysisVADER scores each post in [−1, +1]; > 0.05 positive, < −0.05 negative.Suppressing dissent: flagging people who criticise a government policy.
    Influence maximisationPicks k seed users for widest spread; greedy gives ≥ 63% of optimal.Manipulation: spreading misinformation or microtargeting vulnerable users.

    Safeguard for all three: transparency and purpose limitation.

  10. What is the difference between ARIMA and Facebook Prophet for time series forecasting? Under what conditions would you prefer Prophet over ARIMA? When might ARIMA still be the better choice?

    ARIMA(p, d, q) predicts from past p values and past q errors after differencing d times to make the series stationary. Prophet adds up trend with changepoints, Fourier seasonality and a holiday term: y = g + s + h + ε.

    Prefer Prophet when the series has several seasonalities, holiday effects (Eid, Puja), trend shifts, missing data or outliers, or when thousands of series must be fitted automatically (5,000 SKUs in 12 minutes with applyInPandas).

    ARIMA is still better for a short, stationary series with no strong seasonality and little data, where an expert can tune one important series closely.

  11. Identify three data integration and privacy challenges specific to healthcare big data analytics. For each, describe one technical mitigation strategy (e.g., differential privacy, federated learning, de-identification).
    ChallengeMitigation
    Records carry names, DOB, NID, phone; HIPAA bars research use as-isDe-identification: safe harbour removes the 18 identifiers, or expert determination certifies low risk
    Models need 1M+ records, but data cannot leave each hospital (consent, PDPA)Federated learning: train at each hospital, share only model updates
    Published counts for small areas can reveal one patientDifferential privacy: add calibrated noise to aggregates

    Integration itself: FHIR, Parquet genomics, Kafka wearables and DICOM images meet in one HDFS/S3 lake with a Hive Metastore.

  12. Flu Outbreak Early-Warning System for Bangladesh: Design a big data system to detect flu outbreaks in Bangladesh using Twitter/Facebook posts and pharmacy purchase records from major pharmacy chains. (a) How would you collect and ingest these two data sources? (Specify tools: Kafka, Sqoop, Flume, REST API) (b) What features would you extract from each source for a prediction model? (Name specific NLP features and pharmacy signal metrics) (c) What model would you use, and how would you validate it against ground-truth CDC/DGHS surveillance data? (d) What are the ethical risks of this system? How would you mitigate them?

    Design: sources → Kafka → Spark Streaming → alert engine + Grafana (the CDC pattern).

    PartSocial postsPharmacy sales
    (a) IngestREST APIs (X API v2, Facebook Pages), keyword filter in Bangla and English, producer writes to Kafka topic social_rawSqoop for nightly bulk import from the chains' databases; Flume ships POS logs to Kafka topic pharmacy_sales
    (b) FeaturesDaily flu-keyword post count per district; share of symptom terms (fever, cough, 'jor'); first-person illness flag; VADER/Bangla sentiment; ratio to 4-week baselineDaily paracetamol and cough-syrup units per district; week-on-week % change; z-score vs same week last year

    (c) Model: Prophet per district on DGHS weekly ILI counts, yearly seasonality, Eid holidays, social and pharmacy features as extra regressors; run districts in parallel with applyInPandas. Validate with a rolling backtest against DGHS counts: error (MAE), lead time, hit rate, false alarms, and test on an unseen season (GFT had r² = 0.97 in-sample and still failed).

    (d) Ethics: privacy (keep district counts only, drop user IDs, add differential-privacy noise); panic from false alarms (an officer confirms before any announcement); bias against rural and older people who post less (weight with pharmacy and DGHS data); misuse for watching individuals (purpose limitation, access logs, PDPA consent).

  13. Retail Demand Forecasting Pipeline: A large Bangladeshi supermarket chain needs 90-day demand forecasts for 5,000 store–product SKU combinations. Design the end-to-end big data pipeline: (a) data ingestion from POS systems; (b) storage and partitioning strategy in HDFS/S3; (c) forecasting model choice (ARIMA vs. Prophet vs. LSTM) and justification; (d) how you parallelise model fitting across 5,000 SKUs using Spark; (e) how forecasts are served to the inventory management dashboard. Identify the primary bottleneck in your pipeline.
    StageDesign
    (a) IngestTills send sale events to Kafka topic pos_sales; Sqoop bulk-loads history; Spark aggregates to (sku_id, date, units)
    (b) StorageRaw Parquet on HDFS/S3 partitioned by date; daily aggregate Hive table partitioned by date, bucketed by sku_id; forecasts partitioned by run_date
    (c) ModelProphet: weekly and yearly seasonality, holidays (Eid, Puja, Pohela Boishakh), automatic changepoints, tolerates gaps. ARIMA needs hand tuning per series; LSTM needs much data, GPUs and is a black box
    (d) Parallel fitdaily.groupBy("sku_id").applyInPandas(fit, schema); each group goes to one task, Prophet fits inside the Pandas UDF
    (e) ServeWrite Parquet to Hive/S3; load latest run into a serving table; dashboard (Superset/Grafana) shows yhat with bands and reorder alerts

    Numbers: 8 h = 480 min sequential; 12 min on 20 executors; speedup = 480 / 12 = 40×; 5.76 s per model; 250 models per executor. One at a time that is 250 × 5.76 = 1,440 s = 24 min, so the slide's 12 min implies about 2 models at once per executor (40 slots).

    Bottleneck: model fitting (Prophet via Stan, the 8-hour step). Skewed SKUs with long histories finish last; cap history and add cores.

  14. Kwak et al. found Twitter's average shortest path is 4.12 hops over 41.7M users. If a misinformation tweet is retweeted by a high-PageRank account, estimate how many users it reaches within 3 hops assuming an average out-degree of 45. What graph property makes this estimate an overestimate? [CLO4 — Apply]

    Estimate: 45 + 45² + 45³ = 45 + 2,025 + 91,125 = 93,195 users (0.22% of 41.7M).

    For an overestimate: clustering. Followers overlap, so the tree counts the same people again; most viewers also do not retweet.

    Against: a high-PageRank account may have over a million followers, so hop 1 alone can beat 45.

    From the lecturer’s files

    This discussion question appeared in the old (v1) slides' Part 2 too, with the same CLO tag.

  15. A Prophet model for weekly hospital admissions has strong annual and weekly seasonality but misses a sudden COVID-19 wave onset. Identify which Prophet component should detect this changepoint and explain what prior hyperparameter controls the model's sensitivity to new changepoints. [CLO4 — Analyse]

    Component: the trend g(t). A wave is a structural break, not a repeating cycle or a listed holiday.

    Hyperparameter: changepoint_prior_scale, the scale of the sparse prior on the slope changes δ. Default 0.05 keeps the trend stiff and smooths over the wave; raising it (e.g. 0.5) lets the trend bend.

    Against raising it: the trend then chases noise and the forecast band widens, so tune on held-out weeks.

  16. Design a dengue fever surveillance system for Bangladesh using BioSense-style ED data, Twitter signals, and Prophet forecasting. Specify: data sources, pipeline architecture (Kafka + Spark), model inputs, and how you would validate the system before policy use. [CLO4 — Design]
    • Sources: ED visits (FHIR) as main signal, NS1 lab results, dengue tweets as leading signal, rainfall.
    • Pipeline: Kafka topics → Spark Streaming de-identifies and aggregates per district → Parquet → nightly Prophet per district via applyInPandas → alerts + Grafana.
    • Inputs: weekly dengue-like visits, yearly (monsoon) seasonality, Eid holidays, tweets and rainfall as regressors.
    • Validate: backtest on past seasons and an unseen season; compare with and without Twitter.

    For: earlier warning. Against: tweets skew urban and young, so ED data stays primary.

  17. Live Exercise — Prophet Flu Forecasting in Python. Task (25 minutes, pairs): Fit a Prophet model to synthetic weekly flu incidence data and produce a 12-week forecast. Install: pip install prophet matplotlib pandas
    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from prophet import Prophet
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.date_range("2021-01-04",
                      periods=156, freq="W")
# Annual flu seasonality + noise
ili = (5 + 3*np.sin(
          2*np.pi*np.arange(156)/52
          - np.pi/2)
       + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 156)).clip(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({"ds": dates, "y": ili})

# Optional: add Eid holiday
holidays = pd.DataFrame({
   "holiday": "Eid",
   "ds":       pd.to_datetime([
                 "2021-05-13","2022-05-03",
                 "2023-04-22"]),
   "lower_window": 0,
   "upper_window": 3,
})

m = Prophet(
    yearly_seasonality=True,
    weekly_seasonality=False,
    changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,
    holidays=holidays)
m.fit(df)
future = m.make_future_dataframe(
    periods=12, freq="W")
forecast = m.predict(future)
m.plot(forecast)
m.plot_components(forecast)
plt.show()

    Run the skeleton, then refit with the changes below.

    m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True,
            weekly_seasonality=False,
            changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,   # try 0.5
            holidays=holidays,
            interval_width=0.95)            # 95% band
m.fit(df)
fc = m.predict(m.make_future_dataframe(periods=12, freq="W"))
m.plot(fc); m.plot_components(fc)

    Expected: dates run 2021-01-10 to 2023-12-31 (weeks end Sunday); the forecast covers 2024-01-07 to 2024-03-24 and rises from the yearly low (true curve 2.0) towards about 4.3.

  18. Generate 3 years of synthetic weekly ILI data with annual seasonality + noise.
    The skeleton does it: 156 weekly dates (156 / 52 = 3 years), a sine with period 52 weeks running from 2 to 8 around a mean of 5, plus noise with SD 0.5. Columns must be named ds and y.
  19. Fit Prophet with yearly and weekly seasonality.
    yearly_seasonality=True fits the annual Fourier wave (P = 365.25). Keep weekly_seasonality=False: with one point per week, always a Sunday, there is no within-week pattern to learn.
  20. Plot the forecast with 95% uncertainty intervals.
    Pass interval_width=0.95 (default is 80%), then m.plot(forecast). Expected: data dots, the yhat line and a band from yhat_lower to yhat_upper that widens into the future.
  21. Add a holiday for “Eid” (spike in healthcare visits) and observe the effect.
    Expected effect is near zero: the synthetic data has no Eid spike, and the 2022 window (05-03 to 05-06) contains no Sunday, so it matches no point. Add +3 to the Eid weeks and the components plot shows an Eid bar near +3.
  22. Change changepoint_prior_scale from 0.05 to 0.5 and compare trend flexibility.
    At 0.05 the trend stays nearly flat around 5 (the true trend). At 0.5 it wiggles, absorbs noise and part of the seasonal wave, and the future band widens. Higher reacts faster to real breaks but overfits stable data.

Predicted paper

  1. Write it closed book, then tap each part to check.

    (a (OR))5 marks (tap for the answers)
    A Bangladeshi supermarket chain needs 90-day demand forecasts for 5,000 store-product SKUs. Sales jump in Eid weeks and follow weekly and yearly cycles.
    1. i)
      Why can't time series be treated like ordinary i.i.d. rows? (1)
    2. ii)
      Why choose Prophet over ARIMA here? (1.5)
    3. iii)
      For one SKU in an Eid week the fitted components are g = 500, s = +40, h = +150, e = 0. What is the forecast? (1)
    4. iv)
      How does Spark fit all 5,000 models in parallel? (1.5)
    1. i)
      Order matters (shuffling destroys the signal) and values are autocorrelated (today depends on yesterday), with trend and seasonality. Regression that assumes independent rows is invalid.
    2. ii)
      ARIMA needs a stationary series, struggles with multiple seasonalities, and needs expert choice of (p, d, q) per series, which cannot be done by hand for 5,000 series. Prophet handles trend changepoints, several seasonalities and a holiday list (Eid) with interpretable parameters.
    3. iii)
      y = g + s + h + e = 500 + 40 + 150 + 0 = 690 units.
    4. iv)
      Load all series into one DataFrame, groupBy(sku_id), and call applyInPandas with a function that fits Prophet and forecasts. Each SKU's group goes to one task as a Pandas DataFrame, so the independent fits run in parallel across executors; results are written as Parquet. The slide reports 8 h -> about 12 min on 20 executors.
    (b (OR))5 marks (tap for the answers)
    The health ministry builds a flu early-warning system from tweets, pharmacy paracetamol sales and ER triage notes. Overnight the phrase 'fever' rises from 40 to 12,000 posts an hour.
    1. i)
      Name two syndromic signals and how far ahead of confirmation each peaks. (1)
    2. ii)
      Why did Google Flu Trends fail, and what lesson does that give this system? (1.5)
    3. iii)
      Compute the spike ratio. Is the phrase trending? (1)
    4. iv)
      Give two privacy safeguards for linking pharmacy and ER records. (1.5)
    1. i)
      Social media posts: 7-10 days before ER visits. Pharmacy OTC antipyretic sales: 3-5 days before clinical confirmation. (ER chief complaints via NLP and search volume are also on the slide.)
    2. ii)
      GFT over-predicted flu by about 2x in 2012-13. Lazer et al. gave three causes: big data hubris (r² = 0.97 on the training years did not generalise), algorithm confounding (Google's autocomplete changes shifted the search features), and media amplification (flu news drove searches even when incidence was low). Searches are a proxy for health anxiety, not incidence. Lesson: syndromic data gives early signals that supplement, not replace, clinical surveillance.
    3. iii)
      Spike ratio = current / baseline = 12,000 / 40 = 300x. Yes: trending is judged against the phrase's own baseline, not absolute volume.
    4. iv)
      Any two: de-identification (safe harbour: remove the 18 HIPAA identifiers such as name, NID, phone); differential privacy (calibrated noise on aggregate counts); federated learning (train at each hospital without moving raw records); explicit consent for NID-linked data under PDPA.

    Open it in the mock papers

  2. Write it closed book, then tap each part to check.

    (a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
    A research group tracks Bangla and English posts on X during an election week. They score posts with VADER and look for groups of accounts that retweet each other heavily.
    1. i)
      Why use VADER rather than a generic sentiment model? Give two features it handles. (1)
    2. ii)
      Three posts score compound 0.31, -0.02 and -0.47. Classify each. (1)
    3. iii)
      Give the steps of the Louvain algorithm. (1)
    4. iv)
      Give one ethical risk of this analysis. (1)
    1. i)
      VADER is a lexicon-and-rule analyser tuned for social media. Any two: capitalisation (GREAT > great), punctuation (great!!!), degree modifiers (very good), negation (not good), emojis.
    2. ii)
      Positive if > 0.05, negative if < -0.05, else neutral: 0.31 positive, -0.02 neutral, -0.47 negative.
    3. iii)
      Start with each node as its own community; greedily move each node into the neighbouring community that most increases modularity; aggregate communities into super-nodes and repeat; stop when modularity no longer increases. About O(n log n).
    4. iv)
      Sentiment scoring of political speech can be used to suppress dissent (flag negative posts about the government) or to micro-target vulnerable users; needs transparency and purpose limitation.
    (b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
    A hospital group forecasts weekly admissions with Prophet and also flags unusual weeks. Its model has strong yearly and weekly seasonality but missed the sudden onset of a COVID-19 wave. The residuals after STL decomposition have IQR = 4.
    1. i)
      Write Prophet's model and name each term. (1.5)
    2. ii)
      What do p, d and q mean in ARIMA, and why is ARIMA a weak fit here? (1.5)
    3. iii)
      Flag residuals beyond k x IQR with k = 3. Weeks have residuals 15 and -9. Which is an anomaly? (1)
    4. iv)
      Which Prophet component should catch the COVID wave, which hyperparameter controls it, and how does Isolation Forest find anomalies? (2)
    1. i)
      y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t): g = trend (piecewise linear or logistic, with changepoints), s = seasonality (Fourier series, yearly/weekly), h = holidays and events (e.g. Eid), e = residual noise.
    2. ii)
      AR(p): depends on the past p values; I(d): difference d times to make the series stationary; MA(q): depends on the past q forecast errors. ARIMA assumes stationarity, handles multiple seasonalities poorly and needs manual (p, d, q) choice per series.
    3. iii)
      Threshold = 3 x 4 = 12. |15| > 12, so that week is an anomaly; |-9| = 9 < 12, so it is not.
    4. iv)
      The trend g(t) through its changepoints. changepoint_prior_scale sets the sparse prior on the slope changes: raising it (e.g. 0.05 -> 0.5) makes the trend more flexible. Isolation Forest builds random trees that partition the data; anomalies need fewer splits to isolate, so they have shorter average path lengths.

13 October

Exam morning

  1. Must-know list plus the formula sheet, recalled from memory first and then checked.

    • YARN: RM = one per cluster (Scheduler + ApplicationsManager); NM = one per node (containers, heartbeat); AM = one per application (requests containers). Hadoop 2.0 (2013) replaced the JobTracker (MR only, ~4,000 nodes).
    • Container = {vCPU, RAM} slice on one node; NM kills a container that exceeds its memory limit.
    • YARN failures: NM -> missed heartbeat, containers marked failed, AM re-requests; AM -> RM restarts it (max attempts, default 2); RM -> HA with ZooKeeper (active + standby).
    • Schedulers: FIFO (starves), Capacity (guaranteed queue %, borrows idle capacity), Fair (equal shares, short jobs finish fast). DRF = fairness over CPU and RAM.
    • Containers per queue = min(queue RAM / container RAM, queue vCPU / container vCPU); the smaller one is the bottleneck.
    • Columnar: read = D x k/N; 10 TB, 3 of 100 columns -> 300 GB, 97% less, ~33x.
    • Parquet: row groups (~128 MB) -> column chunks -> pages; footer min/max stats -> predicate pushdown skips row groups.
    • Avro = row, schema evolution (reader/writer schema), Kafka ingest. Parquet = columnar, Spark analytics. ORC = columnar, Hive, highest compression.
    • Gzip is NOT splittable (1 Mapper per file). Bzip2 splittable; LZO splittable with index; Snappy fast (splittable inside Parquet row groups).
    • Spark beats MR on iteration: MR = k x (read + write) on HDFS; Spark reads once and caches. 50 GB x 100 iterations: 10 TB vs 50 GB.
    • Spark architecture: Driver (SparkContext/SparkSession, builds DAG) -> Cluster Manager (YARN/K8s/Mesos/Standalone) -> Executors (tasks + cache).
    • RDD = read-only, partitioned collection created from stable storage or other RDDs; immutable, partitioned, lazy, lineage, resilient (recompute, not replicate).
    • Transformations (lazy): map, filter, flatMap, reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, distinct. Actions: count, collect, first, take, reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach.
    • Lazy evaluation lets Spark pipeline narrow steps and stop early: filter(x > 1000).first().
    • Narrow (1 parent partition, same stage): map, filter, union, coalesce. Wide (shuffle, new stage): groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, repartition, distinct, sortByKey.
    • reduceByKey > groupByKey: it combines locally before the shuffle. Hash partitioner = key.hashCode() % numPartitions.
    • DataFrame = named columns + schema, Catalyst optimiser. HBase is NOT part of the Spark ecosystem.
    • Hive: HiveServer2 (JDBC/ODBC) -> Driver (parse -> semantic -> logical -> optimise -> physical) -> engine MR/Tez/Spark; Metastore (MySQL/PostgreSQL) holds schemas, partitions + HDFS paths, SerDe, stats.
    • Schema-on-read (Hive): schema applied at query, bad value -> NULL, fast load. Schema-on-write (RDBMS): rejected at INSERT. HiveQL: limited ACID (ORC transactional only), minutes of latency. Lecturer's plan: Hive vs SQL is an important exam topic.
    • Partitioning = HDFS sub-directory per value, prunes scans; low-cardinality columns only (user_id -> partition explosion). Dynamic insert: partition columns last in SELECT.
    • Bucketing = hash(col) % N files; bucket map join (same key, same N) avoids a shuffle. Fraction read = partitions read / total.
    • Map-side aggregation: 50 M rows, 200 countries -> 250,000x less shuffle.
    • Presto: in-memory pipeline (no intermediate disk), vectorised 1,024-row batches, cost-based optimiser, connectors.
    • Point-to-point ETL = N(N-1) jobs (50 -> 2,450); bus = N connections.
    • Sqoop = bulk RDBMS <-> HDFS via a MapReduce job whose map tasks each read a primary-key range, incremental last-value. Flume = Source -> Channel (memory/file) -> Sink, logs to HDFS.
    • Kafka = distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Topic -> partitions (ordered, same key -> same partition) -> offsets; consumer tracks its own offset; retention (e.g. 7 days) -> replay from offset 0.
    • RF = R survives R - 1 broker failures; one leader + R - 1 followers. In a consumer group, each partition goes to exactly one consumer (extra consumers idle).
    • Kafka speed: sequential appends (~600 vs ~100 MB/s), zero-copy sendfile (4 -> 2 copies), batching, consumer pull. 50.5 MB/s / 100 B = 505,000 msg/s.
    • Lambda (Marz): Batch (HDFS, accurate, hours) + Speed (stream, seconds, approximate) + Serving (merge). Weakness: two code paths (30-40% effort).
    • Kappa (Kreps): one stream code path over a durable log; reprocess = new job from offset 0, catch up, swap. Not for very slow TB-scale replay, batch-SQL preference, or mandated batch reconciliation.
    • Data lake = raw data, any format, schema-on-read; layers: ingestion, storage, processing, catalogue/governance. No governance -> data swamp.
    • Tufte: data-ink ratio = data ink / total ink (maximise); chartjunk (3-D, gradients, heavy grids, ducks); small multiples; sparklines; lie factor = effect shown / effect in data (1 = truthful).
    • Shneiderman: 'Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand'; 7 data types: 1-D, 2-D, 3-D, temporal, multi-dimensional, tree, network.
    • Chart choice: temporal -> line; categories -> bar (pie only if 4 or fewer and part-of-whole); geography -> choropleth; distribution -> histogram/box; correlation -> scatter.
    • Big-data viz challenges: overplotting (alpha -> hexbin -> KDE), latency (data cube / AQP, trade-off staleness), streaming (Kafka -> Spark window -> TSDB -> Grafana poll / WebSocket push).
    • Tools: Grafana = real-time ops; Tableau/Power BI = business BI; D3.js = custom web SVG; Superset = open-source BI on lakes; Kibana = Elasticsearch logs.
    • Time series: order matters, autocorrelation, trend, seasonality, non-stationarity. ARIMA(p, d, q) = AR lags, differencing, MA errors; needs stationarity and manual tuning.
    • Prophet: y = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t); changepoints in g (changepoint_prior_scale); Fourier seasonality; holidays; scale with groupBy + applyInPandas.
    • Social: Louvain maximises modularity (merge, aggregate, repeat); influence maximisation NP-hard, greedy (1 - 1/e); Kwak: 22.1% reciprocity, 4.12 hops, power law -> Twitter is a news medium. VADER: > 0.05 positive, < -0.05 negative.
    • Health: EHR, genomics (~200 GB/genome), wearables, DICOM (unstructured); HIPAA 18 identifiers, GDPR, PDPA; DP and federated learning. GFT over-predicted 2x: syndromic data supplements, never replaces.

Week 5

YARN, file formats and compression

How a shared Hadoop cluster hands out CPU and RAM to many jobs (YARN), and how the way data is laid out and compressed on disk decides how much of it a query has to read. Part 2 tests the same ideas on LinkedIn's 5,000-node YARN cluster.

  2. YARN fault tolerance
  3. Schedulers and capacity planning
