Compare: 82 pairs

Pairs the slides set against each other. Each shows the key difference; tap it for the table and the scenario cue that tells you which side a question means. The most likely pairs come first.

Most likely to come up

Hadoop 1.x (JobTracker) vs Hadoop 2.x (YARN)

Key differenceHadoop 1.x's single JobTracker mixed resource management with MapReduce job scheduling (MapReduce only, ~4,000-node ceiling); YARN (Hadoop 2.0, 2013) split this into a global ResourceManager and a per-job ApplicationMaster, so any framework can share a 10,000+ node cluster.
Hadoop 1.x (JobTracker)Hadoop 2.x (YARN)
DesignJobTracker = resource mgmt + job scheduling in one monolithResourceManager (global scheduler) separated from per-job ApplicationMaster
Max nodes~4,000>10,000
FrameworksMR onlyAny (Spark, Tez, Samza ...)
Resource unitSlot (fixed)Container (flexible)
AMIn JobTrackerPer-app process
RM HANoYes (ZooKeeper)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a cluster that can only run MapReduce, stalls near 4,000 nodes, or one daemon doing both scheduling and job tracking, the answer is Hadoop 1.x / JobTracker; if Spark, Tez and MapReduce share one cluster, it is YARN.
Week 5, slides P1 s7, s9; P2 s4, s6, s12; P1 s29 (MCQ Q4)
Topic: YARN and its three components

ResourceManager (RM) vs ApplicationMaster (AM)

Key differenceThe ResourceManager is the single global scheduler that hands out containers for the whole cluster, while an ApplicationMaster is a per-job process that negotiates containers from the RM and runs that one job's tasks.
ResourceManager (RM)ApplicationMaster (AM)
How manyOne per cluster, on a dedicated master nodeOne per running job (application)
RoleGlobal cluster resource schedulerThe job's own scheduler
Parts / dutiesScheduler (allocates containers; FIFO/Fair/Capacity) + ApplicationsManager (accepts jobs, starts first container for each AM)Requests containers from RM, tells NM to launch tasks, monitors progress, re-requests for failed tasks, releases containers
Framework knowledgeFramework-agnosticHolds the framework-specific logic (MR AM, Spark AM, Tez AM, Samza AM)
If it failsYARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper Active/Standby RM, failover < 60 sRM restarts the AM (max attempts, default 2)
Slide exampleGrants 80 containers (cluster busy)Spark AM requests 100 containers (4 cores, 8 GB each)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question says 'one per cluster / decides which application gets which containers', the answer is the ResourceManager; if it says 'one per job / requests containers on behalf of the job / restarts failed tasks', it is the ApplicationMaster.
Week 5, slides P1 s10-11; P2 s7, s11; P1 s28 (MCQ Q1 note)
Topic: YARN and its three components

NodeManager failure vs ApplicationMaster failure

Key differenceA NodeManager failure is caught by the RM through missed heartbeats and the job's AM re-requests the lost containers elsewhere, whereas an AM failure is handled by the RM restarting the AM itself (default 2 attempts), recovering state from HDFS checkpoints if supported.
NodeManager failureApplicationMaster failure
Detected byRM, via missing heartbeat (>10 min)RM
State changeAll containers on that node marked failedAM attempt counted (yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts, default 2)
RecoveryAM is notified and re-requests containers elsewhereRM restarts a new AM
Job stateTasks re-run in new containersNew AM recovers state from HDFS checkpoints if the framework supports it (MapReduce: yes; early Spark: no)
Third case (RM failure)-YARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper promotes Standby RM in < 60 s
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question traces a worker node (e.g. NM2 with 5 containers) dying mid-job, the answer is the NodeManager-failure path (heartbeat timeout -> containers failed -> AM re-requests); if the job's coordinator dies, it is the AM-restart path.
Week 5, slides P2 s11; P1 s12; P1 s32 (A2)
Topic: YARN fault tolerance

Capacity Scheduler vs Fair Scheduler

Key differenceThe Capacity Scheduler gives each team's queue a guaranteed percentage of the cluster (lending idle capacity), whereas the Fair Scheduler shares resources equally among running jobs so short jobs finish fast; FIFO simply runs jobs in submission order and lets one long job starve the rest.
Capacity SchedulerFair Scheduler
PolicyCluster divided into queues with guaranteed capacity; elastically borrows unused capacityAll jobs get equal share of resources
Slide exampleEngineering 60% / Finance 40%; a2i queues 60/30/10; LinkedIn 6 queues (production 40%)Latency-sensitive short jobs complete quickly even if a large job is running
Default in / used byHDP/CDH; Yahoo!, LinkedInCloudera; Facebook, Twitter
StrengthSLAs: production queue guaranteed minimum; adhoc queries cannot starve revenue pipelinesSmall jobs get fast turnaround
Contrast with FIFOFIFO: one queue, submission order; one long job starves all othersFIFO not suitable for multi-tenant clusters
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes several teams/departments that each need a guaranteed share (e.g. 60% health batch, 30% streaming, 10% ad hoc), the answer is the Capacity Scheduler; if many short interactive jobs must not wait behind a big one, it is the Fair Scheduler; a single queue in arrival order is FIFO.
Week 5, slides P1 s13-14; P2 s10, s17, s21
Topic: Schedulers and capacity planning

Row store (CSV / JSON / Avro) vs Columnar store (Parquet / ORC)

Key differenceA row store keeps each record's fields together so any query reads every column, while a columnar store keeps each column together so a query reads only the columns it needs (3 of 100 columns -> ~3% of the data).
Row store (CSV / JSON / Avro)Columnar store (Parquet / ORC)
Layout on diskRecord by record (id, name, age, score together)Column by column
SELECT score FROM usersReads ALL columnsReads ONLY the score column
100-col, 10 TB table, 3-col queryCSV reads all 10 TBParquet reads ~300 GB (33x speedup; 97% I/O reduction)
Filter skippingNoneMin/max stats per row group -> predicate pushdown skips row groups
Best forPortability, small data; row-append streaming ingest (Avro)Analytical, read-heavy workloads (Spark, Presto, ML, Hive)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes an analyst query that touches a few columns of a very wide table and is slow on CSV, the answer is to switch to columnar (Parquet/ORC); if it describes appending whole events or exchanging records, a row format (Avro/CSV) fits.
Week 5, slides P1 s6, s16, s17, s22-23; P1 s30 (T/F 1), s31 (D2)
Topic: Row vs columnar storage and Parquet

Avro vs Parquet

Key differenceAvro is a row-oriented format whose reader/writer schema handles schema evolution, so it suits append-heavy streaming ingest, whereas Parquet is columnar with per-row-group statistics, so it suits analytic reads that select few columns and filter.
AvroParquet
OrientationRowColumnar
SchemaSelf-describing (JSON); reader vs writer schemaSelf-describing
Key strengthSchema evolution: missing fields use defaults, extra fields ignored (backward + forward compatible)Row groups (~128 MB) with min/max stats -> predicate pushdown
CodecSnappy / DeflateSnappy / Gzip
Best forStreaming ingest Kafka -> HDFS; data exchangeSpark analytics, Presto, ML pipelines
bKash strategyIngest layer (API versioning)Analytics layer, converted nightly (Parquet+Snappy)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes LinkedIn adding a new field to Kafka events without breaking old consumers, the answer is Avro; if it describes analysts running Spark/Presto queries over a few columns, it is Parquet.
Week 5, slides P1 s17-18, s21, s25-26; P1 s31 (D3)
Topic: File formats: Avro, Parquet, ORC

Splittable (Parquet+Snappy, bzip2, LZO+index) vs Not splittable (Gzip CSV)

Key differenceA splittable file can be read from any point so many Mappers work on it in parallel, whereas a gzip-compressed CSV must be decompressed from the start, so one Mapper reads the whole file.
Splittable (Parquet+Snappy, bzip2, LZO+index)Not splittable (Gzip CSV)
DefinitionHDFS can start reading from any point in the file without decompressing from the beginningMust decompress from the beginning
10 GB fileMultiple Mappers process different parts simultaneously (e.g. 3 row groups -> 3 Mappers)Exactly 1 Mapper - no parallelism
WhyParquet splits at row-group boundaries; bzip2 natively splittableMapReduce cannot split across gzip boundaries even though HDFS stores it in blocks
BenefitEnables data-local task scheduling-
Slide verdictBest practice: Parquet + Snappy for analytics'The Gzip Trap - very common mistake'; avoid raw gzip on large CSV
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a big gzip CSV processed by a single slow Mapper (e.g. telecom CDRs taking 6 hours), the answer is 'not splittable - convert to Parquet+Snappy (or bzip2)'.
Week 5, slides P1 s20-21, s25, s29 (MCQ Q3), s30 (T/F 3), s32 (A1)
Topic: Compression codecs and splittability

Snappy vs Gzip

Key differenceSnappy trades a medium compression ratio for high speed, whereas Gzip compresses more but slowly; neither is splittable on raw files, so both are used inside splittable containers like Parquet.
SnappyGzip
SpeedFastSlow
RatioMediumHigh
Splittable?No (but Parquet row groups are)No
Matrix useAvro ingest; Parquet Spark analyticsParquet ML features
Other codecsLZO: fast/medium, splittable with index; Zstd: fast/high, block-levelBzip2: slowest/highest, splittable; ORC + Zlib for Hive warehouse
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks for a codec for a speed-critical Spark analytics or Kafka ingest pipeline, the answer is Snappy; for storage-heavy ML feature files it lists Gzip; for cold archive, Zstd; if splittability on a raw file is required, bzip2 or LZO+index.
Week 5, slides P1 s20, s25
Topic: Compression codecs and splittability

MapReduce vs Spark

Key differenceMapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS, so iterative jobs pay disk I/O on every pass, whereas Spark caches the working set in memory as RDDs and recovers from lineage, making iterative work 10-100x faster.
MapReduceSpark
Intermediate storageDisk (HDFS) after every stepMemory (spill to disk if needed)
Iterative algorithmsSlow (disk per iteration); K-Means 100 iters = 10 TB I/OFast (cache RDD; 10-100x); 50 GB read once
Fault toleranceRe-execute task from HDFSRecompute from lineage
Programming model / languagesMap + Reduce only; Javamap, filter, join, groupBy, SQL, ML, stream; Python, Scala, Java, R
Streaming / interactiveNot supported natively; not feasible (>30 s)Structured Streaming; Spark Shell (sub-second)
Use whenSingle-pass batch where Spark's ~8 GB/Executor overhead is prohibitive, or stable MR codeML, graph, interactive, streaming, >2 iterations over same data
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes an ML or graph job that loops many times over the same data (K-Means, logistic regression, PageRank), the answer is Spark; a one-pass batch job on a huge cluster with tight memory can stay on MapReduce.
Week 6, slides P1 s6-7, s31-32; P2 s4-5, s10, s16; P1 s34, s36
Topic: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck

HDFS replication (traditional) vs RDD lineage (Spark)

Key differenceHDFS tolerates failures by storing three copies of the data, whereas an RDD stores only how it was derived and recomputes a lost partition from its parents, so there is no replication overhead.
HDFS replication (traditional)RDD lineage (Spark)
What is kept3 copies of the dataThe computation graph (log of transformations)
Recovering a lost partitionRead another copyRe-read the HDFS input for that partition and re-apply the same transformations
OverheadReplication overheadNo data replication overhead - 'the computation is the backup'
Weak spot-Expensive for wide dependencies (many ancestors); checkpoint long chains to HDFS
Slide lesson-Recomputing from lineage is cheaper than maintaining 3x replicated in-memory state
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks how Spark recovers a lost partition without copying data (e.g. an executor holding partitions 3 and 7 crashes), the answer is lineage recomputation; for HDFS block loss, it is replication.
Week 6, slides P1 s13-15; P2 s7-8, s16, s20; P1 s34 (MCQ Q2), s37 (D1)
Topic: RDDs and lineage-based fault tolerance

Transformation vs Action

Key differenceA transformation lazily defines a new RDD and only adds to the DAG, while an action forces the DAG to run and returns a value to the Driver or writes output.
TransformationAction
EvaluationLazy: builds the DAG, does not executeEager: triggers execution of the DAG
ReturnsA new RDDA value to the Driver, or writes to storage
Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, cachecollect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach
RuleNo transformation executes until an action is calledSpark then analyses the full DAG, pipelines, runs only needed partitions
Slide examplerdd.filter(x > 1000) records only.first() stops after the first match
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question shows a chain like filter().map() and asks why nothing ran, the answer is that these are lazy transformations; the first count()/collect()/saveAsTextFile() is the action that triggers the job.
Week 6, slides P1 s17-20; P2 s8; P1 s35 (MCQ Q4), s37 (D2, D3)
Topic: Transformations, actions and lazy evaluation

Narrow dependency vs Wide dependency

Key differenceIn a narrow dependency each child partition needs at most one parent partition, so it pipelines in one stage with no shuffle, whereas a wide dependency needs many parent partitions, forcing a network shuffle and a new stage.
Narrow dependencyWide dependency
Partition mappingEach output partition depends on at most one input partition (1-to-1)Each output partition may depend on multiple input partitions (all-to-all)
Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, union, mapPartitions, coalescegroupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, join (not co-partitioned), repartition, distinct, sortByKey
Data movementNo shuffleShuffle across the network
StagesPipelined within a single stageCreates a stage boundary
RecoveryRecompute only that partition from its single parentMust recompute from all parent partitions (expensive)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question shows a DAG and asks where the stage boundary is, put it at the first wide operation (reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, repartition); map/filter chains stay in one stage.
Week 6, slides P1 s14, s21-22; P2 s9, s16, s20
Topic: Narrow vs wide dependencies, stages and shuffle

reduceByKey vs groupByKey

Key differenceBoth shuffle, but reduceByKey pre-aggregates values on each partition before the shuffle (like a Combiner), so far less data crosses the network than with groupByKey.
reduceByKeygroupByKey
DependencyWide (shuffle)Wide (shuffle)
Before shufflingApplies a local combine (like a MapReduce Combiner)Ships all values per key
Network trafficGreatly reducedLarger
Slide advicePrefer reduceByKeyAvoid when an aggregate is all you need (inference from 'prefer reduceByKey')
How to checkSpark UI (localhost:4040) shuffle read/write bytes - smallerShuffle read/write bytes - larger
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a word count or per-key sum that is slow because of heavy shuffle, the answer is to replace groupByKey with reduceByKey.
Week 6, slides P1 s22; P2 s18 (live exercise Q3)
Topic: Narrow vs wide dependencies, stages and shuffle

DataFrame vs RDD

Key differenceA DataFrame adds named columns and a schema so the Catalyst optimiser can rewrite the query before running it (10-100x faster on structured data), whereas an RDD is schema-less records processed with functional operators.
DataFrameRDD
StructureDistributed collection organised into named columns with a schemaRead-only partitioned collection of records
OptimiserCatalyst (predicate pushdown, join reordering, constant folding)DAG scheduler only
Speed (structured data)10-100x faster than RDDsBaseline
APISQL syntax + Python/Scala method chainingFunctional: map, filter, lambdas
Use whenDefault for structured dataLow-level control needed
RelationshipBuilt on top of RDDs; compiles down to an RDD planRDDs largely replaced by DataFrames/Datasets since Spark 2.0
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes structured tabular data queried with SQL/aggregations, the answer is DataFrame/Spark SQL; if it needs custom low-level per-record control, RDD.
Week 6, slides P1 s26, s36 (T/F 3); P2 s11, s20
Topic: DataFrames, Spark SQL and the ecosystem

Schema-on-write (RDBMS / MySQL) vs Schema-on-read (Hive)

Key differenceSchema-on-write validates data against the table schema when it is loaded and rejects bad rows, while schema-on-read stores raw files as-is and applies the schema only when queried, so bad values silently become NULL.
Very likelyLecturer: important exam topicCLO3
Schema-on-write (RDBMS / MySQL)Schema-on-read (Hive)
When schema enforcedAt INSERT / LOAD timeAt SELECT / query time
Invalid dataRejected immediately (INSERT fails if amount is text)Stored; NULL returned at query ('abc' in amount -> NULL)
Write speed / query speedSlower write (validation); faster queryFast write (raw file copy); slower query (parse per query)
Schemas per dataOne schema per tableMany schemas on same data
Storage formatProprietary (InnoDB pages)Open: ORC, Parquet, CSV, JSON, Avro
Use caseOLTP: e-commerce orders, bankingOLAP: log analysis, batch reporting
From the lecturer’s files

Schema on write vs on read is the first row of the lecturer's “important exam topics” table.

Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes loading raw web logs immediately and defining several tables over them later, or a corrupt column quietly returning NULL, the answer is schema-on-read; if an INSERT is rejected for a type error, it is schema-on-write.
Week 7, slides P1 s13-14; P1 s28 (MCQ Q2), s31 (D3); P2 s6-7
Topic: Schema-on-read and HiveQL vs SQL

SQL (RDBMS) vs HiveQL

Key differenceHiveQL looks like SQL but compiles to distributed batch jobs over HDFS, so it scales to petabytes yet has minute-level latency, limited ACID/UPDATE and no traditional indexes, unlike an RDBMS's millisecond OLTP SQL.
Very likelyLecturer: important exam topicCLO3
SQL (RDBMS)HiveQL
SchemaOn write (checked at INSERT)On read (applied at SELECT)
ACID / UPDATE / DELETEFull; any row, any timeLimited: only ORC tables in ACID (transactional) mode
IndexingB-tree, hash, bitmapPartitions + buckets (no traditional indexes)
Sub-queriesCorrelatedNon-correlated only (some limitations)
LatencyMillisecondsMinutes (MapReduce) / seconds (Tez/Spark)
Execution / data locationSingle-node or MPP; database storage engineDistributed MR/Tez/Spark DAG; HDFS directories
Scale / workloadTerabytes max; OLTPPetabytes; OLAP
From the lecturer’s files

The lecturer's course plan lists this table (schema, ACID, UPDATE/DELETE, indexes vs partitions + buckets, latency) as “important exam topics”.

Spot it in a scenarioIf the question expects millisecond response or row-level UPDATEs from Hive, the answer is the misconception 'HiveQL = SQL'; a COUNT(*) on 1 TB can take 5-10 minutes - use Presto or Spark SQL for interactive latency.
Week 7, slides P1 s16-17; P1 s30 (T/F 1)
Topic: Schema-on-read and HiveQL vs SQL

Partitioning vs Bucketing

Key differencePartitioning splits a table into directories by a low-cardinality column value so WHERE filters skip whole directories, while bucketing hashes a (high-cardinality) column into a fixed number of files so tables bucketed the same way can be joined bucket-to-bucket without a full shuffle.
PartitioningBucketing
Physical unitSeparate HDFS sub-directory per column value (year=2024/month=01/)Fixed number of files (buckets) inside each partition
Decided byValue of the partition columnhash(column) % N
Main benefitPartition pruning: skips non-matching directories, avoids full-table scanBucket map join: bucket i x bucket i, no full sort-merge shuffle
Good columnLow-cardinality, used in WHERE (date, country, region, status)The join key, e.g. user_id (slide example; 'high-cardinality' is general knowledge)
RiskHigh-cardinality key -> partition explosion (100 M directories crash NameNode)Both tables must use same key and same bucket count
DDLPARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT)CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes daily reports filtered by country and date, the answer is partition on (country/date); if it describes repeatedly joining with a 10 M-row user table on user_id, bucket on user_id - often both together.
Week 7, slides P1 s19-24; P1 s29 (MCQ Q3 note), s30 (T/F 2, 4), s31 (D2), s32 (A1)
Topic: Bucketing and bucket map join

Hive (+MapReduce) vs Presto / Trino

Key differenceHive compiles queries into batch MapReduce/Tez jobs that write intermediate results to HDFS (minutes), whereas Presto pipelines data through memory with no intermediate disk writes, giving second-level interactive SQL.
Hive (+MapReduce)Presto / Trino
OriginFacebook, 2008Meta (Facebook), 2013
Execution modelCompiled to MR / Tez / Spark jobsIn-memory pipeline execution (split -> stage -> output)
Intermediate resultsMaterialised to HDFS between every MapReduce stageNo intermediate disk writes
Latency5-15 min (minutes)5-60 sec (seconds); '10x faster than Hive+MapReduce'
OptimisationsPartition pruning, bucketingVectorized execution (1,024-row batches), cost-based optimizer, connector architecture (HDFS, Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3 in one query)
Best forBatch analytics, large ETL jobsInteractive BI dashboards
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes analysts needing sub-minute dashboard queries over petabytes on HDFS, the answer is Presto; a nightly multi-hour ETL is Hive.
Week 7, slides P1 s6, s17, s26; P1 s29 (MCQ Q4 note); P2 s4
Topic: Presto and the SQL-on-Hadoop engines

Point-to-point ETL vs Event-driven pipeline (message bus)

Key differencePoint-to-point ETL wires every pair of systems directly (O(N^2) brittle nightly jobs, no replay), whereas an event-driven pipeline routes everything through one bus like Kafka, so sources and consumers are decoupled, real-time and replayable.
Point-to-point ETLEvent-driven pipeline (message bus)
ConnectionsO(N^2): at 50 systems ~2,450 ETL jobsEach source publishes once to a central bus; consumers subscribe
Schema changeBrittle: breaks its ETL jobsDecoupled
ReplayNone: offline consumer loses dataReplayable from the retained log
LatencyNightly batch, >= 24 hoursReal time
Adding a consumerNew jobs, tightly bound to sourceZero changes to any source system
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes 50 systems with thousands of fragile nightly ETL jobs that break on every schema change, the answer is to replace them with a central Kafka event bus.
Week 8, slides P1 s5-6, s14
Topic: From point-to-point ETL to event pipelines

Sqoop vs Flume

Key differenceSqoop bulk-copies relational database tables to and from HDFS with a parallel MapReduce job, while Flume continuously collects log files from many servers into HDFS through Source-Channel-Sink agents.
SqoopFlume
Direction / dataRDBMS <-> HDFS (Hive, HBase): database tablesLogs -> HDFS: web server, application, IoT logs
TypeBatch (nightly bulk)Batch / micro-batch
MechanismLaunches a MapReduce job; each map task reads a primary-key range; incremental import via last-valueAgent: Source -> Channel -> Sink; fan-in and fan-out
ThroughputGB-TB/hourMB-GB/hour
Slide example01:00 nightly: 10 M bKash rows Oracle -> HDFS Parquetaccess.log from 3 web servers -> /logs/YYYY/MM/DD/
Not forReal-time streaming (use Kafka)-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes syncing 10 million customer records nightly from Oracle to Hadoop, the answer is Sqoop; collecting web-server access logs from many machines into HDFS is Flume.
Week 8, slides P1 s7, s9-12; P1 s32 (MCQ Q1 note), s34 (T/F 1, 4)
Topic: Batch ingestion: Sqoop and Flume

Flume vs Kafka

Key differenceFlume is a specialised log-collection pipe into HDFS, whereas Kafka is a general-purpose durable event log that many consumers can read and replay, which is why Kafka has largely replaced Flume.
FlumeKafka
PurposeOptimised for log collection to HDFSGeneral-purpose event bus
DirectionLogs -> HDFSAny -> Any
ModeBatch / micro-batchReal-time stream
Durability / replayFile channel survives agent crash; no replay (inference: slide credits Kafka with the stronger durability and replay)Stronger durability and replay from any offset
TodayOften replaced by Kafka producers writing directly from applicationsKafka Connect replaces Sqoop and Flume for most use cases
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question needs several independent consumers (fraud, balance, audit) to read the same events in real time and replay them, the answer is Kafka; just shipping server logs into HDFS is Flume.
Week 8, slides P1 s7, s12, s14, s19; P2 s12
Topic: Batch ingestion: Sqoop and Flume

Traditional queue vs Kafka append-only log

Key differenceA traditional queue deletes a message once consumed and the broker tracks delivery, whereas Kafka keeps an append-only log for a retention period and each consumer tracks its own offset, so late or new consumers can replay history.
Traditional queueKafka append-only log
After a message is consumedDeletedRetained for a configured period (days, weeks, or forever)
Late-joining consumerMisses dataReads from offset 0 and replays the entire history
Who tracks read positionBroker (inference from 'the Kafka broker never tracks what a consumer has read')Consumer tracks its own offset; broker never tracks it
Many consumers-Each consumer (group) reads independently at its own offset
Benefit-New pipelines built without re-ingesting from source
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a new analytics team that needs last week's events without re-ingesting from the source database, the answer is Kafka's retained log (start at offset 0).
Week 8, slides P1 s14-15; P2 s5; P1 s32 (MCQ Q2), s34 (T/F 2)
Topic: Kafka: the append-only log

Kafka vs ActiveMQ / RabbitMQ (traditional MOM)

Key differenceActiveMQ and RabbitMQ were built for low-volume transactional messaging with per-message acknowledgements, whereas Kafka uses sequential append-only logs, zero-copy, batching and consumer pull to reach ~10x their throughput with retention and replay.
KafkaActiveMQ / RabbitMQ (traditional MOM)
Designed forSustained 100 MB/s per broker, multi-day retention, replayTransactional messaging: few thousand msgs/sec, guaranteed delivery, complex routing
Producer throughput (paper)50.5 MB/s (505,000 msgs/s)ActiveMQ 4.3 MB/s; RabbitMQ 14.7 MB/s
Consumer throughput22.0 MB/sActiveMQ 4.0; RabbitMQ 8.2 MB/s
AcknowledgementPer batchPer message
Data pathSequential writes + zero-copy sendfile() (2 copies)Disk -> kernel -> user space -> socket -> NIC (4 copies)
ConsumersPull; one log serves all consumersPer-consumer queues
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks why LinkedIn could not use ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ for billions of activity events per day, the answer: they targeted a few thousand msgs/sec without retention or replay; Kafka reached 50.5 MB/s vs 4.3/14.7.
Week 8, slides P2 s4, s9, s11, s22
Topic: Why Kafka is fast

Lambda (Marz, 2011) vs Kappa (Kreps, 2014)

Key differenceLambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer with the same logic implemented twice and merges them in a serving layer, whereas Kappa drops the batch layer and uses one stream-processing code path, reprocessing history by replaying the Kafka log from offset 0.
Lambda (Marz, 2011)Kappa (Kreps, 2014)
Code pathsTwo (batch + stream) - must stay in syncOne (stream only)
Historical reprocessingRe-run batch job on HDFSReplay Kafka log from offset 0
LatencyLow (speed layer) + high (batch layer)Low throughout
ComplexityHigh: two systems, merging layer; 30-40% of effort keeping layers consistentLower: single pipeline
Batch throughput / storageVery high (Spark/Hive on full dataset); HDFS master datasetLimited by stream engine; Kafka (bounded) + S3/Iceberg
Use whenLogic too complex for stream-only; batch ML training; regulatory batch reportsStream engine fast enough to reprocess; single code path worth the stream-storage cost
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a team tired of maintaining the same logic in Spark batch and Spark Streaming, the answer is Kappa; if a regulator mandates separate batch reconciliation or TB+ history is too slow to replay, keep Lambda.
Week 8, slides P1 s21-27; P1 s33 (MCQ Q4), s34 (T/F 3), s35 (D1), s36 (A2); P2 s15, s18
Topic: Lambda and Kappa architectures

Batch layer vs Speed layer

Key differenceThe batch layer periodically recomputes accurate views from the full immutable master dataset (hours stale), while the speed layer processes only recent data with a stream engine to give approximate results within seconds; the serving layer merges the two.
Batch layerSpeed layer
Data handledComplete, immutable master dataset (HDFS); periodically recomputes batch viewsNew data arriving since the last batch job
ToolsHDFS + Spark/Hive (hourly or nightly)Kafka + Spark Streaming / Flink
OutputAccurateApproximate
LatencyHigh: 1-24 hours staleLow: < seconds
NetflixKafka -> S3 -> Spark + Iceberg, ~1 day (ML training, billing)Kafka -> Flink, < 1 minute (dashboards, alerts, A/B counters)
Serving layer (not a processing layer)Query = batch view (up to N hours ago)UNION real-time view (last N hours)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which Lambda layer gives real-time low-latency views, the answer is the speed layer (not the serving layer, which only merges and serves).
Week 8, slides P1 s21-23, s33 (MCQ Q3 note); P2 s15-16

Data lake vs Data warehouse

Key differenceA data lake stores raw data of any format cheaply and applies schema only when read, whereas a data warehouse validates data into a fixed schema before loading (schema-on-write), trading flexibility for clean, fast queries.
Data lakeData warehouse
SchemaNo upfront schema definition (schema-on-read)Schema-on-write: must fit the schema at load (W07 s13)
Data / formatRaw data, any format: structured, semi-structured, unstructured; open files (Parquet, ORC, CSV, JSON, Avro)Validated, structured tables (general knowledge; W07 s13: proprietary storage format)
IngestCheap and quick; transformation on demandSlower writes (validation overhead) (W07 s13)
Storage / processingHDFS or S3/ADLS zones raw -> processed -> curated; Spark, Hive, PrestoEnterprise DW, e.g. Teradata, Oracle (1990s) (W07 P2 s4)
Typical useData science, ML, exploration on raw history (general knowledge)Fixed reports, BI dashboards on cleaned data (general knowledge)
Main riskBecomes a data swamp without governanceRigid: schema must be defined upfront
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes dumping raw logs, images and tables into S3/HDFS for later exploration, the answer is a data lake; cleaned, pre-defined tables for fixed business reports is a warehouse.
Week 8, slides P1 s29-30, s35 (D3); W07 P1 s13; W07 P2 s4
Topic: Data lakes and the data swamp

Data-ink vs Chartjunk

Key differenceData-ink is ink that encodes actual values, while chartjunk is decoration that encodes nothing; Tufte says to maximise the share of data-ink by erasing anything whose removal loses no information.
Data-inkChartjunk
DefinitionInk used to display dataInk that does not convey data
ExamplesBar lengths, data pointsDecorative borders, 3-D effects, gradient fills, redundant legends, heavy gridlines, vibrations, ducks
Erase ruleErasing it reduces informationIf erasing does not reduce information, erase it
EffectRaises data-ink ratio = data ink / total inkLowers the ratio; 3-D distorts quantitative comparison
TrapOne thick bar encoding one value can have a high ratioRatio is about what ink encodes, not how much (not printing cost)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a bar chart with 3-D shading, gradient fills, heavy gridlines and a one-series legend, those are chartjunk - remove them to raise the data-ink ratio.
Week 9, slides P1 s8; P2 s5-6; P1 s26 (MCQ Q1), s29 (D1)
Topic: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, lie factor

Small multiples vs Sparklines

Key differenceSmall multiples repeat the same full chart, on the same scale, for each subset so subsets can be compared side by side, whereas a sparkline is a tiny word-sized trend line placed inline next to a number.
Small multiplesSparklines
WhatSame chart structure repeated across subsets (districts, years) in a grid; trellis/facet chartWord-sized data graphics embedded in text or table cells
ScaleSame axis scale in every panel so magnitudes are comparableTrend shape only, no separate figure
GivesDirect visual comparison across subsetsTemporal context next to a number
Slide exampleDhaka/Ctg/Sylhet 2022 vs 2023 panelsDistrict daily case count with an inline trend
Modern toolsTableau Pages shelf; ggplot2 facet_wrap / facet_gridGrafana stat panel; Bloomberg terminal; GitHub contribution heatmap
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question wants to compare the trend of 50 states or 8 divisions at once, the answer is small multiples; if it wants a trend beside each number in a table, sparklines.

Topic: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, lie factor

Small multiples vs Animation

Key differenceSmall multiples show every subset at once so the eye can compare directly, whereas animation shows one frame at a time and makes the viewer remember earlier frames, so small multiples beat animation.
Small multiplesAnimation
ViewingAll panels visible at onceOne frame at a time
Memory loadEye compares directlyForces the viewer to remember the previous frame
NYT COVID lesson50-state grid was more actionableAnimated map of spreading cases was less actionable
Slide example12 monthly temperature charts in a 3 x 4 grid-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks whether to animate a spreading-disease map or show a grid of state charts, the answer is the small-multiples grid (NYT lesson).

Alpha transparency vs Hexbin aggregation

Key differenceAlpha transparency keeps every point but makes each faint so density shows as darkness (and saturates at extreme density), while hexbin replaces points with hexagon counts, which scales to millions of points.
Alpha transparencyHexbin aggregation
HowEach point drawn at low opacity (alpha = 0.02); dense regions look darker2-D area split into hexagonal grid; count points per hex; colour by count
SophisticationSimplestMiddle
PreservesRelative densityCount per area; 10 M points -> ~10,000 hex cells
WeaknessStill fails at very high densitiesIndividual points inside a cell are hidden (general knowledge)
Interactive at scaleStill draws every pointInteractive and readable
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question has a 10-million-point scatter that is a solid blob and wants an interactive chart with counts, the answer is hexbin; a quick fix for moderate density is alpha.
Week 9, slides P1 s17-18; P1 s28 (T/F 2), s29 (D2)
Topic: Overplotting: alpha, hexbin, KDE

Hexbin vs KDE / 2-D density contour

Key differenceHexbin counts points into discrete hexagonal cells, while KDE estimates a smooth continuous density and draws contours, revealing the shape, modes and tails of the cloud.
HexbinKDE / 2-D density contour
OutputGrid of hexagons coloured by countContour lines or filled contours at probability levels
MethodCounts points in each hexEstimates the continuous probability density of the point cloud
RevealsDensity visible; count per cellShape, modes and tails clearly
SophisticationSecond of threeMost sophisticated of the three
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which overplotting fix best shows the shape and number of peaks (modes) of a distribution, the answer is KDE contours; for counts per area, hexbin.
Week 9, slides P1 s17-18, s29 (D2)
Topic: Overplotting: alpha, hexbin, KDE

Data cube (pre-aggregation) vs Approximate query processing (AQP)

Key differenceA data cube pre-computes exact aggregates in advance so dashboards answer in under a second but can be up to a day stale, whereas AQP samples the live table to give approximate answers in milliseconds.
Data cube (pre-aggregation)Approximate query processing (AQP)
HowMaterialise aggregate tables at all dimension combinations (district x date x product x channel) in advanceReturn a statistically correct estimate by sampling the table
ReadsPre-computed cube (millions of rows), not 100 B-row fact tableA sample
Latency< 1 secondMilliseconds
Trade-offStaleness (up to 24 h; nightly Spark/Hive pre-agg job)Accuracy traded for speed
FitInteractive dashboards on yesterday's dataDashboards, but not financial reconciliation
ToolsSpark / Hive pre-aggregation jobApache DataSketches, BlinkDB
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a Tableau filter over 100 billion Hive rows that must respond in < 1 s and yesterday's numbers are fine, the answer is a data cube; if a fast approximate answer is acceptable, AQP - but never AQP for financial reconciliation.

Poll (Grafana) vs Push (WebSocket + D3.js)

Key differenceGrafana pulls fresh data from the time-series database every few seconds, while a WebSocket + D3 setup has the server push each new value so the chart updates sub-second.
Poll (Grafana)Push (WebSocket + D3.js)
MechanismGrafana polls the TSDB on a scheduleServer pushes updates via WebSocket; browser chart re-renders on each push
Refresh5 s refreshSub-second
Use caseOps dashboards: live driver count every 5 s, server metricsStock tickers, live election counts
EffortNative integration with InfluxDB / PrometheusRequires custom development
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question needs second-level ops monitoring with little coding, the answer is Grafana polling; if it needs sub-second live updates like an election needle, WebSocket push to D3.js.

Tableau vs Grafana

Key differenceTableau is drag-and-drop business BI with only limited scheduled refresh, whereas Grafana is built for real-time operational metrics, polling time-series databases every few seconds.
TableauGrafana
Best forBusiness dashboards, drag-and-drop BIReal-time metrics, ops dashboards
Data sourceSpreadsheets, SQL, Spark, HiveInfluxDB, Prometheus, Elasticsearch
ScaleMillions of rowsMillions of data points
Real-timeLimited (scheduled refresh)Yes (5 s poll)
AudienceBusiness usersOperations / monitoring teams
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes monitoring server metrics and error rates with a 5-second refresh, the answer is Grafana; quarterly business dashboards for managers, Tableau (or Power BI).

Pie chart vs Bar chart

Key differenceA pie chart only works for a few (<= 4) parts of a whole because people judge angles poorly, while a bar chart uses length, which people read accurately, so it wins for comparisons, many categories and time.
Pie chartBar chart
Use only when<= 4 categories and the question is 'what fraction of the whole?'Any comparison; > 5 categories (horizontal bar ordered by value)
PerceptionHumans judge angles and arc lengths poorlyBar lengths judged accurately
Time seriesAvoid (pie listed under Avoid for temporal)Line or bar chart always more readable
3-D variant3-D pie is listed under AvoidGrouped bar for comparison across groups
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question shows a pie chart comparing 8 product categories or months, the answer is to replace it with a (horizontal) bar chart, or a line chart for time.

Louvain (community detection) vs PageRank

Key differenceLouvain finds groups of densely connected nodes by maximising modularity, whereas PageRank scores how important each individual node is; K-Means clusters feature vectors, not graphs.
Louvain (community detection)PageRank
AnswersWhich community/group is a node in?How important is a node?
MethodStart each node alone; greedily merge to maximise modularity; aggregate super-nodes; stop when gain is zeroNode importance score (high-PageRank nodes)
OutputCommunity labelsScore per node
Complexity / scaleO(n log n); billion-node graphs in Spark GraphXGraphX runs PageRank (W06 P1 s29)
K-Means (third distractor)K-Means clusters vectors, not graph topologiesARIMA is a time-series method
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks to find political factions or coordinated bot networks in a follower graph, the answer is Louvain; to rank the most influential accounts, PageRank.

Twitter (Kwak et al. 2010) vs Facebook

Key differenceTwitter is a directed, mostly non-reciprocal follower graph (22.1% mutual) that behaves like a news medium, while Facebook is a mutual-friendship social network (~100% reciprocal).
Twitter (Kwak et al. 2010)Facebook
Graph typeDirected, asymmetricMutual friendship required (undirected)
ReciprocityOnly 22.1% mutual; 77.9% of users have a non-reciprocating follower~100%
Size41.7 million users, 1.47 billion edges (2010)3 billion users
What it isNews medium: 85% of trending topics were headline newsSocial network
CascadesRetweet cascades wide and shallow (one hop from a celebrity)Friendship cascades deep (long chain)
Other findingsPower-law in-degree alpha ~2.276; average path 4.12 hops-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes one-to-many broadcasting where a celebrity's post spreads widely in one hop, the answer is Twitter as a news medium; mutual friendship ties spreading along long chains is Facebook.

ARIMA(p, d, q) vs Facebook Prophet

Key differenceARIMA is a classical model that needs a stationary series and expert-chosen (p, d, q), while Prophet decomposes a series into trend, multiple seasonalities and holidays with automatic changepoints, so analysts can fit thousands of series at scale.
ARIMA(p, d, q)Facebook Prophet
KindClassical statistical: AR(p) past values, I(d) differencing, MA(q) past errorsAdditive decomposable model y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t)
StationarityAssumes stationary input (difference d times)Piecewise trend with automatic changepoints
SeasonalityStruggles with complex multi-seasonal patternsFourier series; multiple seasonalities (annual, weekly, daily)
Holidays-h(t): user-specified events (Eid, Puja, elections, cricket World Cup)
Who tunes itExpert parameter selection (p, d, q); cannot hand-fit 10,000 seriesAnalysts, not statisticians; interpretable parameters; robust to missing data/outliers
Best forShort stationary series, no strong seasonality, small datasetsThousands of business series; one Spark partition per series via applyInPandas
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes 5,000 SKUs with weekly and yearly seasonality and Eid spikes, the answer is Prophet; a short, stationary series with no strong seasonality can use ARIMA.
Week 10, slides P1 s14-17, s31 (MCQ Q1), s34 (D2), s35 (A2); P2 s9-11
Topic: Time series, ARIMA and Prophet at scale

STL decomposition vs Isolation Forest

Key differenceSTL flags points whose residual after removing trend and seasonality is unusually large, which is interpretable but needs regular seasonality, whereas Isolation Forest flags points that random trees isolate in few splits, with no distribution assumption and Spark-scale speed.
STL decompositionIsolation Forest
IdeaDecompose into trend, seasonal, residual (LOESS)Ensemble of random trees isolating points by partitioning feature space
Anomaly ruleResidual whose |value| > k x IQR of residualsFewer splits to isolate -> shorter path length
AssumptionWorks well for regular seasonalityNo assumption about data distribution
StrengthInterpretableScales to millions of observations in Spark MLlib
Slide example-bKash agent: 10 -> 10,000 transactions/hour flagged as possible money laundering
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes millions of mobile agents with no clear seasonal pattern (bKash money laundering), the answer is Isolation Forest; a single seasonal series where you must explain the alert, STL.

Topic: Anomaly detection: STL and Isolation Forest

Traditional surveillance (ILINet) vs Syndromic surveillance

Key differenceTraditional surveillance counts physician-reported cases (accurate but 1-2 weeks late), while syndromic surveillance watches non-clinical signals such as tweets, pharmacy sales and searches for earlier but noisier warnings - a supplement, not a replacement.
Traditional surveillance (ILINet)Syndromic surveillance
Source>3,000 sentinel physicians report weekly ILI countsSocial media, pharmacy OTC sales, ER chief complaints, search query volume
Speed1-2 weeks behind real timeTwitter peaks 7-10 days before ER visits; pharmacy 3-5 days before confirmation
AccuracyGround truthEarly signal; Twitter ~30% higher error
RoleMain recordSupplement, not replace
PipelineClinic -> state health dept -> CDC weekly reportKafka -> Spark Streaming (NLP + aggregation) -> alert engine -> Grafana
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes detecting a flu or dengue outbreak days before hospitals report it, the answer is syndromic surveillance - validated against ILINet/DGHS ground truth.

HIPAA (USA) vs GDPR (EU)

Key differenceHIPAA is the US healthcare-specific law requiring removal of 18 identifiers before research use, while GDPR is the EU's general data-protection law built on data minimisation, purpose limitation and the right to erasure; Bangladesh's PDPA is being modelled on GDPR.
HIPAA (USA)GDPR (EU)
CoversHealthcare data: patient records, medical informationPersonal data generally (general knowledge)
Key requirementDe-identify 18 PHI identifiers before research use; consent requiredData minimisation; purpose limitation; right to erasure
Bangladesh PDPA (third law)-PDPA: under development, based on GDPR principles; NID-linked records require explicit consent
DistractorNot financial data (that is GLBA / Basel III)-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question mentions removing 18 identifiers from US patient records, the answer is HIPAA; a user demanding their data be deleted, GDPR's right to erasure; NID-linked consent in Bangladesh, PDPA.

Also worth knowing

Parquet vs ORC

Key differenceBoth are columnar, but ORC is optimised for Hive (best compression, Hive ACID, vectorized reads) while Parquet is the broader analytics standard across Spark, Presto and ML.
ParquetORC
OrientationColumnarColumnar
CodecSnappy / GzipZlib / Snappy
Best forSpark, Presto, ML pipelines (broader standard for analytics)Hive warehouse, highest compression
Extra featuresPredicate pushdown via row-group stats; Spark-nativeHive ACID support; vectorized reads; pushdown within stripes
Origin-Developed by the Hive team (2013); 2-4x faster reads than SequenceFile
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a Hive SQL warehouse needing ACID and maximum compression, the answer is ORC (+Zlib); if it describes a Spark/Presto/ML pipeline, it is Parquet (+Snappy).

LinkedIn separate clusters (Hadoop 1.x era) vs LinkedIn single YARN cluster

Key differenceRunning each framework on its own cluster left each under-used (45%), whereas consolidating them onto one YARN cluster with Capacity queues raised utilisation to 78% and served 73% more work on the same hardware.
LinkedIn separate clusters (Hadoop 1.x era)LinkedIn single YARN cluster
SetupCluster A MapReduce/Hive ETL, B experimental Spark, C SamzaOne 5,000-node YARN cluster, Capacity Scheduler with 6 queues
Utilisation45% (3 silos)78%
PYMK recompute18 hr on MR14 hours
Ops costThree configurations tripled ops cost; cross-cluster data movement added latencyOne cluster, fair sharing + framework isolation
Workload served-Same capacity served 73% more workload
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a company running separate MapReduce, Spark and streaming clusters that sit idle at different times, the answer is to consolidate onto one YARN cluster with Capacity Scheduler queues.

YARN vs Kubernetes

Key differenceKubernetes has largely replaced YARN for new deployments, but it keeps YARN's three-tier design, and its Pod descends directly from YARN's container.
YARNKubernetes
Timeline2013; cluster OS for EMR, HDInsight, CDP through 20202018-present; largely replaced YARN for new deployments
DesignGlobal scheduler / node agent / per-app masterIdentical three-tier design
Resource unitContainer {vcores, memory}Pod (YARN container is its direct ancestor)
Still dominant whereSpark on YARN in on-premise Hadoop clustersNew deployments
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks what replaced YARN, or where the container idea went, the answer is Kubernetes (Pods); if it is about an on-premise Hadoop cluster running Spark, it is still YARN.

Driver program vs Executor

Key differenceThe Driver runs main() and turns the program into a DAG of tasks and schedules them, while Executors are JVM processes on worker nodes that actually run those tasks and hold cached partitions.
Driver programExecutor
Where it runsThe user's application processJVM processes launched on Worker Nodes
DoesRuns main(); creates SparkContext/SparkSessionExecutes tasks
PlanBuilds the DAG of transformations; coordinates execution; schedules tasksReceives tasks scheduled by the Driver
MemoryHolds the plan (DAG)Stores cached RDD partitions in memory
Third tierCluster Manager allocates resources: YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos, Standalone-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which component builds the DAG or where collect() results land, the answer is the Driver; where tasks run and cached RDD partitions live, it is the Executor.

Topic: Spark architecture

SparkContext vs SparkSession

Key differenceSparkContext was the Spark 1.x entry point for RDDs, while SparkSession (2.x+) is the unified entry point for SQL, DataFrames and RDDs, still exposing the context as spark.sparkContext.
SparkContextSparkSession
VersionEntry point in Spark 1.xEntry point in Spark 2.x+
CoversRDDsUnifies SQL, DataFrames and RDDs under one entry point
RelationshipStill accessible as spark.sparkContextWraps the SparkContext
Slide codesc.textFile(...)SparkSession.builder.appName(...).getOrCreate(); spark.read.parquet, spark.sql
Spot it in a scenarioIf the code starts with SparkSession.builder and uses spark.sql, it is the 2.x+ unified entry point; if it calls sc.textFile on raw RDDs, it uses SparkContext.

Topic: Spark architecture

coalesce vs repartition

Key differencecoalesce reduces the number of partitions without a shuffle (narrow), while repartition reshuffles data across the network (wide) and starts a new stage.
coalescerepartition
Dependency typeNarrowWide
ShuffleNo shuffle (reduces partitions)Requires shuffle
StagePipelined in the same stageCreates a stage boundary
RecoveryRecompute only from the single parent partitionRecompute from all parent partitions
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks for the cheap way to cut partitions before writing output, the answer is coalesce; if it needs a full redistribution, repartition (with a shuffle).
Week 6, slides P1 s21

MEMORY_ONLY vs MEMORY_AND_DISK

Key differenceMEMORY_ONLY keeps partitions in the JVM heap and recomputes any that do not fit, whereas MEMORY_AND_DISK spills those partitions to local disk instead of recomputing them.
MEMORY_ONLYMEMORY_AND_DISK
Stored inJVM heapHeap; overflow to local disk
Partition that does not fitSpill re-computes (recomputed from lineage)Written to local disk, read back
Other levelsMEMORY_ONLY_SER: Kryo-serialised bytes, smaller but slower; OFF_HEAP: native memory, avoids GCDISK_ONLY: local disk, slower reuse
When to cache at allReused in >1 action (iterative ML, interactive queries)Caching single-use RDDs wastes RAM and triggers LRU eviction
BenchmarkLR: Spark MEMORY_ONLY 0.96 s/iter vs Hadoop 127 s/iter (132x)-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question says the cached dataset is bigger than cluster RAM and recomputation is expensive, the answer is MEMORY_AND_DISK; if it fits in RAM and speed is everything, MEMORY_ONLY.
Week 6, slides P2 s10

Hash partitioner vs Range partitioner

Key differenceA hash partitioner spreads keys by hashCode modulo the partition count (the default, but it can hot-spot on skewed keys), while a range partitioner samples keys and assigns ordered ranges, which sortByKey needs.
Hash partitionerRange partitioner
Howkey.hashCode() % numPartitionsSamples key distribution, assigns key ranges to partitions
Default?DefaultUsed by sortByKey()
BehaviourUniform for random keys; can hot-spot on skewed dataEach partition holds a key range (inference: keeps sort order)
Custom optionCustom partitioner: co-partition two RDDs on the same key to eliminate shuffle on join-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question involves sorting by key, the answer is the range partitioner; for ordinary key grouping the default hash partitioner; for joining two RDDs without a shuffle, a custom co-partitioner.
Week 6, slides P2 s10

Spark at GraySort (sort-based shuffle) vs Hadoop MapReduce (hash shuffle)

Key differenceSpark won GraySort mainly through a sort-based shuffle that writes sorted runs once and merges them, whereas MapReduce's shuffle spills and re-reads data several times, costing ~200 TB of extra disk I/O at 100 TB.
Spark at GraySort (sort-based shuffle)Hadoop MapReduce (hash shuffle)
Shuffle behaviourWrites sorted runs to disk once, then mergesSpills, merges and re-reads multiple times (twice per byte)
Extra I/O at 100 TBEliminates ~120 TB of extra I/O~200 TB of additional disk I/O
Result100 TB in 23 min on 206 EC2 nodes (Nov 2013)72 min on 2,100 nodes (Yahoo! 2012)
Other tricksAll 8 SSDs as shuffle dirs; off-heap sort buffers (Unsafe); single wide sortByKey-
Ratio3.1x faster (72 -> 23 min); 206 vs 2,100 nodes (P2 s2 says '3x faster on 3.5x fewer machines' - decks differ)-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks why Spark sorted 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 nodes versus Hadoop's 72 minutes on 2,100, the answer is sort-based shuffle on SSDs plus off-heap buffers and fewer stages, not just caching.
Week 6, slides P2 s13-15

Iterative / working-set workload vs Single-pass ETL

Key differenceSpark's in-memory caching pays off only when the same working set is reused across iterations (10-100x), while for single-pass ETL over data larger than RAM the gain is small (2-5x) - 'a multiplier, not a panacea'.
Iterative / working-set workloadSingle-pass ETL
Spark speedup10-100x (LR 132x, K-Means 30x)Smaller (2-5x) when data is larger than RAM
ExamplesK-Means, logistic regression, graph BFS, interactive queries on the same tableSingle-pass batch jobs on very large clusters
WhyWorking set cached in RAM and reused; MapReduce cannot cache across jobsEach byte read once - nothing to reuse
Better engineSpark (>2 iterations over same data)MapReduce acceptable where Spark's ~8 GB/Executor overhead is prohibitive
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks under what conditions Spark would NOT outperform MapReduce, the answer is a single-pass job over data larger than cluster RAM (or tight memory), not an iterative one.

Zaharia et al. 2010 (HotCloud) vs Zaharia et al. 2012 (NSDI)

Key differenceThe 2010 HotCloud paper was a short proof-of-concept arguing for caching a reusable working set in memory, while the 2012 NSDI paper formalised RDDs with lineage-based fault tolerance and won Best Paper.
Zaharia et al. 2010 (HotCloud)Zaharia et al. 2012 (NSDI)
TitleSpark: Cluster Computing with Working SetsResilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing
VenueUSENIX HotCloud (workshop, short paper)USENIX NSDI, Rank A*; Best Paper Award
Scope4-page proof-of-conceptFormal RDD abstraction
Key ideaWorking set reused across parallel operations; MapReduce cannot cache itLineage-based fault tolerance; narrow vs wide dependencies; persistence levels
Citations>5,000>13,000
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which paper introduced lineage-based fault tolerance formally, the answer is NSDI 2012; the 'working set' motivation is HotCloud 2010.

Static partition insert vs Dynamic partition insert

Key differenceA static insert names the exact partition value in the INSERT, while a dynamic insert lets Hive take partition values from the last SELECT columns so many partitions load in one statement.
Static partition insertDynamic partition insert
Partition valuesWritten in the statement: PARTITION (year=2024, month=1)Inferred from the last SELECT columns: PARTITION (year, month)
SettingsNoneSET hive.exec.dynamic.partition=true; ...partition.mode=nonstrict
Partitions per statementOneAll at once (e.g. all months)
Pitfall-Partition columns must be last in SELECT, in order; otherwise Hive silently assigns values incorrectly
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question needs to load 36 months of raw sales into a partitioned table in one statement, the answer is dynamic partition insert (with nonstrict mode and partition columns last).

Topic: Partitioning and partition pruning

Hive vs Spark SQL

Key differenceHive compiles HiveQL into batch jobs with minute-level latency, whereas Spark SQL optimises queries with Catalyst and runs them in memory in seconds, sharing Hive's Metastore.
HiveSpark SQL
OriginFacebook, 2008Databricks, 2014
Execution modelMR / Tez / Spark (compile-time)Catalyst optimizer, in-memory RDDs
LatencyMinutesSeconds
Best forBatch analytics, large ETL jobsUnified batch + streaming SQL
Shared pieceHive MetastoreReads the same Hive Metastore
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question wants SQL over the same Hive tables but with interactive latency plus streaming in one engine, the answer is Spark SQL.

MapReduce engine vs Tez engine

Key differenceUnder MapReduce, Hive runs a chain of separate jobs that write intermediate results to HDFS, while Tez runs the same query as one DAG of tasks, cutting latency 5-10x with the same results.
MapReduce engineTez engine
Plan shapeChain of MapReduce jobsDAG of tasks
Between stagesMaterialises intermediate data to HDFS between every MR stageDAG-based successor to MapReduce (no per-job HDFS round trip)
SpeedDefault legacy engineFaster; Hive and Pig rewrote on Tez, reducing latency 5-10x
How to choosehive.execution.engine setting (slide shows SET ...=spark)Same setting; Tez = 'DAG of tasks, faster'
Later evolution-LLAP (2016): Hive-on-Tez with persistent in-memory daemon, sub-second queries
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks how switching Hive's execution engine from MapReduce to Tez changes the plan for a top-5 query, the answer is: one DAG instead of chained MR jobs with HDFS writes between them.

Hive Metastore vs HDFS NameNode

Key differenceThe Hive Metastore is a relational DB holding table schemas, partitions and SerDe information, whereas the NameNode holds only HDFS block metadata; the NameNode is the common distractor for 'where is Hive schema stored'.
Hive MetastoreHDFS NameNode
StoresTable schemas, column types, partition info + HDFS path, SerDe, table statistics, privilegesHDFS block metadata
What it isRelational database (MySQL / PostgreSQL)HDFS master
Used forWhere data lives and how to parse it; partition pruning; cost-based optimizer statsLocating file blocks
If lostCannot query any table even though data on HDFS is intact-
LegacyDe facto catalogue for Spark, Presto/Trino, Impala, Athena (AWS Glue)-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks where Hive keeps column names, types and partition locations, the answer is the Metastore (MySQL/PostgreSQL), not the NameNode.

Topic: Hive architecture and query compilation

Pig Latin vs Hive (HiveQL)

Key differencePig Latin is a procedural dataflow language, while HiveQL is declarative SQL that Hive compiles to MapReduce, letting SQL-only analysts query Hadoop without engineers.
Pig LatinHive (HiveQL)
OriginYahoo!, 2008Facebook, 2008 (Thusoo et al. 2009)
StyleDataflow, more expressive than MR but still proceduralDeclarative SQL dialect
Translation-HiveQL translated directly to MapReduce
Who can use itProgrammers (general knowledge; slide only says Pig is procedural)Hundreds of analysts who could write SQL but not Java - self-service access
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which tool let non-programmer analysts query Hadoop with SQL, the answer is Hive; a step-by-step procedural dataflow script is Pig.

Hand-written Java MapReduce vs HiveQL

Key differenceJava MapReduce needs 100+ lines and days per aggregation, whereas HiveQL lets analysts declare the query in SQL and Hive generates the distributed job ('Declare, don't program').
Hand-written Java MapReduceHiveQL
Code for a GROUP BY100+ lines of boilerplateOne SELECT ... GROUP BY
Time-to-insightDays (write, test, debug)Analyst writes SELECT, Hive writes the distributed job
Who writes itJava engineersBusiness analysts, data scientists, BI teams
ExecutionThe job itselfCompiled into MapReduce jobs, Tez DAGs or Spark jobs
Impact-200 analysts replaced 20 Java engineers (democratisation)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes thousands of non-engineers needing to query petabytes, the answer is SQL-on-Hadoop (Hive) instead of Java MapReduce.
Week 7, slides P1 s5; P2 s4, s22

OLTP (RDBMS) vs OLAP (Hive)

Key differenceOLTP systems handle many small real-time reads and writes on validated data with millisecond latency, while OLAP systems like Hive run large batch analytic scans over petabytes with minute-level latency.
OLTP (RDBMS)OLAP (Hive)
Example workloadE-commerce orders, bankingLog analysis, batch reporting, analytics
SchemaSchema-on-writeSchema-on-read
OperationsReal-time reads/writes; UPDATE/DELETE any rowBatch analytics; UPDATE only on ACID tables
LatencyMillisecondsMinutes / seconds
ScaleTerabytes maxPetabytes
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes the live bKash wallet database that must not be slowed down, it is OLTP (copy it out with Sqoop); the nightly analytics over HDFS is OLAP (Hive).
Week 7, slides P1 s13, s16

Partition pruning (Hive) vs Predicate pushdown (Parquet/ORC)

Key differencePartition pruning skips whole directories based on the partition-column value recorded in the Metastore, while predicate pushdown skips row groups within a columnar file using min/max statistics in the footer; the two stack.
Partition pruning (Hive)Predicate pushdown (Parquet/ORC)
What is skippedWhole HDFS sub-directoriesWhole row groups inside a file
UsesPartition metadata (paths) in the MetastoreMin/max column stats in the file footer
Works onWHERE on the partition column onlyWHERE on any column with stats
Slide exampleyear=2024 AND month=01 reads 1 sub-directory, not 36 monthsscore > 90: row group with [60,85] skipped; 10 TB may read only 50 GB
ScopeDirectory levelFile level (then only the needed column chunk)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question filters on the partitioned date column, the saving is partition pruning; if it filters on an ordinary column inside Parquet files, it is predicate pushdown.

HiveQL (Spotify feature engineering) vs Spark MLlib (Spotify ML)

Key differenceAt Spotify, HiveQL did the one-pass SQL aggregation for features (playlist co-occurrence), while Spark did the iterative ALS model training, with Luigi chaining the two.
HiveQL (Spotify feature engineering)Spark MLlib (Spotify ML)
TaskPlaylist co-occurrence aggregationALS matrix factorisation (collaborative filtering)
Nature of workSQL aggregation: GROUP BY song_a, song_b HAVING COUNT(*) > 5Iterative
ScaleOver 2 billion playlists75M users x 30M songs, rank 50
OrchestrationLuigi task (declares output path + dependencies, skips finished outputs)Same Luigi pipeline
LessonNeither alone is sufficientComplementary
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes counting song pairs across billions of playlists, the answer is a HiveQL GROUP BY; training the recommendation model over many iterations is Spark.

Governed data lake vs Data swamp

Key differenceA data swamp is a data lake without governance, where raw files pile up with no catalogue, owners, versions or access control; enforcing a catalogue at ingest, owners, access control, quality checks and a table format keeps it a lake.
Governed data lakeData swamp
CatalogueCatalogue/governance layer (Apache Atlas, AWS Glue, Hive Metastore) tracks schemas, lineage, ownership, accessNo catalogue: analysts cannot find relevant datasets
CurrencyOwners assigned to every datasetNo one knows which files are current vs stale
VersionsTable format (Delta Lake, Iceberg) adds ACIDMultiple copies with different transformations, no version control
PrivacyAccess control enforcedPII mixed with non-sensitive data, violating privacy regulations
QualityAutomated quality checksRaw files accumulate without metadata, owners or quality guarantees
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes analysts unable to find datasets, unclear current files and PII mixed in, the answer is a data swamp - prevent it with a catalogue at ingest, owners, access control, automated checks, Delta/Iceberg.

Flume memory channel vs Flume file channel

Key differenceA memory channel buffers Flume events in RAM (fast but lost on restart), while a file channel persists them on disk so the buffer survives an agent crash.
Flume memory channelFlume file channel
SpeedFastSlower (general knowledge: disk writes)
PersistenceNo persistencePersistent, on disk
Agent crash/restartBuffered events lost (inference from 'no persistence')Survives agent restart / crash
Choose whenSpeed matters and loss is tolerableLogs must not be lost
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question says the Flume agent crashed and no log events may be lost, the answer is the file channel.

Sequential disk I/O (Kafka) vs Random disk I/O

Key differenceKafka only ever appends to the end of a log, so disk access is sequential (~600 MB/s on HDD) instead of random, which is a core reason it runs fast on spinning disks.
Sequential disk I/O (Kafka)Random disk I/O
Throughput (P1 s18)Modern HDDs ~600 MB/s< 1 MB/s
Throughput (P2 s11)~600 MB/s~100 MB/s (6x advantage)
How Kafka gets itNever updates in place; append-only writes; OS page cache prefetches next pagesIn-place updates
ResultNear-disk-bandwidth on spinning disk without SSD-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks why Kafka is fast without SSDs, the answer starts with sequential append-only writes (plus zero-copy, batching, partition parallelism). Note: the two decks give the random-I/O figure as <1 MB/s (P1) and ~100 MB/s (P2) - quote the slide you cite.
Week 8, slides P1 s18; P2 s9, s11

Traditional broker data path vs Kafka zero-copy (sendfile)

Key differenceA traditional broker copies each message through user space (4 copies), while Kafka's sendfile() moves data from the kernel page cache straight to the network card (2 copies), doubling throughput with near-zero CPU.
Traditional broker data pathKafka zero-copy (sendfile)
PathDisk -> kernel buffer -> user space -> socket buffer -> NICDisk -> kernel buffer -> NIC via Linux sendfile()
Copies42
Eliminated-2 user-space copies and 2 context switches
Result-2x throughput, CPU near zero
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks what zero-copy means in Kafka, the answer: sendfile() skips the user-space copy, so 4 copies become 2.
Week 8, slides P1 s18; P2 s9-11

Classic Lambda vs Netflix Kafka-first Lambda (moving to Kappa)

Key differenceNetflix removed classic Lambda's dual-ingestion problem by writing every event to Kafka first so both layers read the same durable log, and gradually shifted batch work to Flink streams (towards Kappa).
Classic LambdaNetflix Kafka-first Lambda (moving to Kappa)
IngestionTwo separate ingestion paths -> data inconsistencyAll events written to Kafka first; speed and batch layers are both consumers of the same topic
ReprocessingRe-run batch job on HDFS7-day Kafka retention lets them replay any window when a Flink/Spark job has a bug
LayersBatch + speed + servingFlink (<1 min), S3 + Spark + Iceberg (~1 day), Cassandra + Druid serving
Direction-Increasingly moved batch jobs to Flink (Kappa simplification)
Burst handling-Kafka's durable log absorbs 5x Super Bowl spikes; Flink catches up
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks how to keep Lambda's batch and speed layers consistent, the answer is Netflix's pattern: one Kafka topic as the single source of truth feeding both layers.
Week 8, slides P2 s15-18, s22

Kafka partition vs Hive partition

Key differenceA Kafka partition is an ordered log segment of a topic that gives parallelism and per-key ordering, while a Hive partition is a directory per column value that lets queries skip data; same word, different jobs.
Kafka partitionHive partition
What it isOrdered append-only log, one of P splits of a topic, stored on a broker (leader + R-1 replicas)HDFS sub-directory per value of the partition column
PurposeParallelism: P producers and up to P consumers in a group; key-level orderingPruning: queries skip non-matching directories
Assigned byProducer: key hash or round-robin (same key -> same partition)Column value (static or dynamic insert)
Scaling noteThroughput scales linearly with partition countHigh-cardinality key -> millions of directories crash NameNode
Spark (for contrast)Spark partition = slice of an RDD processed in parallel by one task on an executor-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question is about consumer parallelism or keeping one driver's GPS pings in order, it means Kafka partitions; if about skipping data in a WHERE clause, it means Hive partitions.

Summary statistics vs Visualisation

Key differenceSummary statistics can be identical for very different data (Anscombe's Quartet), while a plot reveals the actual pattern, so visualise before trusting the numbers - more so at big-data scale.
Summary statisticsVisualisation
Anscombe's QuartetIdentical: mean x 9.0, mean y 7.5, var x 11.0, r 0.816, y = 3 + 0.5xFour different stories: linear, curved, outlier, vertical cluster
At petabyte scaleOpposite trends in sub-populations average out; means meaningless on log-scale dataFirst and most powerful quality check
StreamingDaily average hides sudden regime changesReveals the change
Bangladesh exampleDGHS monthly averages look stable year-over-yearLine chart reveals June-Aug cholera and October dengue peaks

Tufte (1983) vs Shneiderman (1996)

Key differenceTufte tells you what ink belongs on a chart (maximise data-ink, remove chartjunk, avoid lies), while Shneiderman tells you how an interactive visualisation should behave (overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand).
Tufte (1983)Shneiderman (1996)
WorkThe Visual Display of Quantitative Information (book, self-published)The Eyes Have It (IEEE Visual Languages paper)
FocusWhat to show and what to remove (static design)How users interact: overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand
Key conceptsData-ink ratio, chartjunk, lie factor, small multiples, sparklinesMantra, seven data types, seven tasks, treemap (1991), dynamic queries
Modern toolsTableau 'Remove formatting', Grafana minimal theme, D3 no default axesTableau drill-down, Grafana time-range zoom, Google Maps zoom
NYT COVID trackerNo gridlines; 50-state small multiplesNational total first; state dropdown; hover tooltip
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question is about removing 3-D effects or gridlines, cite Tufte; if it is about a dashboard's drill-down flow or tooltips, cite Shneiderman's mantra.

7-day rolling average vs 14-day rolling average

Key differenceBoth smooth out the weekly reporting cycle, but a 7-day average reacts faster to real changes while a 14-day average is smoother and lags more; the choice changes the story the chart tells.
7-day rolling average14-day rolling average
Day-of-week reporting artefactsRemoved (slide: reduces day-of-week artefacts)Removed (general knowledge: any multiple of 7)
Reacts to a real turnSooner (general knowledge)Later (general knowledge)
NoiseMore (general knowledge)Less (general knowledge)
Slide pointNYT's choice: a data quality decision encoded in the visual designChoosing 7 vs 14 changes the story - editorial decision with ethical weight

Community detection vs Influence maximisation

Key differenceCommunity detection groups nodes that are densely linked to each other, whereas influence maximisation chooses a small set of seed nodes that will spread information furthest (NP-hard, greedy (1 - 1/e) approximation).
Community detectionInfluence maximisation
QuestionWhich nodes form a densely connected group?Which k nodes to seed so information spreads to the most users?
AlgorithmLouvain (Blondel 2008), maximise modularityKempe et al. (KDD 2003 Best Paper): NP-hard, greedy approximation with (1 - 1/e) guarantee
RevealsInterest groups, political factions, professional clusters, bot networksSeed users for a product promotion or message
Ethical risk at scaleProfiling group membership (general knowledge; D1 asks for one)Manipulation / microtargeting vulnerable users (slide s12 mentions microtargeting)
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a marketer choosing 50 accounts to start a campaign, the answer is influence maximisation; finding coordinated bot clusters is community detection.

Prophet (decomposable) vs Black-box deep learning (e.g. LSTM)

Key differenceProphet's additive trend + seasonality + holiday components can be inspected and adjusted by domain experts, while black-box deep learning forecasters like LSTM cannot, which is why the slides credit Prophet's trust in public health.
Prophet (decomposable)Black-box deep learning (e.g. LSTM)
Interpretabilityg + s + h structure lets epidemiologists inspect each componentBlack-box
AdjustmentDomain experts can audit and adjust each component (holidays, trend flexibility)-
Public-health outcomeSucceeded where black-box models failed-
FluSightStrong component of ensemblesAlso in the ensemble (Prophet, ARIMA, LSTM, human experts); no single model wins every season

Sequential Prophet on one machine vs Spark vectorised batch forecasting (applyInPandas)

Key differenceFitting thousands of independent forecasts one by one takes hours, but because each series is independent Spark can group by series and run Prophet in parallel with applyInPandas (8 h -> ~12 min).
Sequential Prophet on one machineSpark vectorised batch forecasting (applyInPandas)
Runtime (5,000 SKUs)8+ hours~12 minutes on a 20-executor cluster (40x)
HowFit 5,000 Prophet models one after anotherGroup by sku_id; applyInPandas sends each SKU to one partition; Prophet in a Pandas UDF
Why it works-Each series independent -> embarrassingly parallel
Output-Written to Hive/S3 as Parquet, served to dashboard
CDC example-Prophet on 60 HHS regions simultaneously via applyInPandas
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks how to parallelise 5,000 store-product forecasts, the answer is groupBy(sku_id).applyInPandas(prophet_fit), one series per partition.

Time series data vs i.i.d. tabular data

Key differenceTime series observations are ordered and autocorrelated with trend and seasonality, so shuffling them destroys the signal, whereas i.i.d. tabular rows are independent and order-free.
Time series datai.i.d. tabular data
OrderOrder matters: shuffling rows destroys the signal; timestamps must be keptRows can be shuffled
DependenceAutocorrelation: today correlated with yesterdayIndependent observations (standard regression assumption)
StructureSeasonality, trend must be modelled explicitly-
StationarityMean/variance may change; most models need differencing-
Spot it in a scenarioIf a True/False says shuffling a time series does not change the analysis, it is False; standard regression is invalid because of autocorrelation.

Proxy signal (Google Flu Trends) vs Direct signal (BioSense ED visits)

Key differenceGoogle Flu Trends used search queries as a proxy for flu and failed (2x over-prediction) because searches track anxiety and media, while BioSense uses direct emergency-department observations as the primary signal, adding proxies only as covariates.
Proxy signal (Google Flu Trends)Direct signal (BioSense ED visits)
Data45 flu-related search queriesReal-time ED data from 3,500+ emergency departments (38 M visits in 2019-20)
What it measuresHealth anxiety, not health incidenceDirect medical observation
Track recordr² = 0.97 on 2003-08, then over-predicted flu 2x in 2012-13; discontinuedPrimary signal in post-GFT Prophet nowcasting
Failure causesBig data hubris; algorithm confounding (autocomplete changes); media amplification-
Correct role of proxiesExogenous covariate (e.g. Twitter), not a replacement-
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks why Google Flu Trends failed, the answer: a proxy signal with hubris, autocomplete confounding and media amplification; the fix is direct ED data with proxies as covariates.
