20e9 / 5e6 = 4,000x.
When is a data cube the wrong choice, and what is the alternative?
Why
When the dashboard needs data fresher than the last cube build, or ad-hoc dimensions the cube did not pre-compute. Approximate query processing (sampling, e.g. BlinkDB, DataSketches) answers in milliseconds with an estimate, acceptable for dashboards but not for financial reconciliation.
Topic: Latency: data cubes and AQP

Overplotting: 10 M points to about 10,000 hex cells; alpha = 0.02

Week 9, very likely. Slides: W09 P1 s17-s18
GivenA scatter of 10 million points becomes a grid of about 10,000 hexagonal cells, each coloured by count. Alpha transparency at 0.02 darkens dense regions but saturates.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Reduction = 10,000,000 / 10,000 = 1,000x fewer marks to draw.
  2. Average points per hex = 1,000.
  3. Alpha stacking (general formula): opacity after n overlapping points = 1 - (1 - 0.02)^n; n = 100 gives 0.867, n = 300 gives 0.998: dense regions all look the same black.
Answer1,000x fewer marks; alpha saturates near 0.998 after a few hundred points.
Try it yourself
A Pathao heatmap plots 50 million GPS points into 25,000 hex cells. Given: reduction = points / cells. Find it.
Variant 1
50,000,000 / 25,000 = 2,000x.
With alpha = 0.02, what opacity do 50 overlapping points reach? Given: opacity = 1 - (1 - alpha)^n.
Variant 2
1 - 0.98^50 = 0.636.
Why does hexbin beat alpha transparency at very high density?
Why
Alpha only stacks opacity, and after a few hundred overlaps every dense area is the same black, so differences between 500 and 50,000 points vanish. Hexbin counts points per cell and maps the count to colour, so density differences stay visible and only about 10,000 shapes are rendered.
Topic: Overplotting: alpha, hexbin, KDE

Lie factor: +10% in data drawn as a bar that doubles, lie factor about 10

Week 9, very likely. Slides: W09 P2 s7
GivenLie factor = size of effect shown in graphic / size of effect in data. Y-axis starts at 50; the data rise 10% but the bar appears to double.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Effect in data = +10%.
  2. Effect shown = bar doubles = +100%.
  3. Lie factor = 100 / 10 = 10: the graphic overstates the change 10 times.
AnswerLie factor about 10 (truthful = 1).
Try it yourself
Revenue rises from 50 to 55 (+10%). The chart's y-axis starts at 45, so the bars are drawn 5 and 10 units tall. Given: shown effect = (10 - 5)/5. Find the lie factor.
Variant 1
Shown = +100%; data = +10%; lie factor = 10.
Users fall 20% but the chart's shrinking icon shrinks by only 5%. Lie factor?
Variant 2
5 / 20 = 0.25: it understates the effect.
Why does a truncated y-axis create a large lie factor, and what is the fix?
Why
Bar length is read as the quantity. Cutting the axis at 50 removes the common base, so a small difference fills most of the visible bar. Start bar charts at 0 (the D3 Live Exercise requires it).
Topic: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, lie factor

Data-ink ratio = ink encoding data / total ink

Week 9, likely. Slides: W09 P1 s8; W09 P2 s6
GivenData-ink ratio = ink used to display data / total ink used in the graphic. Example (not on slide): a chart uses 200 units of ink, 60 of which draw the bars.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Ratio = 60 / 200 = 0.3.
  2. Remove the 3-D effect (40 units), redundant legend (20) and heavy gridlines (60): total becomes 200 - 120 = 80.
  3. New ratio = 60 / 80 = 0.75.
Answer0.30 before, 0.75 after removing chartjunk.
Try it yourself
A bar chart uses 500 units of ink; 150 draw data. Given: ratio = data ink / total ink. Find the ratio.
Variant 1
150 / 500 = 0.3.
From that chart you erase 250 units of gridlines and borders without touching data. New ratio?
Variant 2
150 / 250 = 0.6.
Does a high data-ink ratio mean 'use less ink'?
Why
No. It is about what the ink encodes, not how much is used: one thick bar showing one important value can have a ratio near 1. The rule is: if erasing an element loses no information, erase it.
Topic: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, lie factor

Live Exercise: D3 bar chart, y-axis from 0, scaleLinear range [260, 20]

Week 9, likely. Slides: W09 P2 s17 (Live Exercise)
Given5 topics x 7 days = 35 random values; count = floor(random x 50,000) + 10,000. y = d3.scaleLinear().domain([0, max]).range([260, 20]); bar height = 260 - y(count). Suppose max = 50,000.
Show the 4 steps
  1. Count range: 10,000 to 59,999 (random in [0, 1)).
  2. Pixels per unit = (260 - 20) / 50,000 = 0.0048 px.
  3. Count 25,000: y = 260 - 25,000/50,000 x 240 = 140; height = 260 - 140 = 120 px.
  4. Because the domain starts at 0, bar heights are proportional to counts (lie factor 1).
AnswerA 25,000 bar is 120 px tall and its top sits at y = 140.
Try it yourself
Same scale (domain [0, 50,000], range [260, 20]). Given: height = count / 50,000 x 240. Height of a 40,000 bar?
Variant 1
40,000/50,000 x 240 = 192 px.
A student sets the domain to [30,000, 50,000]. Bars of 35,000 and 40,000: heights, and the lie factor of the 40,000 vs 35,000 comparison?
Variant 2
Heights 60 px and 120 px: drawn +100% for a +14.3% change, lie factor 7.
Which Tufte and Shneiderman rules does the exercise apply, and why?
Why
Tufte: no gridlines (or one light reference line), flat colour, y-axis from 0, so ink encodes data and lengths are truthful. Shneiderman: a hover tooltip gives details on demand, and the dropdown filter is the zoom-and-filter step.
Topic: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, lie factor

Pie chart rule: only for 4 or fewer categories and part-of-whole questions

Week 9, likely. Slides: W09 P1 s15; W09 P1 s28 (T/F 1)
GivenPie charts only when there are <= 4 categories and the question is 'what fraction of the whole?'. Above 5 categories use a horizontal bar chart ordered by value.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Count categories and identify the question type.
  2. Example: 8 districts' share of dengue cases: 8 > 4, so use a horizontal bar chart sorted by value.
  3. Example: a 3-way split of revenue by channel as a fraction of total: a pie is acceptable.
AnswerPie only for <= 4 categories and part-to-whole; otherwise bar (or line for time).
Try it yourself
A bKash report shows the share of 3 transaction types (send money, cash out, payment) in total volume. Given the <= 4 rule, is a pie acceptable?
Variant 1
Yes: 3 categories and a part-of-whole question.
A report shows monthly sales for 12 months. Pie or not, and what instead?
Variant 2
No: it is a time series, and 12 slices is far above 4. Use a line chart.
Why are pie charts read less accurately than bar charts?
Why
Humans judge angles and arc lengths far less accurately than lengths along a common baseline. A bar chart puts every value on one axis, so small differences are visible.
Topic: Shneiderman's mantra and choosing the chart

NYT COVID tracker: 7-day rolling average; 800 M loads in 2020

Week 9, likely. Slides: W09 P2 s14-s15
GivenThe NYT used 7-day rolling averages to remove day-of-week reporting artefacts; the tracker loaded 800 million times in 2020; 6 million readers per day. Sample daily cases (not on slide): 120, 135, 128, 300, 140, 131, 126.
Show the 3 steps
  1. 7-day average = sum / 7 = 1,080 / 7 = 154.3.
  2. The 300 spike (a reporting backlog) moves the average far less than it moves the daily line.
  3. 800 M loads / 366 days (2020 leap year) = 2,185,792 loads per day.
Answer7-day average = 154.3; about 2,185,792 loads per day.
Try it yourself
Daily dengue cases for 7 days: 210, 190, 205, 400, 195, 200, 180. Given: 7-day average = sum / 7. Compute it.
Variant 1
1,580 / 7 = 225.7.
Next day's count is 220, and 210 drops out of the window. New 7-day average?
Variant 2
(1,580 - 210 + 220) / 7 = 227.1.
Why do the slides call rolling averages an editorial decision?
Why
The window length changes the story: 7-day smooths weekday reporting dips; 14-day hides more noise but reacts more slowly to a real surge. The choice decides what readers see, so it carries ethical weight.
Topic: Case study: NYT COVID-19 tracker

Week 10

Discussion Q1: misinformation reach within 3 hops at out-degree 45

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P2 s15 (Discussion Q1); W10 P2 s6
GivenTwitter: average shortest path 4.12 hops over 41.7 M users. A tweet is retweeted by a high-PageRank account. Assume an average out-degree of 45 and estimate reach within 3 hops.
Show the 5 steps
  1. Hop 1: 45 users.
  2. Hop 2: 45^2 = 2,025.
  3. Hop 3: 45^3 = 91,125.
  4. Total within 3 hops = 45 + 2,025 + 91,125 = 93,195, about 0.22% of 41.7 M users.
  5. It is an overestimate: real networks are clustered (followers share followers), so the same users are counted many times; reciprocity (22.1%) and overlapping neighbourhoods mean paths loop back.
AnswerUpper bound 93,195 users; an overestimate because of clustering/overlapping neighbourhoods (the tree assumption ignores repeated users).
Try it yourself
A Bangla-language rumour starts at an account whose followers each have 30 followers on average. Given: reach in h hops = d + d^2 + ... + d^h. Reach within 2 hops?
Variant 1
30 + 900 = 930.
Same d = 30, 3 hops: what does hop 3 add, and what is the new total?
Variant 2
30^3 = 27,000; total 27,930.
Why does a tweet from a high-PageRank account spread further than one from an account with more raw followers?
Why
PageRank weights followers by their own influence: being followed by influential users who re-share matters more than a big but passive audience. Kwak et al. found PageRank and follower-count rankings differ substantially.
Topic: Social media as a graph: communities, influence, Twitter's shape

Analytical A1: flu early-warning for Bangladesh from social posts and pharmacy sales

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P1 s35 (Analytical A1); W10 P2 s15 (Discussion Q3)
GivenSources: Twitter/Facebook posts and pharmacy purchase records. Validate against DGHS ground truth. Example: 120 pharmacies upload hourly; 2 million posts per day (assumptions).
Show the 5 steps
  1. Ingest: social posts via REST API -> Kafka; pharmacy POS: Kafka producers (real time) or nightly Sqoop from their RDBMS.
  2. Load: 120 pharmacies x 24 uploads = 2,880 files/day; 2 M posts / 86,400 = 23.1 posts/s.
  3. Features: keyword counts (flu, fever, can't taste), VADER sentiment, spike ratio vs baseline per district; pharmacy: daily antipyretic units, ratio to a 7-day baseline.
  4. Model: Prophet with social and pharmacy signals as covariates (they lead by days); validate by back-testing against DGHS case counts week by week.
  5. Ethics: privacy (aggregate by district, de-identify), misinformation-driven false alarms, Bangla-English code-switching bias.
AnswerKafka ingestion, NLP + pharmacy ratio features, Prophet with exogenous signals, validation on DGHS history, privacy by aggregation.
Try it yourself
Antipyretic sales in a district average 400 units/day over the last 7 days; today 1,000 units sold. Given: spike = today / baseline. Spike ratio?
Variant 1
1,000 / 400 = 2.5x.
An alert fires when the ratio exceeds 2.0. Another district sells 700 against a baseline of 380. Does it alert?
Variant 2
700 / 380 = 1.84 < 2.0, so no alert.
Why validate against DGHS ground truth before using the system for policy?
Why
Proxy signals can drift for non-medical reasons (Google Flu Trends over-predicted 2x). Back-testing on past DGHS counts shows whether the lead time is real and how often false alarms happen before anyone acts on them.
Topic: Syndromic surveillance and the Google Flu Trends lesson

Genomics storage: 200 GB per genome x 10,000 patients = 2 PB

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P1 s21
GivenA single whole-genome sequence is about 200 GB. A clinical study of 10,000 patients. DICOM images are 200 MB to 2 GB each.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Total = 200 GB x 10,000 = 2,000,000 GB.
  2. = 2,000 TB = 2 PB.
  3. With HDFS 3x replication: 6 PB of raw disk.
Answer2 PB (6 PB raw with 3x replication).
Try it yourself
A Bangladesh study sequences 2,500 patients at 200 GB each. Given: total = genomes x size. Total storage?
Variant 1
2,500 x 200 = 500,000 GB = 500 TB.
A hospital stores 50,000 CT scans averaging 500 MB. Total, and with 3x replication?
Variant 2
50,000 x 0.5 GB = 25,000 GB = 25 TB; 75 TB replicated.
Why are genomics and imaging not handled with plain SQL tables?
Why
Genomes are huge and processed by specialised pipelines (Parquet + GATK on Spark); DICOM images are unstructured binary files analysed by deep learning (CNN, ViT). They need distributed file/object storage and ML, not row-column queries.
Topic: Healthcare big data, privacy and AlphaFold

Kwak 2010: 41.7 M users, 1.47 B edges, 22.1% reciprocity, alpha 2.276

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P2 s4-s7; W10 P1 s7
Given41.7 M users, 1.47 billion following edges, 106 M tweets. 77.9% of users have a follower they do not follow back; 22.1% of relationships mutual. Power law P(k) ∝ k^-2.276. Top 0.05% have >1 M followers. 85% of trending topics are news; median trend lasts 17.5 h.
Show the 5 steps
  1. Average out-degree = 1.47e9 / 41.7e6 = 35.25 follows per user.
  2. Mutual relationships = 22.1% of 1.47 B = 324.87 million.
  3. Top 0.05% of 41.7 M = 20,850 users with >1 M followers.
  4. Power law: doubling k cuts P(k) by 2^2.276 = 4.84x.
  5. Of 200 trending topics, 85% = 170 news, 15% = 30 memes.
AnswerAverage 35.3 follows per user; 20,850 celebrities; P(k) falls 4.8x when k doubles.
Try it yourself
A graph has 2 million users and 70 million directed edges. Given: average out-degree = edges / users. Compute it.
Variant 1
70e6 / 2e6 = 35.
In that graph 22.1% of edges are reciprocated. How many mutual edges?
Variant 2
0.221 x 70e6 = 15,470,000.
Why do the low reciprocity and fast trending make Twitter a 'news medium' rather than a social network?
Why
Most following is one-way broadcasting from a few hubs to many followers (77.9% asymmetry, power-law in-degree), and 85% of trending topics are headline news peaking within 15 minutes. It behaves like a news wire, which is why it became a public-health surveillance signal.
Topic: Social media as a graph: communities, influence, Twitter's shape

Vectorised Prophet: 5,000 SKUs, 8 h to about 12 min on 20 executors (40x)

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P1 s19; W10 P1 s35 (Analytical A2)
Given90-day forecasts for 5,000 store-product SKUs. Sequential Prophet on one machine: 8+ hours. Spark applyInPandas, grouped by sku_id, on a 20-executor cluster: about 12 minutes.
Show the 5 steps
  1. Speedup = 8 x 60 / 12 = 40x.
  2. Models per executor = 5,000 / 20 = 250.
  3. Sequential time per model = 480 min / 5,000 = 5.76 s.
  4. One model at a time per executor would take 250 x 5.76 s = 24 min; the measured 12 min is half that, which implies about 2 models running at once per executor (multi-core executors; inference, not stated on the slide).
  5. Forecast output rows = 5,000 x 90 = 450,000.
Answer40x speedup; 250 models per executor; 450,000 forecast rows.
Try it yourself
A chain has 12,000 SKUs; Prophet takes 6 s per SKU on one machine. Given: sequential time = SKUs x time per model. How long sequentially?
Variant 1
12,000 x 6 = 72,000 s = 20 h.
Run that on 40 executors with perfect parallelism. Models per executor and wall-clock time?
Variant 2
12,000 / 40 = 300 models; 300 x 6 s = 1,800 s = 30 min.
Why is fitting thousands of Prophet models 'embarrassingly parallel'?
Why
Each SKU's series is fitted independently with no data shared between models. Spark groups rows by sku_id, sends each group to one task, and runs Prophet inside a Pandas UDF, so all models fit at once across the cluster.
Topic: Time series, ARIMA and Prophet at scale

Trend and anomaly spikes: 10 to 10,000 per hour = 1,000x; #QurbaniEid 1,200x

Week 10, very likely. Slides: W10 P1 s12, s18
GivenA phrase normally appears 10 times/hour and suddenly 10,000 times/hour: trending regardless of absolute volume. #QurbaniEid showed a 1,200x spike over 6 hours with 92% positive sentiment. A bKash agent's hourly volume jumps from 10 to 10,000 transactions.
Show the 4 steps
  1. Spike ratio = current rate / baseline = 10,000 / 10 = 1,000x.
  2. The rule is relative: a phrase going 1,000 to 10,000 (10x) trends less than one going 10 to 10,000.
  3. #QurbaniEid: if the baseline was 50 per hour, 1,200x gives 60,000 per hour.
  4. 92% positive of 60,000 tweets = 55,200 positive.
Answer1,000x spike ratio; same arithmetic flags the bKash agent for Isolation Forest review.
Try it yourself
A hashtag's baseline is 25 posts/hour; it now has 15,000/hour. Given: spike = current / baseline. Spike ratio?
Variant 1
15,000 / 25 = 600x.
A hashtag has 40,000 posts in a spike; VADER marks 92% positive. How many are not positive?
Variant 2
40,000 x 0.08 = 3,200.
Why does trend detection use the ratio to the baseline instead of the absolute count?
Why
Big topics are always high-volume, so absolute counts would always show the same things. A ratio to each phrase's own history finds sudden change, which is what 'trending' means. (High sentiment like 92% positive also helped show the spike was organic, not coordinated.)
Topic: Sentiment (VADER), trend detection and ethics

AlphaFold scale: 170,000 PDB structures -> 200 M predictions; 250 M UniProt sequences

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s25-s26, s32
GivenTrained on 170,000 experimentally determined structures; released 200 million predicted structures (2022). MSA search over 250 million UniProt sequences (>200 GB compressed). Training used 128 TPU v3 cores. Median GDT > 92%.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Predictions per training structure = 200,000,000 / 170,000 = 1,176x.
  2. Average compressed size per UniProt sequence = 200 GB / 250 M = 800 bytes.
  3. Each prediction searches all 250 M sequences to build the MSA, which is why it is a big data problem.
AnswerAbout 1,176x more predicted structures than training structures; about 800 bytes per sequence.
Try it yourself
A lab predicts 2 million structures from a model trained on 20,000. Given: ratio = predicted / trained. Ratio?
Variant 1
2,000,000 / 20,000 = 100x.
If X-ray crystallography takes 6 months per protein, how many protein-years would 200 M structures take?
Variant 2
200 M x 0.5 = 100,000,000 protein-years.
Why is AlphaFold a big data problem and not just a deep learning one?
Why
Its input for each protein is a multiple sequence alignment built by searching 250 M sequences from millions of genomes, and training used the whole PDB plus UniRef90. The model works because of that scale of evolutionary data.
Topic: Healthcare big data, privacy and AlphaFold

Clinical ML claims: readmission down 20%, sepsis 6 h early, AUROC > 0.90

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s23-s24
GivenGradient boosting on discharge records reduces 30-day readmissions by 20%. Streaming sepsis model detects onset 6 hours before clinical criteria. ICU mortality model AUROC > 0.90. Needs 1 million+ records. HIPAA Safe Harbour removes 18 identifiers.
Show the 3 steps
  1. Readmissions: 1,500 per year x (1 - 0.20) = 1,200; 300 avoided.
  2. Sepsis onset by clinical criteria at 14:00 -> model alert at 08:00.
  3. De-identification: a record with name, DOB, phone, NID and zip has all 5 removed under Safe Harbour (part of the 18).
Answer1,500 readmissions become 1,200 (300 avoided); sepsis flagged 6 hours earlier.
Try it yourself
A Dhaka hospital has 800 readmissions per year. Given: the model cuts readmissions by 20%. How many remain?
Variant 1
800 x 0.8 = 640.
Clinical criteria would flag sepsis at 03:00. When does the streaming model flag it?
Variant 2
6 hours earlier: 21:00 the previous evening.
Why do these models need streaming infrastructure and a million records?
Why
Sepsis warning only helps if vitals are scored as they arrive (Kafka + Spark Streaming); a nightly batch would be too late. A million+ records are needed so the model generalises across patients rather than memorising one hospital.
Topic: Healthcare big data, privacy and AlphaFold

Google Flu Trends: r² = 0.97 in training, then over-predicted by 2x

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s29; W10 P2 s14-s15
GivenGFT correlated 45 search queries with ILINet; initial r² = 0.97 on 2003-2008 data. In 2012-13 it over-predicted flu by 2x. Twitter signals arrive 2 weeks earlier than ILINet but with 30% higher error.
Show the 4 steps
  1. r² = 0.97: 97% of variance explained in training (r ≈ 0.985).
  2. Over-prediction by 2x: true ILI rate 3% -> GFT predicted 6%.
  3. Twitter error: if ILINet-based error is 10%, Twitter's is 10 x 1.3 = 13% (30% higher), but 2 weeks sooner.
  4. Three causes (Lazer 2014): big-data hubris, autocomplete changed the features, media coverage drove searches.
Answerr^2 = 0.97 in-sample, yet a 2x over-prediction out of sample.
Try it yourself
True ILI in a week was 2.4%. GFT over-predicted by 2x. Given: predicted = 2 x true. What did GFT report?
Variant 1
2 x 2.4 = 4.8%.
A model's correlation with ground truth is r = 0.9. What fraction of variance does it explain, and does that guarantee future accuracy?
Variant 2
0.9^2 = 0.81 (81%). No: in-sample fit does not guarantee out-of-sample accuracy when the data-generating process changes.
Why must syndromic signals supplement, not replace, clinical surveillance?
Why
Proxy data measure behaviour (searching, tweeting) that can shift for reasons unrelated to illness, such as media panic or a search-engine change. They give lead time, not ground truth, so they are combined with ILINet/BioSense reports.
Topic: Syndromic surveillance and the Google Flu Trends lesson

Influence maximisation: greedy achieves at least (1 - 1/e) of optimal

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s10
GivenChoosing k seed nodes for maximum spread is NP-hard (Kempe et al., KDD 2003); the greedy algorithm guarantees at least (1 - 1/e) of the optimal spread.
Show the 3 steps
  1. 1 - 1/e = 1 - 0.3679 = 0.6321, about 63%.
  2. If the best possible seeding reaches 100,000 users, greedy reaches at least 63,212.
  3. Greedy: repeatedly add the node with the largest marginal gain in spread.
AnswerGreedy reaches at least 63.2% of optimal.
Try it yourself
A campaign's optimal 10-seed spread is 40,000 users. Given: greedy >= 0.632 x optimal. Minimum greedy spread?
Variant 1
0.632 x 40,000 = 25,280.
Greedy reached 25,000 users. What is the most the optimal spread could be?
Variant 2
25,000 / 0.632 = 39,557 (39,549 with the exact 1 - 1/e = 0.6321).
Why settle for an approximation instead of the optimal seed set?
Why
Finding the optimum is NP-hard: checking every k-subset of millions of nodes is infeasible. Greedy runs in practical time with a proven 63% guarantee.
Topic: Social media as a graph: communities, influence, Twitter's shape

STL anomaly rule: flag |residual| > k x IQR of residuals

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s18
GivenSTL splits a series into trend, seasonal and residual, and flags residuals whose absolute value exceeds k x IQR. Example (not on slide): residual Q1 = -0.65, Q3 = 1.25, k = 3.
Show the 3 steps
  1. IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 1.25 - (-0.65) = 1.9.
  2. Threshold = 3 x 1.9 = 5.7.
  3. New residuals to check (quartiles come from the agent's history): Residuals [1.2, -0.8, 0.5, 2.0, -1.5, 9.4, 0.3, -0.2]: only 9.4 has |r| > 5.7, so that hour is the anomaly.
AnswerIQR 1.9, threshold 5.7; the residual 9.4 is flagged.
Try it yourself
bKash residuals for one agent have Q1 = -2 and Q3 = 4. Given: IQR = Q3 - Q1 = 6 and k = 2. What is the flag threshold?
Variant 1
2 x 6 = 12: flag |residual| > 12.
With that threshold (12), which residuals are flagged: 5, -14, 11, 30?
Variant 2
-14 and 30 (|-14| = 14 > 12, 30 > 12).
Why flag the residual and not the raw value?
Why
The raw value includes trend and seasonality: a high Friday-evening value may be normal. Once STL removes the expected trend and season, what is left is the unexplained part, so a big residual means truly unusual behaviour. IQR is robust to the outliers it is trying to find.
Topic: Anomaly detection: STL and Isolation Forest

Syndromic lead times: Twitter 7-10 days, pharmacy 3-5 days, CDC lag 1-2 weeks

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s28; W10 P2 s13
GivenPhysician reports reach CDC 1-2 weeks after symptoms. Twitter posts with 'flu', 'fever', 'can't taste' peak 7-10 days before ER visits. OTC antipyretic sales spike 3-5 days before clinical confirmation. ILINet: >3,000 sentinel physicians; BioSense: 3,500+ EDs.
Show the 4 steps
  1. ER visits peak on 20 October.
  2. Twitter signal peaks 7-10 days earlier: 10-13 October.
  3. Taking 20 October as the clinical confirmation date, the pharmacy spike comes 3-5 days earlier: 15-17 October.
  4. Traditional report reaches CDC 1-2 weeks after symptoms: 27 October to 3 November (if symptoms start 20 October).
AnswerTwitter about 10-13 Oct, pharmacy 15-17 Oct, ER peak 20 Oct, CDC reports 27 Oct-3 Nov.
Try it yourself
Dengue ER visits in Dhaka peak on 15 September. Given: social posts peak 7-10 days before ER visits. When does the social signal peak?
Variant 1
5-8 September.
Clinical confirmation is on 12 March. Given: pharmacy sales spike 3-5 days earlier. When is the spike?
Variant 2
7-9 March.
Why do pharmacy sales lead clinical confirmation?
Why
People self-medicate with paracetamol or ibuprofen as soon as symptoms start, days before they see a doctor and long before a diagnosis is reported. Sales data capture illness at that earlier stage.
Topic: Syndromic surveillance and the Google Flu Trends lesson

Live Exercise: synthetic weekly ILI = 5 + 3 sin(2πt/52 - π/2) + noise

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P2 s17 (Live Exercise); W10 P2 s10, s15 (Discussion Q2)
Given156 weekly points (3 years). ili = 5 + 3 sin(2π t / 52 - π/2) + N(0, 0.5), clipped at 0. Fit Prophet with yearly and weekly seasonality, forecast 12 weeks, add an Eid holiday (upper_window 3), change changepoint_prior_scale 0.05 -> 0.5.
Show the 7 steps
  1. t = 0: 5 + 3 sin(-π/2) = 2 (trough).
  2. t = 13: 5 + 3 sin(0) = 5.
  3. t = 26: 5 + 3 sin(π/2) = 8 (peak).
  4. Period 52 weeks = 1 year; 156 / 52 = 3 seasons.
  5. Forecast 12 weeks beyond week 155 (weeks 156-167).
  6. changepoint_prior_scale 0.05 -> 0.5 is 10x looser: the trend bends more easily (more flexible, risk of overfitting).
  7. Discussion Q2: a sudden COVID wave is a trend changepoint, caught by g(t); the changepoint_prior_scale sets how readily new changepoints are accepted.
AnswerTrough 2 at week 0, mean 5 at week 13, peak 8 at week 26; 3 full seasons; prior scale raised 10x.
Try it yourself
Same formula. Given: sin(2π·39/52 - π/2) = sin(π) = 0. What is the expected ILI at week 39?
Variant 1
5 + 3 x 0 = 5.
A model's yearly Fourier seasonality uses N = 10 terms (each with a cos and a sin coefficient). How many seasonal coefficients are fitted? Add weekly with N = 3.
Variant 2
Yearly 2 x 10 = 20; weekly 2 x 3 = 6; total 26.
Why does Prophet's g + s + h structure suit epidemiologists better than a black-box model?
Why
Each component can be inspected and adjusted on its own: trend changepoints, annual flu season, holiday effects such as Eid. Domain experts can audit and tune it without ARIMA expertise, and the additive form absorbs spikes without corrupting the trend.
Topic: Time series, ARIMA and Prophet at scale

Social and surveillance scale: YouTube 500 h/min, 500 M tweets/day, BioSense 38 M visits

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s8; W10 P2 s10, s14
GivenYouTube: 500 hours uploaded per minute. Twitter/X: 500 M tweets/day. BioSense 2019-20: 38 million ED visits; Prophet ran on 60 HHS regions in parallel; 3,500+ EDs. Facebook ran Prophet on 500,000+ series.
Show the 4 steps
  1. YouTube per day = 500 x 60 x 24 = 720,000 hours of video.
  2. Tweets per second = 500e6 / 86,400 = 5,787.
  3. ED visits per ED = 38e6 / 3,500 = 10,857 per season.
  4. 500,000 Prophet series on 1,000 executors = 500 series each.
Answer720,000 hours/day of video; about 5,787 tweets/s; about 10,857 visits per ED.
Try it yourself
A platform receives 100 million posts per day. Given: per second = daily / 86,400. Rate?
Variant 1
100e6 / 86,400 = 1,157 posts/s.
60 HHS regions are forecast in parallel with applyInPandas on 12 executors. How many region models per executor?
Variant 2
60 / 12 = 5.
Why does the slide say social media's graph, not the individual post, is the main analytical object?
Why
Influence, communities and cascades are properties of who follows and retweets whom. Single posts are short and noisy; the network structure explains how information spreads.
Topic: Social media as a graph: communities, influence, Twitter's shape

VADER compound score thresholds: > 0.05 positive, < -0.05 negative

Week 10, likely. Slides: W10 P1 s11
GivenVADER outputs a compound score in [-1, +1]: positive if > 0.05, negative if < -0.05, otherwise neutral. Sample scores (not on slide): 0.62, 0.04, -0.03, -0.41, 0.05.
Show the 6 steps
  1. 0.62: positive.
  2. 0.04: neutral.
  3. -0.03: neutral.
  4. -0.41: negative.
  5. 0.05: neutral.
  6. Share positive = 1/5 = 20%. Note 0.05 itself is neutral (the rule is strictly greater).
Answer1 positive, 3 neutral, 1 negative.
Try it yourself
Three tweets score 0.30, -0.06 and 0.05. Given the thresholds, classify each.
Variant 1
0.30 positive; -0.06 negative; 0.05 neutral.
'great' scores 0.62. Name two VADER rules that would raise the score of 'GREAT!!!'.
Variant 2
Capitalisation (GREAT > great) and punctuation (great!!! > great) both intensify it.
Why use VADER instead of a general-purpose sentiment model on tweets?
Why
VADER is a lexicon-and-rule model tuned for social media: it handles capitals, exclamation marks, degree words, negation and emojis, which dominate short noisy posts. It is cheap enough to run as a Spark UDF on every tweet.
Topic: Sentiment (VADER), trend detection and ethics

The same firm loads its 5 M-row trips table from MySQL into HDFS nightly and also wants a fraud check on payments within 1 second. Name the tool for each, choose Lambda or Kappa for the whole system, and give one weakness of your choice.
Trips table: Sqoop (incremental import by last-value, parallel map tasks, retry on failure). Payments: Kafka topic + Spark Streaming (milliseconds, RF for fault tolerance, replay from offset). Architecture: Lambda, because a real nightly batch path exists (batch = Sqoop + HDFS + Hive; speed = Kafka + Spark Streaming; serving merges). Risk: replaying TB+ of records may take days, and all batch jobs must be rewritten. Not suitable if: health regulators require a separate batch reconciliation, or batch SQL is preferred. A prediction, not the real paper

Predicted Paper A (most likely chapters as main questions: W6, W8, W5, W7; W9 and W10 as ORs)

Built from how much the slides stress each chapter; the reasoning is shown on every question. The real paper can pick any chapter, so the plan and the pool still cover all six weeks.

Question 1Week 6, 10 marks
Why predicted: Spark has the most pooled topics and teacher-drawn figures of any chapter (RDD lineage, narrow/wide, lazy evaluation all in both parts). Uses the slide examples: RDD-paper benchmark (127 s vs 0.96 s) and the bKash fraud pipeline (P1 s24).
(a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
bKash's fraud team trains a logistic-regression model for 10 iterations over the same transaction data. On MapReduce each iteration takes 127 s; on Spark with the data cached in memory it takes 0.96 s (the RDD paper's benchmark).
  1. i)
    Why is MapReduce slow for this kind of algorithm? (1)
  2. ii)
    What does Spark do differently? (1)
  3. iii)
    Calculate the per-iteration speedup and the total time of each system for 10 iterations. (1)
  4. iv)
    When should the team call cache(), and when is caching a mistake? (1)
  1. i)
    MapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS and reads it back at the next step, so each of the 10 iterations pays a full disk read and write of the data.
  2. ii)
    Spark reads the data from HDFS once, caches it as an RDD in executor memory, and runs iterations 2 onward from RAM. Intermediate results stay in memory.
  3. iii)
    Speedup = 127 / 0.96 = 132x. Totals: MapReduce 10 x 127 = 1,270 s; Spark 10 x 0.96 = 9.6 s.
  4. iv)
    Cache an RDD that is reused by more than one action (iterative ML, interactive queries). Caching a single-use RDD wastes RAM and pushes other cached data out (LRU eviction).
(b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
The fraud pipeline on the slide is: txns = textFile -> map(parse) -> filter(amount > 50000) -> map((sender, 1)) -> reduceByKey(+) -> filter(count > 3) -> count(). It runs on 8 partitions.
  1. i)
    Which of these calls are transformations and which is the action? When does Spark actually start work? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Is reduceByKey a narrow or wide dependency? How many stages does the job have, and where is the boundary? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    reduceByKey uses the default hash partitioner. A sender key has hashCode 1,234,567. Which partition gets it? (1)
  4. iv)
    The executor holding one partition of the parsed RDD crashes. How does Spark rebuild it without replicas, and why would losing a partition after reduceByKey cost more? (2)
  1. i)
    Transformations: map, filter, map, reduceByKey, filter (textFile is lazy too). Action: count(). Nothing runs until count() is called; until then Spark only records the DAG (lazy evaluation).
  2. ii)
    Wide: an output partition needs records for its keys from every input partition, so data is shuffled. 2 stages: stage 1 = textFile, map, filter, map (pipelined); the boundary is the shuffle at reduceByKey; stage 2 = reduce, filter, count.
  3. iii)
    Partition = key.hashCode() % numPartitions = 1,234,567 % 8. 8 x 154,320 = 1,234,560, remainder 7, so partition 7.
  4. iv)
    Spark follows the lineage: it re-reads that partition's HDFS block and re-applies map(parse) for that one partition only (narrow dependency, one parent). After reduceByKey each output partition depends on all 8 parent partitions, so if the shuffle output is lost, Spark must recompute the parents of all 8 partitions. Long lineages should be checkpointed to HDFS.
Question 2Week 8, 10 marks
Why predicted: Kafka and Lambda/Kappa are the two highest-scoring W8 topics (both in P1 and P2, 5 pool items for Lambda/Kappa alone). Slide numbers: 50 systems -> 2,450 jobs; bKash wallet topics with 3 consumers; Lambda serving-layer merge rule.
(a)5 marks (tap for the answers)
A bank connects 50 internal systems with nightly point-to-point ETL jobs. It moves to Kafka: every wallet transaction goes to topics wallet-credit and wallet-debit, read by fraud detection, the balance updater and an audit writer.
  1. i)
    Give two problems of point-to-point ETL. (1)
  2. ii)
    How many point-to-point jobs can 50 systems need, and how many connections with a central bus? (1)
  3. iii)
    A traditional queue and a Kafka partition both receive the same message. What happens to it after it is read, and why does that matter for a consumer that joins late? (1.5)
  4. iv)
    How do fraud detection, the balance updater and the audit writer each receive every event? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Any two: brittle (a schema change breaks the jobs), no replay (an offline consumer loses data), no real time (nightly, latency of 24 h or more), tight coupling between source and consumer.
  2. ii)
    N(N-1) = 50 x 49 = 2,450 jobs. With a bus each system connects once: 50 connections.
  3. iii)
    A queue deletes a message once it is consumed, so a late consumer misses it. Kafka appends it to an immutable log and keeps it for the retention period (e.g. 7 days); a late consumer starts at offset 0 and replays the history.
  4. iv)
    Each service is its own consumer group. Every group reads all partitions of the topic and tracks its own offset, so the three read the same log independently; inside one group each partition goes to exactly one consumer.
(b)5 marks (tap for the answers)
An e-commerce firm wants accurate nightly revenue reports and a live sales dashboard that is less than a minute old. The team builds a Lambda architecture: nightly Spark jobs on HDFS plus a Flink job reading Kafka.
  1. i)
    Name the three Lambda layers and say what each produces. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    The last batch view counted 1,200,000 orders up to 02:00; the speed layer has counted 85,000 orders since then. What does the serving layer return? (1)
  3. iii)
    What is Lambda's main engineering weakness? (1)
  4. iv)
    The CTO proposes Kappa. How would Kappa reprocess history after a bug fix? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Batch layer: keeps the immutable master dataset on HDFS and recomputes accurate batch views (hours old). Speed layer: stream processor over recent data, low-latency approximate real-time views. Serving layer: merges batch and real-time views to answer queries.
  2. ii)
    Result = batch view UNION real-time view = 1,200,000 + 85,000 = 1,285,000 orders.
  3. iii)
    Dual code paths: the same business logic is written twice (batch and stream) and must be kept in sync; teams report 30-40% of effort goes into that, plus two clusters and a merge step.
  4. iv)
    Kappa keeps one stream code path over a durable log (Kafka with long retention, or Iceberg on S3). Deploy the fixed job version, start it at offset 0, let it replay all history and catch up to live events, then swap it into production and retire the old job.
OR
(a (OR)) Week 95 marks (tap for the answers)
DGHS publishes a monthly dengue bar chart for 8 divisions with 3-D bars, a gradient fill, heavy gridlines and a legend for its single series. Of 800 units of ink, 200 draw the bars.
  1. i)
    Define Tufte's data-ink ratio. (1)
  2. ii)
    Name three chartjunk elements in this chart. (1)
  3. iii)
    Find the ratio now, and after 400 units of junk are erased. (1.5)
  4. iv)
    The director wants to compare the 8 divisions' 24-month trends. What does Tufte recommend, and what must the panels share? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Data-ink ratio = ink used to display data / total ink in the graphic. The goal is to maximise it: every non-data mark must justify itself.
  2. ii)
    3-D effect, gradient fill, heavy gridlines (also the redundant one-series legend).
  3. iii)
    Now: 200 / 800 = 0.25. After erasing 400 units: total ink 400, data ink 200, ratio 200 / 400 = 0.5.
  4. iv)
    Small multiples: the same line chart repeated once per division in a grid. All panels must use the same axis scale, so magnitudes can be compared across divisions.
(b (OR)) Week 95 marks (tap for the answers)
The same dashboard must show (1) confirmed cases by district over 24 months, (2) the hospitalisation rate updated every 5 minutes. The fact table in Hive has 100 billion rows and filters take minutes.
  1. i)
    Which chart suits requirement (1), and which Shneiderman data type is it? (1)
  2. ii)
    How should the dashboard follow Shneiderman's mantra? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    The team pre-aggregates the 100-billion-row table into a 2-million-row data cube. How many times fewer rows does a filter read? (1)
  4. iv)
    Give the cube's trade-off, and name the tool for requirement (2). (1.5)
  1. i)
    Temporal data, so a line chart (or district small multiples of line charts). Avoid a pie chart for time series.
  2. ii)
    Overview first: national total chart on top. Zoom and filter: district dropdown and date-range slider (dynamic queries). Details on demand: hover or click shows the exact date and count.
  3. iii)
    100,000,000,000 / 2,000,000 = 50,000x fewer rows.
  4. iv)
    Trade-off: staleness. The cube is rebuilt by a nightly job, so it can be up to 24 h old (and only answers the pre-chosen dimensions). For the 5-minute rate use Grafana, which polls a time-series DB (InfluxDB/Prometheus) on a short refresh.
Question 3Week 5, 10 marks
Why predicted: YARN is in both parts with three drawn figures and leads the pool; format/compression carries the chapter's main worked numbers. Uses the a2i queue example, the LinkedIn capacity exercise, and pool A1 (telecom CDR) almost verbatim.
(a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
The a2i programme shares one 200-node YARN cluster (each node 64 GB RAM, 16 vCPU) between queue A 60% (nightly MapReduce on health records), queue B 30% (Spark streaming), queue C 10% (ad-hoc Hive).
  1. i)
    Which scheduler gives each queue a guaranteed share, and what happens to a queue's idle capacity? (1)
  2. ii)
    Why would FIFO be a poor choice here? (1)
  3. iii)
    Queue B runs Spark executors of {8 GB, 4 vCPU}. How many can run at once, and which resource is the bottleneck? (1)
  4. iv)
    What is DRF and why does this cluster need it? (1)
  1. i)
    Capacity Scheduler: each queue is guaranteed its percentage, and unused capacity is lent elastically to other queues (reclaimed when needed, by pre-emption).
  2. ii)
    FIFO runs jobs in submission order, so one long nightly batch job starves the streaming and ad-hoc work. It does not suit a multi-tenant cluster.
  3. iii)
    Queue B = 0.30 x 200 = 60 nodes: RAM 3,840 GB / 8 = 480; vCPU 960 / 4 = 240. Max = min = 240 executors; CPU is the bottleneck.
  4. iv)
    Dominant Resource Fairness (Ghodsi 2011) defines fairness across several resources (CPU and RAM), not memory alone. Here some jobs are CPU-heavy and some RAM-heavy, so sharing by one resource would be unfair.
(b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
A Dhaka telecom stores 10 TB of daily call-detail records on HDFS as gzip-compressed CSV. A Hive query that selects 4 of the 80 columns takes 6 hours.
  1. i)
    Give two specific reasons this is slow. (2)
  2. ii)
    Propose a new format, codec and partitioning scheme. (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Estimate the I/O reduction from going columnar. (1)
  4. iv)
    How can Parquet skip whole groups of rows for WHERE duration > 600? (1.5)
  1. i)
    1) Gzip is not splittable: each file is read by exactly one Mapper, so there is no parallelism within a file. 2) CSV is a row store: the query reads all 80 columns from disk to use 4.
  2. ii)
    Parquet + Snappy (or ORC + Zlib if the workload is Hive only), partitioned by date, e.g. dt=YYYY-MM-DD/ (optionally region=). Columnar, splittable at row-group boundaries, and date filters prune whole directories.
  3. iii)
    Read = 10 TB x 4/80 = 0.5 TB = 500 GB. Reduction = 1 - 4/80 = 95%, about 20x less data. (Ignores compression differences.)
  4. iv)
    Predicate pushdown: the reader first reads only the file footer, which holds min/max statistics per column chunk per row group. Any row group whose max duration is 600 or less is skipped with no I/O; in the rest only the needed column chunks are read.
Question 4Week 7, 10 marks
Why predicted: Partitioning and Hive architecture both score 9 (partitioning is 'the most used feature' on P2 s10). Uses the slide's sales table (year/month, 36 months) and the 32-bucket DDL on P1 s24.
(a)5 marks (tap for the answers)
An online retailer's Hive table sales holds 36 months of data, PARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT). The finance report runs SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sales WHERE year=2024 AND month=1.
  1. i)
    What is partitioning, and how does it speed up this query? (1)
  2. ii)
    What fraction of the table does the report read? (1)
  3. iii)
    A developer suggests partitioning by user_id instead. What goes wrong? (1.5)
  4. iv)
    Where does Hive learn which partitions exist and their HDFS paths? What else does that component store? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Partitioning stores each value of the partition columns in its own HDFS sub-directory (year=2024/month=01/). When the WHERE clause filters on those columns, Hive reads only the matching directories and skips the rest (partition pruning).
  2. ii)
    1 partition of 36 = 1/36 = about 2.78%; the other 35 are skipped.
  3. iii)
    user_id has very high cardinality: 100 M users would create 100 M HDFS directories, overloading the NameNode with metadata (partition explosion). Partition on low-cardinality columns used in WHERE, such as date or country.
  4. iv)
    The Metastore, a relational DB (MySQL/PostgreSQL). It also stores table schemas and column types, SerDe/format information, table statistics for the optimiser, and privileges. If it is lost, no table can be queried even though the data on HDFS is intact.
(b)5 marks (tap for the answers)
Analysts join sales with a 10 M-row users table on user_id. Both tables are declared CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS STORED AS ORC. One analyst also loaded a CSV where the amount column contains the text 'abc'.
  1. i)
    What is bucketing, and how is it different from partitioning? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Which bucket file holds user_id 1,000,007? (1)
  3. iii)
    Why can Hive join these tables without a full shuffle? State the condition. (1.5)
  4. iv)
    What does a query return for the 'abc' amount, and what would MySQL have done? (1)
  1. i)
    Bucketing splits each partition into a fixed number N of files by hash(column) % N. Partitioning creates directories by column value and skips data; bucketing does not skip directories, it co-locates rows with the same key to make joins and sampling cheaper.
  2. ii)
    1,000,007 % 32: 32 x 31,250 = 1,000,000, remainder 7, so bucket 7 (in both tables).
  3. iii)
    Bucket map join: bucket i of sales can only match bucket i of users, so Hive joins bucket 0 with 0, 1 with 1, and so on, with no sort-merge shuffle. Condition: both tables bucketed on the join key with the same number of buckets (general knowledge: Hive also accepts one count being a multiple of the other).
  4. iv)
    Hive is schema-on-read: the file is stored as-is and the bad value comes back as NULL at query time. MySQL is schema-on-write: the INSERT is rejected immediately.
OR
(a (OR)) Week 105 marks (tap for the answers)
A Bangladeshi supermarket chain needs 90-day demand forecasts for 5,000 store-product SKUs. Sales jump in Eid weeks and follow weekly and yearly cycles.
  1. i)
    Why can't time series be treated like ordinary i.i.d. rows? (1)
  2. ii)
    Why choose Prophet over ARIMA here? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    For one SKU in an Eid week the fitted components are g = 500, s = +40, h = +150, e = 0. What is the forecast? (1)
  4. iv)
    How does Spark fit all 5,000 models in parallel? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Order matters (shuffling destroys the signal) and values are autocorrelated (today depends on yesterday), with trend and seasonality. Regression that assumes independent rows is invalid.
  2. ii)
    ARIMA needs a stationary series, struggles with multiple seasonalities, and needs expert choice of (p, d, q) per series, which cannot be done by hand for 5,000 series. Prophet handles trend changepoints, several seasonalities and a holiday list (Eid) with interpretable parameters.
  3. iii)
    y = g + s + h + e = 500 + 40 + 150 + 0 = 690 units.
  4. iv)
    Load all series into one DataFrame, groupBy(sku_id), and call applyInPandas with a function that fits Prophet and forecasts. Each SKU's group goes to one task as a Pandas DataFrame, so the independent fits run in parallel across executors; results are written as Parquet. The slide reports 8 h -> about 12 min on 20 executors.
(b (OR)) Week 105 marks (tap for the answers)
The health ministry builds a flu early-warning system from tweets, pharmacy paracetamol sales and ER triage notes. Overnight the phrase 'fever' rises from 40 to 12,000 posts an hour.
  1. i)
    Name two syndromic signals and how far ahead of confirmation each peaks. (1)
  2. ii)
    Why did Google Flu Trends fail, and what lesson does that give this system? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Compute the spike ratio. Is the phrase trending? (1)
  4. iv)
    Give two privacy safeguards for linking pharmacy and ER records. (1.5)
  1. i)
    Social media posts: 7-10 days before ER visits. Pharmacy OTC antipyretic sales: 3-5 days before clinical confirmation. (ER chief complaints via NLP and search volume are also on the slide.)
  2. ii)
    GFT over-predicted flu by about 2x in 2012-13. Lazer et al. gave three causes: big data hubris (r² = 0.97 on the training years did not generalise), algorithm confounding (Google's autocomplete changes shifted the search features), and media amplification (flu news drove searches even when incidence was low). Searches are a proxy for health anxiety, not incidence. Lesson: syndromic data gives early signals that supplement, not replace, clinical surveillance.
  3. iii)
    Spike ratio = current / baseline = 12,000 / 40 = 300x. Yes: trending is judged against the phrase's own baseline, not absolute volume.
  4. iv)
    Any two: de-identification (safe harbour: remove the 18 HIPAA identifiers such as name, NID, phone); differential privacy (calibrated noise on aggregate counts); federated learning (train at each hospital without moving raw records); explicit consent for NID-linked data under PDPA.
A prediction, not the real paper

Predicted Paper B (hedge: W10 promoted to a main question; W7 and W9 as ORs)

Built from how much the slides stress each chapter; the reasoning is shown on every question. The real paper can pick any chapter, so the plan and the pool still cover all six weeks.

Question 1Week 5, 10 marks
Why predicted: Covers the W5 material Paper A skips: the Hadoop 1 limits, LinkedIn's case numbers (45% -> 78%) and the bKash format strategy (Avro -> Parquet+Snappy -> ORC+Zstd, 60% smaller).
(a)5 marks (tap for the answers)
Before YARN, LinkedIn ran three separate clusters: MapReduce for Hive ETL, an experimental Spark cluster and Samza stream nodes. In 2013 it merged them into one 5,000-node YARN cluster with the Capacity Scheduler.
  1. i)
    Why couldn't the Hadoop 1.x cluster simply run Spark and Samza too? (1)
  2. ii)
    Give the role of each YARN component in one line. (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Average utilisation rose from 45% to 78%. How much more workload does the same hardware now serve? (1)
  4. iv)
    LinkedIn turned on pre-emption. What does it do, and what went wrong at first? (1.5)
  1. i)
    The JobTracker bundled resource management with MapReduce-specific scheduling, so only MapReduce jobs could get cluster resources; it was also a single bottleneck with a ceiling of about 4,000 nodes.
  2. ii)
    ResourceManager: one per cluster, schedules containers globally (Scheduler + ApplicationsManager). NodeManager: one per node, launches and monitors containers and heartbeats to the RM. ApplicationMaster: one per application, requests containers from the RM and tells NMs which tasks to run.
  3. iii)
    78 / 45 = 1.733, so about 73% more workload on the same capacity.
  4. iv)
    Pre-emption lets a queue borrow idle capacity from other queues and takes it back when the owner needs it. Aggressive pre-emption killed long-running Spark jobs, so LinkedIn added a 30-second grace period and checkpoint-on-preempt hooks.
(b)5 marks (tap for the answers)
bKash's data lake ingests Kafka events as Avro, converts them nightly to Parquet+Snappy partitioned by dt= and region=, and moves data older than 2 years to ORC+Zstd. The old system kept everything as gzip CSV.
  1. i)
    Why Avro at the ingest layer? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What do Parquet+Snappy and the dt=/region= layout give the analytics layer? (1)
  3. iii)
    50 TB of cold CSV moves to ORC+Zstd, which the slide says is 60% smaller. How much storage remains? (1)
  4. iv)
    Why was the old gzip CSV a problem for MapReduce/Hive jobs? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Avro is a self-describing row format with schema evolution: the reader-schema / writer-schema protocol gives backward and forward compatibility, so when the API adds a field old readers do not break (missing fields take defaults, extra fields are ignored). Row format also suits appending events.
  2. ii)
    Columnar reads of only the needed columns, predicate pushdown from row-group statistics, splittable files (Snappy inside row groups), and partition pruning on date and region.
  3. iii)
    50 TB x (1 - 0.60) = 20 TB.
  4. iv)
    Gzip is not splittable: MapReduce cannot start reading in the middle of a gzip stream, so each file, however large, goes to exactly one Mapper (a 10 GB file = 1 Mapper). Use Parquet+Snappy or bzip2 instead.
Question 2Week 6, 10 marks
Why predicted: Covers the remaining slide examples: filter(x>1000).first() (pool D3), the 10 iterations over 100 GB 'about 3 hours' number (P2 s4), and GraySort (P2 s14-15, 32x per node in Key Takeaways).
(a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
An analyst runs rdd.filter(lambda x: x > 1000).first() on a 1 TB dataset and is surprised it returns in seconds. A colleague says the same 10-iteration job over 100 GB on MapReduce spent about 3 hours on disk I/O.
  1. i)
    What is lazy evaluation? (1)
  2. ii)
    Why does first() return so quickly here? (1)
  3. iii)
    Check the colleague's figure: 10 iterations over 100 GB at 100 MB/s. (1)
  4. iv)
    Name two transformations and two actions. (1)
  1. i)
    Transformations such as filter and map only record a step in the DAG and return a new RDD; nothing executes until an action (count, collect, first, saveAsTextFile) is called.
  2. ii)
    When first() triggers the DAG, Spark pipelines the filter and stops as soon as it finds the first matching element; it never filters the whole 1 TB. Without lazy evaluation the full filter would run first.
  3. iii)
    Reads only: 10 x 100 GB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 10,000 s = about 2.8 h, the slide's 'about 3 hours'. Counting the writes too doubles it to 20,000 s = about 5.6 h.
  4. iv)
    Transformations: map, filter (also flatMap, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, distinct). Actions: count, collect (also first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach).
(b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
In November 2013 Databricks sorted 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 EC2 nodes. The previous Hadoop record was 72 minutes on 2,100 nodes. The sort is a single sortByKey.
  1. i)
    Why is the shuffle the bottleneck of a distributed sort, and what did Spark change in it? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Spark was 3.1x faster on 10.2x fewer nodes. What is its efficiency per node relative to Hadoop? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Define narrow and wide dependencies with one example each, and say how each affects stages. (1.5)
  4. iv)
    Why should a word count use reduceByKey rather than groupByKey? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Every record crosses the network between map and reduce sides, and MapReduce's shuffle spills, merges and re-reads intermediate data on disk many times (about 200 TB of extra I/O at 100 TB). Spark used a sort-based shuffle that writes sorted runs once and then merges, spread over 8 SSDs per node, with off-heap sort buffers that avoid GC pauses.
  2. ii)
    Per-node efficiency = 3.1 x 10.2 = about 31.6, about 32x (72/23 = 3.13 and 2,100/206 = 10.19 give 31.9).
  3. iii)
    Narrow: each output partition depends on at most one input partition (map, filter, union); no shuffle, pipelined in one stage. Wide: an output partition depends on many input partitions (groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, sortByKey); needs a shuffle and starts a new stage.
  4. iv)
    reduceByKey combines values locally on each partition before the shuffle (like a MapReduce Combiner), so only one partial sum per key per partition crosses the network. groupByKey ships every (word, 1) pair, so it moves far more data.
OR
(a (OR)) Week 74 marks (tap for the answers)
By 2008 Facebook had hundreds of analysts who knew SQL but not Java. Today a ministry wants district-wise counts from a 30-million-row health table: SELECT district, COUNT(*) FROM visits GROUP BY district (64 districts).
  1. i)
    What problem did Hive solve? (1)
  2. ii)
    What do HiveServer2 and the Driver do? (1)
  3. iii)
    With map-side aggregation each mapper emits partial counts per district instead of one row per record. By what factor does the shuffle shrink (treat it as one mapper)? (1)
  4. iv)
    Why do production teams run the Metastore as a highly available service? (1)
  1. i)
    Every query used to be a Java MapReduce program (100+ lines for a GROUP BY, days to insight). Hive lets analysts write declarative SQL-like HiveQL, which Hive compiles into MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs.
  2. ii)
    HiveServer2 is the JDBC/ODBC server that authenticates users and accepts queries from Beeline and BI tools. The Driver runs the pipeline: parser -> semantic analyser -> logical planner -> optimiser -> physical plan, and submits the jobs.
  3. iii)
    30,000,000 rows / 64 partial counts = 468,750x less shuffle data.
  4. iv)
    Without it Hive cannot find where any table lives or how to parse it, so Metastore corruption means no table can be queried even though the HDFS data is intact.
(b (OR)) Week 76 marks (tap for the answers)
Table play_events is partitioned by dt (30 days kept) and country (50 countries). A dashboard asks for plays on dt='2024-10-01' in BD and IN. It takes 6 minutes on Hive+MapReduce; Presto does it in seconds.
  1. i)
    List the compiler steps Hive goes through for this query. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What fraction of partitions does the query read? (1)
  3. iii)
    Give the design decisions that make Presto faster for this dashboard. (2)
  4. iv)
    Give one advantage and one risk of Hive's schema-on-read. (1.5)
  1. i)
    Parse HiveQL into an AST -> semantic analysis (resolve columns and types against the Metastore, note dt and country are partition columns) -> logical plan (filter, aggregate) -> physical plan of MR/Tez jobs with partition pruning -> submit to YARN.
  2. ii)
    Total = 30 x 50 = 1,500 partitions; it reads 2, so 2 / 1,500 = about 0.13%; 1,498 are skipped.
  3. iii)
    No intermediate disk writes: data flows as an in-memory pipeline (Hive+MR writes to HDFS between stages). Vectorised execution over batches of 1,024 rows. Cost-based optimiser using table statistics for join order and strategy. Connector architecture: one SQL engine over HDFS/Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3.
  4. iv)
    Advantage: raw files load fast with no ETL at ingest, and several tables (schemas) can be defined over the same files as needs change. Risk: data-quality problems stay silent until query time; a corrupt value comes back as NULL instead of an error, so pipelines need separate validation.
Question 3Week 10, 10 marks
Why predicted: W10 is CLO4 (problem solving), is the last chapter taught, and has two papers plus a case study. Promoted to a main question here as the hedge against Paper A's ranking. Uses VADER thresholds, Louvain steps, Prophet terms and the STL k x IQR rule.
(a)4 marks (tap for the answers)
A research group tracks Bangla and English posts on X during an election week. They score posts with VADER and look for groups of accounts that retweet each other heavily.
  1. i)
    Why use VADER rather than a generic sentiment model? Give two features it handles. (1)
  2. ii)
    Three posts score compound 0.31, -0.02 and -0.47. Classify each. (1)
  3. iii)
    Give the steps of the Louvain algorithm. (1)
  4. iv)
    Give one ethical risk of this analysis. (1)
  1. i)
    VADER is a lexicon-and-rule analyser tuned for social media. Any two: capitalisation (GREAT > great), punctuation (great!!!), degree modifiers (very good), negation (not good), emojis.
  2. ii)
    Positive if > 0.05, negative if < -0.05, else neutral: 0.31 positive, -0.02 neutral, -0.47 negative.
  3. iii)
    Start with each node as its own community; greedily move each node into the neighbouring community that most increases modularity; aggregate communities into super-nodes and repeat; stop when modularity no longer increases. About O(n log n).
  4. iv)
    Sentiment scoring of political speech can be used to suppress dissent (flag negative posts about the government) or to micro-target vulnerable users; needs transparency and purpose limitation.
(b)6 marks (tap for the answers)
A hospital group forecasts weekly admissions with Prophet and also flags unusual weeks. Its model has strong yearly and weekly seasonality but missed the sudden onset of a COVID-19 wave. The residuals after STL decomposition have IQR = 4.
  1. i)
    Write Prophet's model and name each term. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What do p, d and q mean in ARIMA, and why is ARIMA a weak fit here? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Flag residuals beyond k x IQR with k = 3. Weeks have residuals 15 and -9. Which is an anomaly? (1)
  4. iv)
    Which Prophet component should catch the COVID wave, which hyperparameter controls it, and how does Isolation Forest find anomalies? (2)
  1. i)
    y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t): g = trend (piecewise linear or logistic, with changepoints), s = seasonality (Fourier series, yearly/weekly), h = holidays and events (e.g. Eid), e = residual noise.
  2. ii)
    AR(p): depends on the past p values; I(d): difference d times to make the series stationary; MA(q): depends on the past q forecast errors. ARIMA assumes stationarity, handles multiple seasonalities poorly and needs manual (p, d, q) choice per series.
  3. iii)
    Threshold = 3 x 4 = 12. |15| > 12, so that week is an anomaly; |-9| = 9 < 12, so it is not.
  4. iv)
    The trend g(t) through its changepoints. changepoint_prior_scale sets the sparse prior on the slope changes: raising it (e.g. 0.05 -> 0.5) makes the trend more flexible. Isolation Forest builds random trees that partition the data; anomalies need fewer splits to isolate, so they have shorter average path lengths.
Question 4Week 8, 10 marks
Why predicted: Pool A1 (bank pipeline) is the W8 design question; the Kafka paper's benchmark table gives a ready calculation (50.5 MB/s at 100 B = 505,000 msg/s).
(a)5 marks (tap for the answers)
A commercial bank must (1) copy 10 million customer records from Oracle to Hadoop every night, (2) decide on card-swipe fraud within 200 ms, and (3) keep a risk dashboard no more than 5 minutes old.
  1. i)
    Which tool handles (1), and how does it work inside? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Which tools handle (2)? (1)
  3. iii)
    The nightly import runs with 4 map tasks splitting on customer_id. How many rows does each read if keys are evenly spread? (1)
  4. iv)
    Lambda or Kappa for the whole system? Justify. (1.5)
  1. i)
    Apache Sqoop. sqoop import launches a MapReduce job whose map tasks each read a primary-key range of the table in parallel over JDBC and write to HDFS (Parquet/Avro/CSV) or Hive. Incremental import with check-column and last-value copies only new rows.
  2. ii)
    Kafka carries the swipe events; Spark Streaming (or Flink) consumes them and scores each event within the 200 ms budget. Sqoop is batch and Flume is for logs, so neither fits.
  3. iii)
    10,000,000 / 4 = 2,500,000 rows per map task.
  4. iv)
    Lambda fits: there is a genuine nightly batch (Sqoop + Hive/Spark for accurate risk reports, regulatory reconciliation) beside a low-latency stream for fraud and the dashboard. Kappa would suit if a single stream engine could also replay the full history fast enough, but a regulator-mandated batch reconciliation is one of the slide's 'Kappa not suitable' cases.
(b)5 marks (tap for the answers)
In 2010 LinkedIn found ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ could not carry billions of activity events a day. In the Kafka paper's benchmark (one broker, 100-byte messages) the producer throughputs were ActiveMQ 4.3 MB/s, RabbitMQ 14.7 MB/s, Kafka 50.5 MB/s.
  1. i)
    Explain the two storage decisions behind Kafka's speed. (2)
  2. ii)
    How many messages per second is Kafka's 50.5 MB/s, and how many times ActiveMQ's throughput? (1)
  3. iii)
    What does 'consumer pull' mean, and why does it help the broker? (1)
  4. iv)
    The bank later dumps every raw file into S3 with no catalogue or owners. What does the lake become, and give one prevention step. (1)
  1. i)
    Sequential writes: Kafka only appends to segment files, so disks run at sequential speed (about 600 MB/s vs about 100 MB/s random), helped by the OS page cache. Zero-copy: sendfile() sends data from the kernel page cache straight to the NIC, cutting 4 copies to 2 and skipping user space, so CPU stays near zero.
  2. ii)
    50.5 MB/s / 100 B = 50,500,000 / 100 = 505,000 messages/s. 50.5 / 4.3 = about 11.7x ActiveMQ.
  3. iii)
    Consumers fetch data and track their own offsets (stored in __consumer_offsets); the broker keeps no per-consumer queues or per-message ACKs, so one log serves any number of consumers cheaply.
  4. iv)
    A data swamp: nobody can find datasets or tell current from stale copies, and PII is mixed in. Prevention: enforce a data catalogue at ingest (Hive Metastore/Glue/Atlas), with owners, access control, quality checks or a table format like Delta/Iceberg.
OR
(a (OR)) Week 95 marks (tap for the answers)
An analyst reports that four regional sales datasets have the same mean, variance and correlation (r = 0.816), so 'they behave the same'. Another report shows revenue up 5%, but the bar is drawn 40% taller because the y-axis does not start at 0.
  1. i)
    What does Anscombe's quartet say about the analyst's conclusion? (1)
  2. ii)
    A manager wants the share of revenue from 9 product lines. Is a pie chart right? What should be used? (1)
  3. iii)
    Compute the lie factor of the revenue chart and say what it means. (1)
  4. iv)
    Define small multiples and sparklines, with one use each. (2)
  1. i)
    Four datasets with identical summary statistics look completely different when plotted (linear, curved, one outlier, a vertical cluster). Plot the data before trusting the statistics.
  2. ii)
    No. Pies only suit 4 or fewer categories and a 'fraction of the whole' question; people judge angles poorly. Use a horizontal bar chart.
  3. iii)
    Lie factor = effect shown / effect in data = 40% / 5% = 8. Above 1, so the chart overstates the change eightfold.
  4. iv)
    Small multiples: the same chart structure repeated for each subset (district, year) on the same scale, for side-by-side comparison, e.g. a 50-state grid of case curves. Sparklines: word-sized line charts embedded in text or table cells, adding trend context, e.g. a tiny 7-day trend beside each district's case count.
(b (OR)) Week 95 marks (tap for the answers)
bKash fraud operations want a live chart of transaction volume. Events arrive in Kafka at 3,000 transactions per second, are aggregated by Spark Structured Streaming in 1-minute tumbling windows, stored in a time-series DB and shown in Grafana with a 5-second refresh. A second screen plots millions of transactions as a scatter.
  1. i)
    Describe the four-step streaming visualisation architecture. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    How many transactions does each 1-minute window summarise? (1)
  3. iii)
    When would you push updates over WebSocket instead of Grafana's polling? (1)
  4. iv)
    The scatter is a solid blob. Give three fixes in increasing sophistication. (1.5)
  1. i)
    1) Events arrive in a Kafka topic. 2) Spark Structured Streaming or Flink aggregates them over a window. 3) Results are written to a time-series DB (InfluxDB, Prometheus, Elasticsearch). 4) Grafana or Kibana polls the DB every few seconds and redraws.
  2. ii)
    3,000 x 60 = 180,000 transactions per window.
  3. iii)
    When sub-second updates are needed (stock tickers, live election counts): the server pushes each update and a D3.js chart re-renders on every push. Polling every 5 s is enough for ops dashboards.
  4. iv)
    Alpha transparency (e.g. 0.02, denser areas darker, fails at extreme density); hexbin aggregation (count per hexagon, about 10 M points -> about 10,000 cells); KDE / 2-D density contours (shows shape, modes and tails).
For the last ten minutes

Must-know list and formula sheet

The must-know list first, then every formula from weeks 5–10. Each topic's one-line answer sits at the top of the topic; you can run through all 36 at the end.

Must-know list 40 lines. Tick each one you can say from memory.

  • YARN: RM = one per cluster (Scheduler + ApplicationsManager); NM = one per node (containers, heartbeat); AM = one per application (requests containers). Hadoop 2.0 (2013) replaced the JobTracker (MR only, ~4,000 nodes).
  • Container = {vCPU, RAM} slice on one node; NM kills a container that exceeds its memory limit.
  • YARN failures: NM -> missed heartbeat, containers marked failed, AM re-requests; AM -> RM restarts it (max attempts, default 2); RM -> HA with ZooKeeper (active + standby).
  • Schedulers: FIFO (starves), Capacity (guaranteed queue %, borrows idle capacity), Fair (equal shares, short jobs finish fast). DRF = fairness over CPU and RAM.
  • Containers per queue = min(queue RAM / container RAM, queue vCPU / container vCPU); the smaller one is the bottleneck.
  • Columnar: read = D x k/N; 10 TB, 3 of 100 columns -> 300 GB, 97% less, ~33x.
  • Parquet: row groups (~128 MB) -> column chunks -> pages; footer min/max stats -> predicate pushdown skips row groups.
  • Avro = row, schema evolution (reader/writer schema), Kafka ingest. Parquet = columnar, Spark analytics. ORC = columnar, Hive, highest compression.
  • Gzip is NOT splittable (1 Mapper per file). Bzip2 splittable; LZO splittable with index; Snappy fast (splittable inside Parquet row groups).
  • Spark beats MR on iteration: MR = k x (read + write) on HDFS; Spark reads once and caches. 50 GB x 100 iterations: 10 TB vs 50 GB.
  • Spark architecture: Driver (SparkContext/SparkSession, builds DAG) -> Cluster Manager (YARN/K8s/Mesos/Standalone) -> Executors (tasks + cache).
  • RDD = read-only, partitioned collection created from stable storage or other RDDs; immutable, partitioned, lazy, lineage, resilient (recompute, not replicate).
  • Transformations (lazy): map, filter, flatMap, reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, distinct. Actions: count, collect, first, take, reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach.
  • Lazy evaluation lets Spark pipeline narrow steps and stop early: filter(x > 1000).first().
  • Narrow (1 parent partition, same stage): map, filter, union, coalesce. Wide (shuffle, new stage): groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, repartition, distinct, sortByKey.
  • reduceByKey > groupByKey: it combines locally before the shuffle. Hash partitioner = key.hashCode() % numPartitions.
  • DataFrame = named columns + schema, Catalyst optimiser. HBase is NOT part of the Spark ecosystem.
  • Hive: HiveServer2 (JDBC/ODBC) -> Driver (parse -> semantic -> logical -> optimise -> physical) -> engine MR/Tez/Spark; Metastore (MySQL/PostgreSQL) holds schemas, partitions + HDFS paths, SerDe, stats.
  • Schema-on-read (Hive): schema applied at query, bad value -> NULL, fast load. Schema-on-write (RDBMS): rejected at INSERT. HiveQL: limited ACID (ORC transactional only), minutes of latency. Lecturer's plan: Hive vs SQL is an important exam topic.
  • Partitioning = HDFS sub-directory per value, prunes scans; low-cardinality columns only (user_id -> partition explosion). Dynamic insert: partition columns last in SELECT.
  • Bucketing = hash(col) % N files; bucket map join (same key, same N) avoids a shuffle. Fraction read = partitions read / total.
  • Map-side aggregation: 50 M rows, 200 countries -> 250,000x less shuffle.
  • Presto: in-memory pipeline (no intermediate disk), vectorised 1,024-row batches, cost-based optimiser, connectors.
  • Point-to-point ETL = N(N-1) jobs (50 -> 2,450); bus = N connections.
  • Sqoop = bulk RDBMS <-> HDFS via a MapReduce job whose map tasks each read a primary-key range, incremental last-value. Flume = Source -> Channel (memory/file) -> Sink, logs to HDFS.
  • Kafka = distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Topic -> partitions (ordered, same key -> same partition) -> offsets; consumer tracks its own offset; retention (e.g. 7 days) -> replay from offset 0.
  • RF = R survives R - 1 broker failures; one leader + R - 1 followers. In a consumer group, each partition goes to exactly one consumer (extra consumers idle).
  • Kafka speed: sequential appends (~600 vs ~100 MB/s), zero-copy sendfile (4 -> 2 copies), batching, consumer pull. 50.5 MB/s / 100 B = 505,000 msg/s.
  • Lambda (Marz): Batch (HDFS, accurate, hours) + Speed (stream, seconds, approximate) + Serving (merge). Weakness: two code paths (30-40% effort).
  • Kappa (Kreps): one stream code path over a durable log; reprocess = new job from offset 0, catch up, swap. Not for very slow TB-scale replay, batch-SQL preference, or mandated batch reconciliation.
  • Data lake = raw data, any format, schema-on-read; layers: ingestion, storage, processing, catalogue/governance. No governance -> data swamp.
  • Tufte: data-ink ratio = data ink / total ink (maximise); chartjunk (3-D, gradients, heavy grids, ducks); small multiples; sparklines; lie factor = effect shown / effect in data (1 = truthful).
  • Shneiderman: 'Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand'; 7 data types: 1-D, 2-D, 3-D, temporal, multi-dimensional, tree, network.
  • Chart choice: temporal -> line; categories -> bar (pie only if 4 or fewer and part-of-whole); geography -> choropleth; distribution -> histogram/box; correlation -> scatter.
  • Big-data viz challenges: overplotting (alpha -> hexbin -> KDE), latency (data cube / AQP, trade-off staleness), streaming (Kafka -> Spark window -> TSDB -> Grafana poll / WebSocket push).
  • Tools: Grafana = real-time ops; Tableau/Power BI = business BI; D3.js = custom web SVG; Superset = open-source BI on lakes; Kibana = Elasticsearch logs.
  • Time series: order matters, autocorrelation, trend, seasonality, non-stationarity. ARIMA(p, d, q) = AR lags, differencing, MA errors; needs stationarity and manual tuning.
  • Prophet: y = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t); changepoints in g (changepoint_prior_scale); Fourier seasonality; holidays; scale with groupBy + applyInPandas.
  • Social: Louvain maximises modularity (merge, aggregate, repeat); influence maximisation NP-hard, greedy (1 - 1/e); Kwak: 22.1% reciprocity, 4.12 hops, power law -> Twitter is a news medium. VADER: > 0.05 positive, < -0.05 negative.
  • Health: EHR, genomics (~200 GB/genome), wearables, DICOM (unstructured); HIPAA 18 identifiers, GDPR, PDPA; DP and federated learning. GFT over-predicted 2x: syndromic data supplements, never replaces.
Short on time? 10 things you can skip

Low-yield detail by the slide evidence. Skip only if the clock forces it; everything else stays in.

  • Paper citations, author lists, venues, citation counts and timelines (Vavilapalli, Zaharia, Thusoo, Kreps, Tufte, Shneiderman, Kwak, Taylor & Letham): know the idea each paper introduced, not the bibliography.
  • Company scale trivia not used by any pool question: Spotify 1 M tables / 600 B events, Netflix 4,000 topics / 2,000 brokers, Facebook 7,500 queries/day, LinkedIn 30,000 jobs/day, NYT 6 M readers.
  • Python/D3/PySpark live-exercise skeleton code line by line (know what each exercise demonstrates, not the syntax).
  • Spotify Discover Weekly details (Word2Vec, Annoy, CNN audio embeddings).
  • W6 P2 persistence levels beyond MEMORY_ONLY vs MEMORY_AND_DISK; GraySort hardware specs (i2.8xlarge, SSD totals).
  • Hive 2010 paper extras: compact/bitmap indexes, LLAP, Iceberg REST catalog, AWS Glue; Kafka extras: ksqlDB, tiered storage, Schema Registry details.
  • Netflix A/B-testing pipeline step list; Timeline Server REST details; DRF maths.
  • AlphaFold architecture details (Evoformer, GDT score, TPU counts): know only 'protein 3D structure from sequence, trained on PDB, MSA over 250 M sequences'.
  • Prophet trend and Fourier formulas written out symbol by symbol (know g/s/h/e meanings and changepoint_prior_scale).
  • University-curricula slides (Harvard CS171, Stanford CS246, CMU 15-721, MIT 6.830) and quote-of-the-week slides.

The order follows how heavily the slides stress each topic, but every week still gets its own blocks, weeks 9 and 10 included, and the multiple-choice and true-or-false sweep covers all six. A prediction is a guess, so nothing is dropped because of it.
